A patient, sophisticated attacker spent *years* building trust in a project, pressuring an overwhelmed maintainer to hand over access, and then injected a backdoor into critical infrastructure. The vulnerability wasn't in the code. It was in the human system around the code. It was in the fact that a single exhausted maintainer was susceptible to social engineering precisely because they were alone, under-resourced, and desperate for help.

So when we talk about sustainability, we need to talk about all of it: the money, the labor, the governance, the identity, and the trust architecture. Because all of them are failing simultaneously. And they're failing not because open source is broken — they're failing because open source *succeeded* beyond anyone's imagination, and the structures we built for a gift economy cannot bear the weight of global infrastructure.

**[SLIDE 3: Enter the Machine]**

Now let's add AI to this picture, because AI isn't waiting for us to solve the sustainability crisis before it starts reshaping the landscape.

In the last eighteen months, AI-generated code has gone from a novelty to a daily reality for most of us in this room. GitHub's own figures — and we should read them with some skepticism, since GitHub has a commercial interest in making Copilot look indispensable — suggest that Copilot is now generating nearly half of all code in the languages where it's enabled. Even if the real number is lower, the trajectory is undeniable.

What does this mean for open source?

The optimistic view — and there is a genuinely optimistic view that deserves more than a paragraph — is that AI dramatically lowers the barrier to contribution. Someone who understands a problem domain but isn't fluent in Rust can still submit a meaningful pull request to a Rust project. AI can generate boilerplate, write tests, draft documentation, triage issues. Maintainers I've spoken with report that AI-assisted code review has cut their triage time significantly. One told me it was the first time in three years she didn't dread opening her notifications. That's real. For people drowning in maintenance load, AI isn't a threat — it's a life raft.

But there's a shadow side, and I think we need to look at it directly.

First: the contribution quality problem. Maintainers are already reporting a surge in low-quality, AI-generated pull requests from people who are essentially using open source projects as a proving ground for their AI tools. They generate a PR, submit it, and move on — leaving the maintainer to review, test, and usually reject code that was produced without genuine understanding of the project's architecture or goals. One maintainer described it to me as "automated littering." The cost of saying no is still borne by humans. AI has lowered the barrier to contribution, but it has also lowered the barrier to *noise* — and for an overwhelmed maintainer, noise is the enemy.

Second: the provenance problem. This is the one that should keep all of us up at night, because it strikes at the legal and ethical foundations of open source itself. When a human writes code and contributes it to a project, there's a relatively clear chain of authorship and intent. When an AI generates code, trained on a corpus that includes open source code under various licenses, that chain dissolves. If Copilot generates a function that is substantially similar to GPL-licensed code and a developer submits it to an Apache-licensed project, what just happened legally? We don't have clear answers. The courts are only beginning to grapple with this — the Doe v. GitHub class action is still unresolved, and the EU AI Act's provisions on training data transparency are untested. Meanwhile, maintainers face a practical question right now: how do you review a pull request when you can't verify the provenance of the code? The honest answer, today, is that you can't. And that's a crisis of trust layered on top of an existing crisis of trust.

Third: the homogenization risk. AI models are trained on existing code. They are, by definition, pattern-matching engines that reproduce what has been done before. Think about what that means for a field that has been driven by creative outliers. Would React have emerged from an AI trained on the jQuery-era DOM manipulation patterns that dominated at the time? Would Git have emerged from an AI trained on centralized version control systems? Open source has historically been a space for radical, opinionated, sometimes-brilliant experiments that no product manager would have approved. If we increasingly rely on AI to generate contributions, we risk converging on a median — a world where every new project looks like a weighted average of every old project. The code will be competent. It will also be boring. And boring is how ecosystems stagnate.

So let me say clearly what I think: AI is, at this moment, a net positive for open source *productivity* and a net negative for open source *culture*. It makes the mechanical work easier while making the human dynamics harder. That balance can shift — but only if we're intentional about shifting it.

**[SLIDE 4: A Vision for the Next Decade]**

So — sustainability is fractured, AI is reshaping the terrain, and the old social contract is breaking down. Where does this leave us?

I want you to imagine something with me. It's 2034. You're a developer, and you've just found a bug in a critical open source library. You open the project page and you see: a team of four paid maintainers, funded through a combination of public infrastructure investment and an industry consortium. You see a clear governance charter. You see a contribution policy that specifies how AI-generated code should be disclosed and reviewed. You see a provenance attestation on every recent commit. You see a mentorship program that onboarded twelve new contributors last quarter. You submit your bug report, and within a day, a human being responds — not because they're a volunteer sacrificing their weekend, but because this is their job, and it's a job that is respected and compensated like the critical work it is.

That's not a fantasy. Every piece of that vision exists in embryonic form today. The question is whether we grow it or let it die.

Here's how.

**First: professionalize maintenance — and name who's responsible for the failure to do so.**

The Sovereign Tech Fund in Germany is directly funding maintenance work on critical open source projects as a matter of public interest. This is the model. Not grants. Not one-time sponsorships. Ongoing, structural, infrastructure-grade investment. It needs to scale globally — and it needs to be matched by the companies that have built empires on open source labor.

Let me be direct: if your company generates revenue from open source dependencies and contributes nothing back — no funding, no engineering time, no maintainer support — you are free-riding on a public good. That's not an accusation; it's an economic description. And the open source community needs to stop being polite about it. We should be publishing league tables. We should be making the asymmetry visible and uncomfortable. Shame is an underrated incentive mechanism.

At the same time, we need to break the single-maintainer model. Not by asking more volunteers to show up, but by building governance structures and tooling that make shared authority safe and efficient. The `xz` attack succeeded because one person held all the keys. That's not a human failing — it's a design failing.

**Second: make AI open, or lose the commons.**

Here's the argument I want you to carry out of this room: if the future of code generation is AI, then the future of open source depends on that AI itself being open. Full stop. Open-weight models like LLaMA and Mistral, open training datasets, open fine-tuning frameworks — these aren't side projects. They're the new battleground for the commons. If the tools that generate code are proprietary, trained on open source code, and controlled by three companies, then we haven't solved the sustainability problem. We've just added a new extraction layer on top of it. We've built a proprietary tollbooth on a public road.

The open source community should be *building* these tools, not just being subject to them. And we need practical infrastructure now: provenance attestation standards for AI-generated code, clear project-level policies on disclosure and review, and a unified community voice in the legal and policy debates that will define the next decade of copyright and licensing law. Because if we don't define those terms, they will be defined for us by entities whose interests are not aligned with the commons.

**Third: protect the human core.**

This is the pillar that matters most, and it's the one that no amount of funding or tooling can substitute for.

The thing that makes open source genuinely different from proprietary software is not the license. It's the community. It's the fact that a project is a living system of humans who share context, values, and purpose. AI can generate code. It cannot generate trust. It cannot generate the shared understanding that allows a group of strangers across six time zones to collaborate on something complex and beautiful and useful.

In a world where AI generates an increasing share of the code, the *human* contributions become more valuable, not less. Code review, architectural judgment, mentorship, governance, the slow work of building a community where people feel ownership and belonging — these are the things that will distinguish living projects from abandoned repositories full of machine-generated commits.

So what does recommitting to community look like in 2034? It looks like projects that treat onboarding a new contributor as seriously as shipping a new feature. It looks like governance that is transparent, distributed, and resilient to the kind of social engineering that compromised `xz`. It looks like making the experience of contributing so genuinely rewarding — technically, socially, humanly — that people choose it over the frictionless alternative of letting an AI do it for them.

Because here's the truth we need to face: if contributing to open source feels like feeding code into a machine, people will stop doing it. And no amount of AI-generated pull requests will replace what's lost when the humans leave.

**[SLIDE 5: Closing]**

Open source has always been, at its heart, an act of faith. Faith that if you share your work freely, others will build on it. Faith that collaboration beats competition. Faith that the commons can hold.

That faith is being tested now, in new ways and at new scales. The sustainability crisis is real. The AI disruption is real. The erosion of trust is real.

But I've spent twenty years in this community, and I have never seen a moment with more potential to get this right. We have funding models that are maturing. We have governance frameworks that are evolving. We have a generation of developers who grew up on open source and understand its value intuitively. And yes, we have AI — which, if we are intentional and brave, can be a tool that amplifies human contribution rather than replacing it.

The future of open source will not be determined by technology. It will be determined by choices. Choices about what we fund. Choices about what we build. Choices about who we include. Choices about what we refuse to accept.

So here's my ask. Don't just consume open source. Don't just contribute to open source. *Fight for* open source. Fight for the maintainers. Fight for the commons. Fight for the idea that the most important software in the world should belong to everyone.

Because open source was never just a licensing model. It was a promise — that we could build something together that none of us could build alone. That promise is worth keeping.

Thank you.

**[END]**

Let's start with sustainability, and let's go deeper than the usual "we need to pay maintainers" talking point. Yes, we need to pay maintainers. But the sustainability crisis in open source is not simply a funding problem. It's a structural problem. It's an incentive design problem. And increasingly, it's an identity problem.

The traditional open source social contract went something like this: a developer scratches an itch, shares the code, a community forms, companies adopt it, and everyone benefits from the commons. You become a product manager, a tech support agent, a community moderator, a documentation writer, a release engineer, and a therapist for people who open issues in all caps at 2 AM demanding to know why you broke their production system with a patch release. That's not a job description anyone signed up for. And it's not a job description that scales.

And here's what we don't talk about enough: the *identity crisis* underneath all of this. Think about the archetype of the open source creator twenty-five years ago — the lone hacker, building something brilliant and weird in their spare time, sharing it because sharing was the point. Now think about what we actually ask of maintainers today. We ask them to be infrastructure stewards. We ask them to operate critical systems with the rigor and availability expectations of a Fortune 500 company, but with the resources of a hobbyist. That shift — from craftsperson to invisible infrastructure operator — carries a real psychological cost. The joy of creation gets buried under the weight of obligation. And when the joy dies, maintainers leave. Not because they can't do the work, but because the work has become something they never wanted.

A patient, sophisticated attacker spent *years* building trust in a project, pressuring an overwhelmed maintainer to hand over access, and then injected a backdoor into critical infrastructure. The vulnerability wasn't in the code. It was in the human system around the code — in the fact that a single exhausted maintainer was susceptible to social engineering precisely because they were alone, under-resourced, and desperate for help.

Projects routinely outlive their creators' capacity — or desire — to care for them. The bus factor isn't just about sudden disappearance. It's about the slow, quiet erosion of commitment that happens when a person's life simply moves on, and the code doesn't.

So when we talk about sustainability, we need to talk about all of it: the money, the labor, the governance, the identity, and the trust architecture. Because all of them are failing simultaneously.

**[SLIDE 3: The Accelerant]**

Now let's add AI to this picture, because AI isn't waiting for us to solve the sustainability crisis before it starts reshaping the landscape. It's an accelerant — intensifying dynamics that were already in motion.

Someone who understands a problem domain but isn't fluent in Rust can still submit a meaningful pull request to a Rust project. AI can generate boilerplate, write tests, draft documentation, triage issues. It can, in theory, alleviate exactly the maintenance load asymmetry I was just describing. And we're already seeing this. Some maintainers report that AI tools have genuinely reduced their burden. That's real, and it matters.

But there's a shadow side, and I think we need to look at it directly.

First: the contribution quality problem. Maintainers are already reporting a surge in low-quality, AI-generated pull requests from people using open source projects as a proving ground for their AI tools. They generate a PR, submit it, and move on — leaving the maintainer to review, test, and usually reject code produced without genuine understanding of the project's architecture or goals. One maintainer described it to me as "automated littering." The cost of saying no is still borne by humans.

Second: the provenance problem. When a human writes code and contributes it to an open source project, there's a relatively clear chain of authorship and intent. When an AI generates code, trained on a corpus that includes open source code under various licenses, the provenance becomes murky. Who is the author? What license applies? If Copilot generates a function substantially similar to GPL-licensed code and a developer submits it to an Apache-licensed project, what just happened legally? We don't have clear answers yet. The courts don't have clear answers. And the volume of AI-generated code is scaling far faster than our legal and normative frameworks can adapt.

Third — and this is the one that connects our two themes most directly — there's the training data reciprocity problem. Open source code trains AI systems. Those AI systems then generate code used overwhelmingly in proprietary products. The value flows one direction: out of the commons and into closed systems, with no return flow. This isn't hypothetical. It's happening right now, at enormous scale. It is, in a very real sense, a new and more efficient form of the same value extraction that has plagued open source for decades — only now it's automated.

And there's an emergent risk I want to flag: class stratification within open source itself. AI could create a two-tier system where experienced maintainers direct AI tools to do sophisticated work while a growing population of "contributors" submits machine-generated PRs they don't fully understand. That's not democratization. That's the illusion of participation layered on top of a deepening divide.

I'm not saying AI is bad for open source. I'm saying AI is a powerful force being applied to open source without sufficient intentionality about the consequences. And that should concern us.

**[SLIDE 4: The Reconstruction]**

So — sustainability is fractured, AI is accelerating the disruption, and the old social contract is breaking down. What do we actually do?

I want to propose a vision built on three pillars. These aren't silver bullets. They're design principles for the next era of open source — and they only work if they reinforce each other.

**Pillar one: Professionalize maintenance without corporatizing it.**

We need to create legitimate, well-compensated roles for open source maintenance that don't require maintainers to either work for free or get absorbed into a corporate OSPO. The model I find most promising is *infrastructure-grade funding* — treating critical open source projects the way we treat other public infrastructure. The Sovereign Tech Fund in Germany is pioneering this approach, directly funding maintenance work on critical projects as a matter of public interest. This needs to scale globally. Governments, industry consortia, and foundations need to build permanent funding mechanisms — not grants, not sponsorships, but ongoing, structural investment.

But funding without governance reform is just money poured into a broken structure. We need better frameworks for *distributed maintenance* — governance structures that make it safe and efficient to share authority, so that funding can flow to teams rather than burning out individuals. This means better tooling for permissions, review workflows, and decision-making. And it means cultural change in how we think about project ownership.

This pillar also means embracing something we rarely discuss: graceful project lifecycle management. Not every project should live forever. A sustainable ecosystem needs clear norms for archiving, transferring, and sunsetting projects — so that maintainers can step away without guilt, and users can plan accordingly. Sustainability isn't just about keeping things alive. It's about knowing when and how to let go.

This pillar creates the stable foundation that makes the next two possible.

**Pillar two: Build an intentional framework for AI in open source.**

We cannot afford to let the integration of AI into open source happen by default. We need explicit community norms, and we need them soon.

Projects should be empowered to set clear policies on AI-generated contributions — not to ban them, necessarily, but to establish expectations around disclosure, review standards, and quality thresholds. We need to end the "automated littering" by making the social contract around AI contributions explicit.

We need technical infrastructure for code provenance — not hand-waving, but real systems. Cryptographic attestation frameworks like Sigstore, extended to distinguish human-authored and AI-generated contributions, could give projects and users the transparency they need to make informed decisions. This is tractable engineering, not science fiction.

And we need the open source community to have a strong, unified voice in the ongoing legal and policy debates around AI training data, copyright, and licensing — especially on the reciprocity question. If open source code trains AI systems, the community should have a say in the terms. Because if we don't define those terms, they will be defined for us by entities whose interests are not aligned with the commons.

I'd also argue that the open source community should be *building* the AI tools, not just being subject to them. Open-weight models like LLaMA and Mistral, open training datasets, open fine-tuning frameworks — these are the leverage points. If the future of code generation is AI, then the future of open source depends on that AI itself being open. Otherwise, we've just created a new proprietary layer that sits on top of the commons and extracts value from it. Sound familiar?

This pillar protects the commons. And it only works if pillar one has created the professional capacity to enforce and maintain these frameworks.

**Pillar three: Recommit to community as the core asset.**

This is the one that's easiest to say and hardest to do. But I believe it's the most important — because it's what makes the other two pillars worth building.

The thing that makes open source genuinely different from proprietary software is not the license. It's the community. It's the fact that a project is a living system of humans who share context, values, and purpose. AI can generate code. It cannot generate trust. It cannot generate the shared understanding that allows a group of strangers across six time zones to collaborate on something complex and beautiful and useful.

In the next decade, the open source projects that thrive will be the ones that invest deliberately in their human communities. That means mentorship programs. That means inclusive governance. That means codes of conduct that are actually enforced. That means making contributing a genuinely rewarding human experience — not just technically, but socially and emotionally. Because if contributing to open source feels like feeding code into a machine, people will stop doing it. And no amount of AI-generated pull requests will replace what's lost.

Community is also the immune system that protects against the threats we've discussed — the `xz`-style social engineering attacks, the maintenance load asymmetry, the erosion of trust. A project with a strong, distributed, well-supported community is resilient in ways that no technical solution alone can replicate.

**[SLIDE 5: The Promise]**

I want to leave you with this.

Open source has always been, at its heart, an act of faith. Faith that if you share your work freely, others will build on it. Faith that collaboration beats competition. Faith that the commons can hold.

That faith has been tested before. It's being tested now, in new ways and at new scales. The sustainability crisis is real. The AI disruption is real. The erosion of trust is real.

But I've spent twenty years in this community, and I have never seen a moment with more potential to get this right. We have funding models that are maturing. We have governance frameworks that are evolving. We have a generation of developers who grew up on open source and understand its value intuitively. And yes, we have AI — which, if we are intentional and brave, can be a tool that amplifies human contribution rather than replacing it.

The future of open source will not be determined by technology. It will be determined by choices. Choices about what we fund. Choices about what we build. Choices about who we include. Choices about what we refuse to accept.

So here's my ask — and I want to be specific. Don't just consume open source. Don't just contribute to open source. Find one project you depend on, and ask its maintainer what they actually need. Not what you want to give — what *they* need. Then provide it. Maybe it's funding. Maybe it's code review. Maybe it's taking over the documentation. Maybe it's just telling them their work matters. Start there. And then fight for the structures that make that kind of support sustainable and systemic — not charity, but architecture.

Because open source was never just a licensing model. It was a promise — that we could build something together that none of us could build alone. That promise is the bridge. And it's worth holding up — not with our bare hands, but with the kind of structural support it has always deserved.

Thank you.

**[SLIDE 1: Title]**

Here's a question to start: what happens when the internet's most critical infrastructure depends on someone who isn't there anymore?

Two numbers frame the answer. Two billion, four hundred million. That's how many open source packages were downloaded from npm last *week*. Not last year. Last week.

Now: one. That's how many maintainers kept `core-js` running for years — a library that roughly 75% of the top 10,000 websites depend on. One person. Maintaining critical infrastructure while struggling financially, burning out publicly, posting on GitHub Issues asking for help that mostly didn't come.

If you've ever shipped a security advisory at 2 AM, you've met someone like that maintainer. Maybe you've *been* that maintainer — replying with patience while the inbox explodes, while strangers in all caps demand to know why you broke their production system with a patch release.

We have built a civilization-scale dependency on software held up by the digital equivalent of volunteers bracing a bridge with their bare hands. And we've been doing it so long that we've confused the bridge staying up with the bridge being structurally sound.

That's what I want to talk about today. Not just the problem — you've heard the problem — but what comes next. Because we are standing at an inflection point. Sustainability crises, shifting community dynamics, and the sudden eruption of AI-generated code are converging to reshape open source within this decade.

Here's the thesis I want you to carry through the next fourteen minutes: **We can choose the future of open source, or we can let it be chosen for us.** I'd prefer we choose.

**[SLIDE 2: The Sustainability Crisis — Beyond the Memes]**

Let's start with sustainability. And let's go deeper than "we need to pay maintainers."

Yes, we need to pay maintainers. But the sustainability crisis is not simply a funding problem. It's structural. It's an incentive design problem. And increasingly, it's an identity problem.

The traditional open source social contract went something like this: a developer scratches an itch, shares the code, a community forms, companies adopt it, everyone benefits from the commons. Beautiful in theory.

In practice, the value chain became radically asymmetric. Companies capture billions from open source dependencies. Maintainers capture GitHub stars. Maybe a sponsorship that covers their coffee budget.

The numbers are stark. The Linux Foundation's 2024 census estimated that rebuilding widely-used open source from scratch would cost over $8.8 trillion. Meanwhile, Tidelift's maintainer survey found that 60% of maintainers are unpaid volunteers, and nearly half have quit or considered quitting due to burnout. The total funding flowing back to independent maintainers is a rounding error against the value they create.

But funding is only one dimension. The deeper issue is what I call *maintenance load asymmetry*. When you publish a popular library, you don't just write code. You become a product manager, a tech support agent, a community moderator, a documentation writer, a release engineer, and a therapist — all at once, all unpaid. That's not a job description anyone signed up for. And it doesn't scale.

We've also seen the trust layer fracture. The `xz` backdoor earlier this year was a masterclass in exploiting open source social dynamics. A patient, sophisticated attacker spent *years* building trust, pressuring an overwhelmed solo maintainer to hand over access, then injected a backdoor into critical infrastructure. The vulnerability wasn't in the code. It was in the human system around the code — in the fact that a single exhausted person was susceptible to social engineering precisely because they were alone, under-resourced, and desperate for help.

Contrast that with projects that have gotten governance right. The Python Software Foundation runs a structured steering council with term limits and transparent decision-making. The Rust project distributes authority across working groups with codified escalation paths. These projects aren't immune to problems, but they're resilient. They have a bus factor greater than one.

So when we talk about sustainability, we need to talk about all of it: money, labor, governance, and trust. I think of it as a **Sustainability Triad** — though it's really four legs holding up one table. Funding stability means multi-year commitments, not one-off grants. Labor sustainability means shared maintainership and, yes, something resembling sick leave for the people who keep the internet running. Governance means codified decision-making, shadow boards, transparent escalation. And trust means security practices and social structures that can withstand adversarial pressure.

All four are failing simultaneously. And now we're adding AI to the mix.

**[SLIDE 3: Enter the Machine]**

AI isn't waiting for us to solve the sustainability crisis before it starts reshaping the landscape.

In the last eighteen months, AI-generated code has gone from novelty to daily reality. GitHub reports that Copilot now generates nearly half of all code in the languages where it's enabled. Half. Let that land.

The optimistic view — and there is a genuinely optimistic view — is that AI dramatically lowers the barrier to contribution. Someone who understands a problem domain but isn't fluent in Rust can submit a meaningful pull request to a Rust project. AI can generate boilerplate, write tests, draft documentation, triage issues. In theory, it alleviates exactly the maintenance load I just described.

We're already seeing it. Projects are experimenting with AI-assisted code review and automated dependency updates. Some maintainers report that these tools have genuinely reduced their burden. That's real.

But there's a shadow side, and we need to look at it directly.

**The contribution quality problem.** Maintainers are reporting a surge in low-quality, AI-generated pull requests from people using open source projects as a proving ground for their tools. Generate a PR, submit it, move on — leaving the maintainer to review, test, and usually reject code produced without understanding of the project's architecture. One maintainer described it to me as "automated littering." The cost of saying no is still borne by humans.

**The provenance problem.** This is the one that keeps me up at night. When a human writes code and contributes it, there's a relatively clear chain of authorship and intent. When AI generates code — trained on a corpus that includes open source under various licenses — provenance becomes murky. Who is the author? What license applies? If Copilot generates a function substantially similar to GPL-licensed code and a developer submits it to an Apache-licensed project, what just happened legally? We don't have clear answers. The courts don't have clear answers. And the volume of AI-generated code is scaling far faster than our legal frameworks can adapt.

**The homogenization risk.** AI models reproduce patterns from existing code. Open source has historically been a space for radical experimentation — weird, opinionated, sometimes-brilliant approaches no product manager would approve. If we increasingly rely on AI to generate contributions, we risk converging on a median. We risk losing the creative outliers that have driven the most important innovations in our field.

I'm not saying AI is bad for open source. I'm saying it's a powerful force being applied without sufficient intentionality about the consequences.

If AI changes the game, we need to change the rules we play by. That's what the next section is about.

**[SLIDE 4: A Vision for the Next Decade — Three Pillars]**

Sustainability is fractured. AI is reshaping the terrain. The old social contract is breaking down. What do we actually do?

I want to propose a vision built on three pillars — not silver bullets, but design principles for the next era of open source.

**Pillar One: Professionalize maintenance without corporatizing it.**

We need legitimate, well-compensated roles for open source maintenance that don't require maintainers to either work for free or get absorbed into a corporate open source program office. The most promising model is what I'd call *infrastructure-grade funding* — treating critical open source the way we treat other public infrastructure.

The Sovereign Tech Fund in Germany is pioneering this, directly funding maintenance of critical projects as a matter of public interest. The European Commission's Next Generation Internet initiative is doing similar work. These need to scale globally. Governments, industry consortia, and foundations need to build permanent funding mechanisms — not grants, not sponsorships, but ongoing structural investment.

At the same time, we need better frameworks for *distributed maintenance*. The single-maintainer model is a single point of failure. Projects need governance structures that make it safe and efficient to share authority — better tooling for permissions, review workflows, and decision-making.

Here's what this looks like concretely. In the next twelve to twenty-four months, I'd like to see three major foundations pilot dual-maintainer requirements for critical packages. Within three to five years, infrastructure-grade funding should cover the top one thousand most-depended-on packages globally. By the end of the decade, we should be able to measure meaningful reductions in maintainer burnout and improvements in security response times.

**Sustainable maintenance demands stable, scalable funding and governance — not charity, not hobbyist labor.**

We cannot let AI integration happen by default. We need explicit norms, and we need them soon.

First, **require provenance disclosure.** AI-generated contributions should include a provenance tag — a lightweight, human-readable certificate indicating what tools were used and what human review occurred. This isn't bureaucracy; it's traceability.

Second, **publish an AI contribution policy.** Every project should state its expectations: disclosure standards, review criteria for AI-generated code, and licensing alignment requirements. Think of it as a CONTRIBUTING.md for the AI era.

Third, **invest in open tooling for provenance and compliance.** PR provenance dashboards that flag AI-assisted submissions. Automated license compatibility checks. Model cards attached to the tools themselves. These aren't hypothetical — prototypes exist. They need adoption.

Beyond policy, the open source community should be *building* the AI tools, not just being subject to them. Open-weight models like LLaMA and Mistral, open training datasets, open fine-tuning frameworks — these are leverage points. If the future of code generation is AI, then the future of open source depends on that AI itself being open. Otherwise, we've created a new proprietary layer sitting on top of the commons, extracting value from it. Sound familiar?

**AI must be governed, not guessed at.**

**Pillar Three: Recommit to community as the core asset.**

This is the easiest to say and hardest to do. But I believe it's the most important.

What makes open source genuinely different from proprietary software is not the license. It's the community — the living system of humans who share context, values, and purpose. AI can generate code. It cannot generate trust. It cannot generate the shared understanding that allows strangers across six time zones to collaborate on something complex and beautiful and useful.

The projects that thrive in the next decade will invest deliberately in their human communities. Mentorship programs that pair experienced contributors with newcomers. Inclusive governance that reflects the diversity of the people who depend on the software. Codes of conduct that are actually enforced. Contribution experiences that are rewarding not just technically, but socially and emotionally.

Because if contributing to open source feels like feeding code into a machine, people will stop doing it. And no amount of AI-generated pull requests will replace what's lost.

**Communities build what code alone cannot.**

**[SLIDE 5: Your Role — A 90-Day Challenge]**

Before I close, I want to make this concrete. What can you do in the next ninety days?

**If you're an engineer:** Adopt a provenance disclosure practice for AI-assisted code in your projects. Mentor one newcomer. Participate in the governance of a project you depend on — even if it's just showing up to a community call.

**If you're an engineering leader:** Fund maintenance, not just features. Advocate for multi-year open source sustaining commitments in your organization. Support your team members who contribute upstream.

**If you're at a foundation or in policy:** Champion infrastructure-grade funding. Promote licensing transparency for AI training data. Help build the governance templates that projects desperately need.

**[SLIDE 6: Closing]**

Open source has always been an act of faith. Faith that if you share your work freely, others will build on it. Faith that collaboration beats competition. Faith that the commons can hold.

That faith is being tested now — in new ways, at new scales. The sustainability crisis is real. The AI disruption is real. The erosion of trust is real.

But I have never seen a moment with more potential to get this right. Funding models are maturing. Governance frameworks are evolving. A generation of developers who grew up on open source understands its value intuitively. And yes, we have AI — which, if we are intentional and brave, can amplify human contribution rather than replace it.

The future of open source will not be determined by technology. It will be determined by choices. What we fund. What we build. Who we include. What we refuse to accept.

So here's my ask. Don't just consume open source. Don't just contribute to open source. *Fight for* open source. Fight for the maintainers. Fight for the commons. Fight for the idea that the most important software in the world should belong to everyone.

Because open source was never just a licensing model. **It was a promise — that together, we could build something none of us could build alone.** That promise is worth keeping.

Thank you.

**[SLIDE 1: Title]**

Eleven people mass-transit systems, banking infrastructure, hospital networks, and roughly ninety-six percent of the world's top million web servers. Eleven people maintained OpenSSL when Heartbleed was discovered in 2014. Eleven volunteers, most of them part-time, standing between the global economy and catastrophe.

We like to tell ourselves that story is ancient history. That we've learned. That we've grown up. But three years ago, a single developer mass-deleted his seventeen-line npm package called "left-pad," and thousands of builds broke worldwide. Two years ago, the maintainer of `core-js`—a package downloaded thirty million times per week—posted from prison, asking if anyone could help keep the project alive. So let me ask you honestly: Have we actually learned anything?

I think we have. I think we're *starting* to. But I also think we're standing at an inflection point—one shaped by three forces colliding simultaneously: a sustainability crisis that's been building for decades, a community model under unprecedented strain, and the arrival of AI-generated code at a scale none of us fully predicted. And how we navigate the next five to ten years will determine whether open source remains the bedrock of modern software—or becomes its most dangerous single point of failure.

Let's talk about all three.

**[SLIDE 2: The Sustainability Problem]**

Here's the uncomfortable truth about open source sustainability: we have not solved it. We've created a dozen mechanisms to *partially address* it, and then we've congratulated ourselves and moved on.

GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective, Tidelift, foundation membership models—these are real tools, and they've helped real maintainers. I don't want to diminish that. But let's look at the data. The Tidelift maintainer survey from 2023 found that sixty percent of open source maintainers are unpaid volunteers. Forty-six percent have considered quitting. And the most common reason isn't technical burnout—it's the emotional weight of maintaining critical infrastructure while feeling invisible.

We have built an economic model where the most critical software on the planet is maintained by people we do not pay, do not support, and frequently abuse in GitHub issues.

And the structural problem goes deeper than money. Even when funding exists, it tends to flow to *projects*, not to *people*. It flows to the exciting new framework, not to the person quietly maintaining the cryptographic library underneath it. We have a visibility problem layered on top of a funding problem layered on top of a cultural problem that tells maintainers they should be grateful for the exposure.

I want to name that cultural problem directly, because I think it's the root: **we have confused the freedom of open source with the idea that it should be free of cost.** The open source ethos was never "labor should be donated." It was "knowledge should be shared." Those are profoundly different propositions.

So what does real sustainability look like? I think it requires three shifts.

First, **corporate consumers of open source need to move from sponsorship to obligation.** Not legally—I'm not arguing for license changes, though others are, and I respect that conversation. I mean culturally. If your company's revenue depends on a piece of open source software, contributing back—in money, in engineering time, in maintainer support—should be as non-negotiable as paying your cloud bill. It's infrastructure. Treat it like infrastructure.

Second, **we need to fund people, not just projects.** The best investment in open source sustainability isn't a grant to a GitHub repository. It's a salary for a maintainer. It's health insurance. It's the ability for someone to do this work without choosing between maintaining critical software and paying rent. Foundations like the Linux Foundation and Apache have started moving in this direction. We need more of it, and we need it from the companies that benefit most.

Third, **we need to normalize succession planning.** Open source projects should not be single points of human failure. We need mentorship pipelines, co-maintainer models, and a culture that treats "I need to step back" not as abandonment but as a healthy part of a project's lifecycle.

**[SLIDE 3: The Community Question]**

Which brings me to community—because sustainability isn't just about money. It's about people choosing to show up.

Open source communities are under strain in ways that aren't always visible from the outside. The xz-utils incident I mentioned earlier wasn't just a security story. It was a *community* story. A maintainer, overwhelmed and undersupported, was socially engineered over the course of years by someone who showed up, contributed, gained trust, and then exploited it. The attack vector wasn't a buffer overflow. It was human loneliness.

We need to sit with that for a moment.

The open source community model—built on trust, on volunteerism, on the radical idea that strangers on the internet can build great things together—is one of the most remarkable social experiments in human history. And it works. It has produced software that runs the world. But it works because of *people*, and people are not infinitely resilient.

I see three threats to open source community health right now.

**Maintainer burnout**, which we've discussed. **Toxic interaction patterns**—the entitlement, the demanding issues, the "I found a bug, fix it now" attitude that treats maintainers as unpaid customer support. And increasingly, **a loss of on-ramp for new contributors.** As projects mature and codebases grow more complex, the barrier to meaningful contribution rises. First-time contributors face intimidating code review processes, unclear documentation, and sometimes outright hostility.

If we want open source to thrive for the next decade, we need to invest in community architecture as deliberately as we invest in software architecture. That means codes of conduct with actual enforcement. It means dedicated community management roles, funded and valued. It means mentorship programs that don't just exist on paper but are actively maintained. And it means creating genuine pathways for new contributors—not "good first issues" that have been sitting untouched for three years, but real, structured onboarding.

The projects that will thrive are the ones that treat community health as a first-class engineering concern.

**[SLIDE 4: The AI Question]**

Now. The elephant in the room. The elephant that's also writing code, opening pull requests, and generating documentation at three in the morning.

AI-generated code is already reshaping open source, and we are not ready for the conversation we need to have about it.

Let me break this into three dimensions: volume, quality, and ownership.

**Volume.** GitHub reported that in 2024, the number of AI-assisted pull requests on the platform increased by over forty percent year-over-year. Copilot, Claude, GPT-based tools—developers are using them daily. This means more code is being generated, faster, by more people. In theory, this is wonderful. More contributions, more fixes, more features. In practice, it means maintainers are now drowning in pull requests they didn't ask for, generated by tools that don't understand project conventions, architectural decisions, or the subtle human context behind a codebase.

We are adding volume without adding understanding. And for already-overwhelmed maintainers, more pull requests is not a gift. It's a burden.

**Quality.** AI-generated code is getting better—rapidly. But "better" is not "good enough for critical infrastructure." AI tools generate code that *looks* correct, passes surface-level review, and sometimes contains subtle bugs that a human reviewer might miss precisely because the code *looks* so polished. We are entering an era where the cost of code review is going up, not down, because the surface quality of submissions masks deeper issues.

And this connects directly to security. The xz-utils attack worked because a human built trust over time. What happens when AI-generated contributions—perfectly formatted, well-tested, seemingly benign—are submitted at scale across thousands of projects? The attack surface isn't shrinking. It's expanding.

**Ownership.** And then there's the question no one has fully answered: Who owns AI-generated code? If a model trained on GPL-licensed code generates a function, is that function GPL-licensed? If a developer uses an AI tool to contribute to an Apache-licensed project, and the AI's training data included code under incompatible licenses, what happens? We don't know. The legal frameworks haven't caught up. And until they do, every AI-generated contribution to an open source project carries a small asterisk of legal uncertainty.

Now—I don't want to be a doomer about this. AI tools are genuinely powerful, and they can be genuine force multipliers for open source. Automated documentation generation, test creation, bug triage, translation—these are areas where AI can take real burden off maintainers. The key is intentionality. We need AI tools that are *designed for* the open source context, not just enterprise developer productivity tools that happen to interact with open source repositories.

Imagine an AI assistant that doesn't just generate code but understands a project's contribution guidelines, respects its architectural patterns, and helps new contributors learn the codebase rather than bypassing the learning entirely. That's the future I want to build toward.

**[SLIDE 5: A Vision for the Next Decade]**

So where does all of this leave us? Let me try to paint a picture of the open source ecosystem I believe we can build—if we're deliberate about it.

In the next decade, I want to see an open source world where **maintainership is a recognized, compensated profession**—not a side project, not a hobby, not a sacrifice. Where the people who maintain the software the world runs on are valued the way we value the people who maintain bridges and power grids.

I want to see **corporate participation that goes beyond logos on a website.** Companies embedding engineers in open source projects. Companies funding not just features they need but the maintenance, security, and community work that makes those features possible.

I want to see **AI as a tool in service of maintainers, not a firehose pointed at them.** AI that reduces toil. AI that helps with the unglamorous work—dependency updates, security patches, documentation, accessibility. AI that makes maintainers' lives easier rather than more complicated.

I want to see **communities that are genuinely welcoming**—not in the shallow, performative sense, but in the structural sense. Where there are real pathways from first contribution to core maintainer. Where the knowledge of how to build and maintain great software is passed down deliberately, not accidentally.

And I want to see **an honest reckoning with the economics of open source.** We cannot keep building trillion-dollar industries on top of unpaid labor and calling it a community. Community is real. Community matters. But community is not a substitute for structural support.

**[SLIDE 6: Closing]**

I'll leave you with this.

Open source is not just a development methodology. It's not just a licensing model. At its best, it is a statement of belief—that we build better things together than apart, that knowledge shared is knowledge multiplied, and that the commons is worth protecting.

But a commons requires stewardship. It requires investment. It requires people who show up not just to take, but to tend.

The code is open. **The question is whether we are.**

Thank you.

I see three threats to community health right now.

**Maintainer burnout**, which we've discussed. **Toxic interaction patterns**—the entitlement, the demanding issues, the attitude that treats maintainers as unpaid customer support. And **a loss of on-ramp for new contributors.** As codebases grow complex, the barrier to meaningful contribution rises. First-time contributors face intimidating review processes, unclear documentation, and sometimes outright hostility.

Let me tell you about a junior developer—call her Anika—who tried to contribute to a major infrastructure project last year. She found a "good first issue" tag, spent a weekend writing a patch, submitted her PR, and waited. Three weeks later, a maintainer left a single comment: "This doesn't follow our patterns." Real, structured onboarding—not three-year-old "good first issues" but genuine pathways from first contribution to core maintainer.

2. **Licensing transparency.** Flag when generated code may carry licensing implications.
3. **Human-in-the-loop review.** No AI-generated PR merges without human sign-off.
4. **Project-aware tooling.** AI assistants that understand contribution guidelines, not just syntax.
5. **Risk assessment.** A lightweight checklist for evaluating AI-generated contributions to security-critical projects.

And I want to see a cross-foundation working group—OpenSSF, Linux Foundation, Apache—draft best-practice guidelines for AI-generated contributions, with a public, versioned FAQ and a living policy document. This isn't hypothetical. This is work that needs to start this year.

The future I want: AI that serves maintainers, not one that's a firehose pointed at them. AI-assisted triage that flags high-risk PRs. AI-generated test scaffolding aligned with project conventions. AI-powered onboarding that adapts to a contributor's background. Tools designed *for* the open source context, not enterprise productivity tools that happen to touch open source repos.

**[SLIDE 5: A Roadmap for the Next Decade]**

So where does this leave us? Let me sketch a roadmap—not just a vision, but milestones.

**2026–2027:** Pilot paid maintainer programs in three to five critical ecosystems. Launch AI governance pilots. Publish a "sustainability scorecard" for projects—open, auditable metrics on maintainer health, funding sources, and contributor pipeline.

**2031 and beyond:** Broad adoption of standardized governance for AI-generated contributions. Measurable improvements in maintainer longevity and project health. A world where maintainership is a recognized, compensated profession—not a side project, not a sacrifice.

This isn't utopian. Pieces of it already exist. The Python Software Foundation funds developer-in-residence positions. The Sovereign Tech Fund in Germany invests in critical open source infrastructure. Companies like Sentry and Astral are building businesses that fund maintainers directly. These are proof points. We need to scale them.

**[SLIDE 6: Closing]**

I'll close with this.

Open source is not just a development methodology. It's not just a licensing model. At its best, it is a statement of belief—that we build better things together than apart, that knowledge shared is knowledge multiplied, and that the commons is worth protecting.

But a commons requires stewardship. It requires investment. It requires people who show up not just to take, but to tend.

So here's my ask. **If you're an individual contributor:** mentor someone. Review a PR on a project you depend on. Show up. **If you're a maintainer:** you are not alone, and you deserve support—demand it. **If you're a company:** fund a maintainer this quarter. Not a logo on a sponsorship page. A person. **If you're a foundation:** start the AI governance working group. Don't wait.

The code is open. The question is whether we are.

Join the work. Protect the commons.

Thank you.

# The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question

**A Conference Talk**

---

**[SLIDE 1: Title]**

Good morning.

I want to start with a number. Eleven.

Eleven people maintained the code securing mass-transit systems, banking infrastructure, hospital networks, and roughly ninety-six percent of the world's top million web servers. Eleven volunteers, most of them part-time, maintained OpenSSL when Heartbleed was discovered in 2014. Eleven people standing between the global economy and catastrophe.

We like to tell ourselves that story is ancient history. That we've learned. That we've grown up. But three years ago, a single developer mass-deleted his seventeen-line npm package called "left-pad," and thousands of builds broke worldwide. Two years ago, the maintainer of `core-js`—a package downloaded thirty million times per week—posted from prison, asking if anyone could help keep the project alive. And just last year, a lone, burned-out maintainer nearly succeeded in planting a backdoor in `xz-utils` that would have compromised SSH on most Linux distributions on Earth.

The names of the libraries change. The nature of the crisis does not. We keep building skyscrapers on foundations maintained by volunteers, and then acting surprised when the foundations crack.

So let me ask you honestly: Have we actually learned anything?

I think we have. I think we're *starting* to. But I also think we're standing at an inflection point—one shaped by three forces colliding simultaneously: a sustainability crisis that's been building for decades, a community model under unprecedented strain, and the arrival of AI-generated code at a scale none of us fully predicted. How we navigate the next five to ten years will determine whether open source remains the bedrock of modern software—or becomes its most dangerous single point of failure.

Let's talk about all three.

**[SLIDE 2: The Sustainability Problem]**

Here's the uncomfortable truth about open source sustainability: we have not solved it. We've created a dozen mechanisms to *partially address* it, and then we've congratulated ourselves and moved on.

GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective, Tidelift, foundation membership models—these are real tools, and they've helped real maintainers. I don't want to diminish that. But let's look at the data. The Tidelift maintainer survey from 2023 found that sixty percent of open source maintainers are unpaid volunteers. Forty-six percent have considered quitting. And the most common reason isn't technical burnout—it's the emotional weight of maintaining critical infrastructure while feeling invisible.

We have built an economic model where the most critical software on the planet is maintained by people we do not know, do not pay, do not support, and frequently abuse in GitHub issues.

And the structural problem goes deeper than money. Even when funding exists, it tends to flow to *projects*, not to *people*. It flows to the exciting new framework, not to the person quietly maintaining the cryptographic library underneath it. We have a visibility problem layered on top of a funding problem layered on top of a cultural problem that tells maintainers they should be grateful for the exposure.

I want to name that cultural problem directly, because I think it's the root: **we have confused the freedom of open source with the idea that it should be free of cost.** The open source ethos was never "labor should be donated." It was "knowledge should be shared." Those are profoundly different propositions.

So what does real sustainability look like? I think it requires three shifts.

First, **corporate consumers of open source need to move from sponsorship to obligation.** Not legally—I'm not arguing for license changes, though others are, and I respect that conversation. I mean culturally. If your company's revenue depends on a piece of open source software, contributing back—in money, in engineering time, in maintainer support—should be as non-negotiable as paying your cloud bill. It's infrastructure. Treat it like infrastructure. And here's a concrete challenge for every engineering leader in this room: if you have a budget for AWS and a budget for Datadog but zero budget for the open source libraries that glue them together, your risk model is broken. Allocate one percent of your cloud spend to the open source projects that run on that cloud. One percent. Start there.

Second, **we need to fund people, not just projects.** The best investment in open source sustainability isn't a grant to a GitHub repository. It's a salary for a maintainer. It's health insurance. It's the ability for someone to do this work without choosing between maintaining critical software and paying rent. Foundations like the Linux Foundation and Apache have started moving in this direction. We need more of it, and we need it from the companies that benefit most.

Third, **we need to normalize succession planning.** Open source projects should not be single points of human failure. We need mentorship pipelines, co-maintainer models, and a culture that treats "I need to step back" not as abandonment but as a healthy part of a project's lifecycle.

**[SLIDE 3: The Community Question]**

Which brings me to community—because sustainability isn't just about money. It's about people choosing to show up.

Open source communities are under strain in ways that aren't always visible from the outside. The xz-utils incident I mentioned earlier wasn't just a security story. It was a *community* story. A maintainer, overwhelmed and undersupported, was socially engineered over the course of years by someone who showed up, contributed, gained trust, and then exploited it. The attack vector wasn't a buffer overflow. It was human loneliness.

We need to sit with that for a moment.

The open source community model—built on trust, on volunteerism, on the radical idea that strangers on the internet can build great things together—is one of the most remarkable social experiments in human history. And it works. It has produced software that runs the world. But it works because of *people*, and people are not infinitely resilient.

I see three threats to open source community health right now.

**Maintainer burnout**, which we've discussed. **Toxic interaction patterns**—the entitlement, the demanding issues, the "I found a bug, fix it now" attitude that treats maintainers as unpaid customer support. And increasingly, **a loss of on-ramp for new contributors.** As projects mature and codebases grow more complex, the barrier to meaningful contribution rises. First-time contributors face intimidating code review processes, unclear documentation, and sometimes outright hostility.

If we want open source to thrive for the next decade, we need to invest in community architecture as deliberately as we invest in software architecture. That means codes of conduct with actual enforcement. It means dedicated community management roles, funded and valued. It means mentorship programs that don't just exist on paper but are actively maintained. And it means creating genuine pathways for new contributors—not "good first issues" that have been sitting untouched for three years, but real, structured onboarding.

The projects that will thrive are the ones that treat community health as a first-class engineering concern.

**[SLIDE 4: The AI Question]**

Now. The ghost in the machine. The ghost that is currently writing code, opening pull requests, and generating documentation at three in the morning.

AI-generated code is already reshaping open source, and we are not ready for the conversation we need to have about it.

Let me break this into three dimensions: volume, quality, and accountability.

**Volume.** GitHub reported that in 2024, the number of AI-assisted pull requests on the platform increased by over forty percent year-over-year. Copilot, Claude, GPT-based tools—developers are using them daily. This means more code is being generated, faster, by more people. In theory, this is wonderful. More contributions, more fixes, more features. In practice, it means maintainers are now drowning in pull requests they didn't ask for, generated by tools that don't understand project conventions, architectural decisions, or the subtle human context behind a codebase.

We are adding volume without adding understanding. And for already-overwhelmed maintainers, more pull requests is not a gift. It's a burden.

**Quality.** AI-generated code is getting better—rapidly. But "better" is not "good enough for critical infrastructure." AI tools generate code that *looks* correct, passes surface-level review, and sometimes contains subtle bugs that a human reviewer might miss precisely because the code *looks* so polished. We are entering an era where the cost of code review is going up, not down, because the surface quality of submissions masks deeper issues.

And this connects directly to security. The xz-utils attack worked because a human built trust over time. What happens when AI-generated contributions—perfectly formatted, well-tested, seemingly benign—are submitted at scale across thousands of projects? The attack surface isn't shrinking. It's expanding.

**Accountability.** Here's the question no one has fully answered: when AI-generated code breaks production, who is on the hook? If Copilot writes a vulnerability, who bears responsibility? The maintainer who merged it? The junior developer who prompted it? The corporation that sold the tool and trained it on open source code in the first place? Right now, the answer, in practice, is this: the unpaid volunteer maintainer cleans up the mess. That is not a sustainable model. That is not even a fair one.

Now—I don't want to be a doomer about this. AI tools are genuinely powerful, and they can be genuine force multipliers for open source. Automated documentation generation, test creation, bug triage, translation—these are areas where AI can take real burden off maintainers. The key is intentionality. We need AI tools that are *designed for* the open source context, not just enterprise developer productivity tools that happen to interact with open source repositories.

Imagine an AI assistant that doesn't just generate code but understands a project's contribution guidelines, respects its architectural patterns, and helps new contributors learn the codebase rather than bypassing the learning entirely. That's the future I want to build toward.

**[SLIDE 5: A Vision for the Next Decade]**

So where does all of this leave us? Let me try to paint a picture of the open source ecosystem I believe we can build—if we're deliberate about it.

In the next decade, I want to see an open source world where **maintainership is a recognized, compensated profession**—not a side project, not a hobby, not a sacrifice. Where the people who maintain the software the world runs on are valued the way we value the people who maintain bridges and power grids.

I want to see **corporate participation that goes beyond logos on a website.** Companies embedding engineers in open source projects. Companies funding not just features they need but the maintenance, security, and community work that makes those features possible.

I want to see **AI as a tool in service of maintainers, not a firehose pointed at them.** AI that reduces toil. AI that helps with the unglamorous work—dependency updates, security patches, documentation, accessibility. AI that makes maintainers' lives easier rather than more complicated.

I want to see **communities that are genuinely welcoming**—not in the shallow, performative sense, but in the structural sense. Where there are real pathways from first contribution to core maintainer. Where the knowledge of how to build and maintain great software is passed down deliberately, not accidentally.

And I want to see **an honest reckoning with the economics of open source.** We cannot keep building trillion-dollar industries on top of unpaid labor and calling it a community. Community is real. Community matters. But community is not a substitute for structural support.

That vision is not going to build itself. So let me speak directly to the people in this room.

**To the junior developers:** Don't just generate code and throw it over the wall. Learn the project's context. Read the contributing guide. Understand *why* the code is shaped the way it is before you try to reshape it. Your first pull request should cost you effort. That's not a bug—it's how you become someone a project can trust.

**To the engineering managers and directors:** Put open source contribution on your promotion rubrics. Make it count. Give your engineers twenty-percent time for upstream work, and then actually protect that time. And when you're planning next year's budget, remember: one percent of your cloud spend. Start there.

**To the maintainers:** You are doing some of the most important work in our industry. You are allowed to set boundaries. You are allowed to say no. And you deserve to be paid.

**[SLIDE 6: Closing]**

I'll leave you with this.

Open source is not just a development methodology. It's not just a licensing model. At its best, it is a statement of belief—that we build better things together than apart, that knowledge shared is knowledge multiplied, and that the commons is worth protecting.

But a commons requires stewardship. It requires investment. It requires people who show up not just to take, but to tend.

The code is open. **The question is whether we're willing to pay the price to keep it that way.**

Thank you.
