Five years ago, I opened an issue on a library I depended on—a library maintained by one person, in their spare time, for free—and I titled it "Critical bug, needs immediate fix." No greeting. No context about my own attempts to solve it. Just a demand, dressed up as urgency. I think about that issue sometimes. I think about it because I was part of the problem, and if we're being honest with ourselves, a lot of us in this room have been too.

I think we're *starting* to learn. But I also think we're standing at an inflection point—one shaped by three forces colliding simultaneously: a sustainability crisis that's been building for decades, a community model under unprecedented strain, and the arrival of AI-generated code at a scale none of us fully predicted. How we navigate the next five to ten years will determine whether open source remains the bedrock of modern software—or becomes its most dangerous single point of failure.

Let's talk about all three.

**[SLIDE 2: The Sustainability Problem]**

Here's the uncomfortable truth about open source sustainability: we have not solved it. We've created a dozen mechanisms to *partially address* it, and then we've congratulated ourselves and moved on.

GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective, Tidelift, foundation membership models—these are real tools, and they've helped real maintainers. I don't want to diminish that. But let's look at the data. The Tidelift maintainer survey from 2023 found that sixty percent of open source maintainers are unpaid volunteers. Forty-six percent have considered quitting. And the most common reason isn't technical burnout—it's the emotional weight of maintaining critical infrastructure while feeling invisible.

We have built an economic model where the most critical software on the planet is maintained by people we do not pay, do not support, and frequently abuse in GitHub issues.

And the structural problem goes deeper than money. Even when funding exists, it tends to flow to *projects*, not to *people*. It flows to the exciting new framework, not to the person quietly maintaining the cryptographic library underneath it. We have a visibility problem layered on top of a funding problem layered on top of a cultural problem that tells maintainers they should be grateful for the exposure.

I want to name that cultural problem directly, because I think it's the root: **we have confused the freedom of open source with the idea that it should be free of cost.** The open source ethos was never "labor should be donated." It was "knowledge should be shared." Those are profoundly different propositions.

So why hasn't this changed? Because there's a genuine collective action problem, and naming it matters. Any single company that starts paying for its open source dependencies bears a real cost while its competitors free-ride. Procurement systems don't have a line item for "software we got for free." The cost of failure—a Heartbleed, an xz-utils—gets externalized to the entire ecosystem, while the cost of prevention lands on whoever volunteers first. This is the tragedy of the commons, and we will not solve it with goodwill alone.

Real sustainability requires three shifts.

First, **corporate consumers of open source need to move from sponsorship to obligation.** Not legally—though the EU's Cyber Resilience Act is already pushing in that direction, and we should be paying attention. I mean culturally. If your company's revenue depends on a piece of open source software, contributing back—in money, in engineering time, in maintainer support—should be as non-negotiable as paying your cloud bill. It's infrastructure. Treat it like infrastructure. Companies like Bloomberg, embedding engineers directly in open source projects they depend on, show that this model works. We need it to become normal, not exceptional.

Second, **we need to fund people, not just projects.** The best investment in open source sustainability isn't a grant to a GitHub repository. It's a salary for a maintainer. It's health insurance. It's the ability for someone to do this work without choosing between maintaining critical software and paying rent.

Third, **we need to normalize succession planning.** The xz-utils attack succeeded precisely because a single overwhelmed maintainer had no supported path to share or transfer responsibility. Open source projects should not be single points of human failure. We need mentorship pipelines, co-maintainer models, and a culture that treats "I need to step back" not as abandonment but as a healthy part of a project's lifecycle.

**[SLIDE 3: The Community Question]**

Which brings me to community—because sustainability isn't just about money. It's about people choosing to show up.

The xz-utils incident wasn't just a security story. It was a *community* story. A maintainer, overwhelmed and undersupported, was socially engineered over the course of years by someone who showed up, contributed, gained trust, and then exploited it. The attack vector wasn't a buffer overflow. It was human loneliness.

We need to sit with that for a moment.

The open source community model—built on trust, on volunteerism, on the radical idea that strangers on the internet can build great things together—is one of the most remarkable social experiments in human history. And it works. It has produced software that runs the world. But it works because of *people*, and people are not infinitely resilient.

I see three threats to open source community health right now. **Maintainer burnout**, which we've discussed. **Toxic interaction patterns**—the entitlement, the demanding issues, the attitude that treats maintainers as unpaid customer support. And increasingly, **a loss of on-ramp for new contributors.** As projects mature and codebases grow more complex, the barrier to meaningful contribution rises. First-time contributors face intimidating code review processes, unclear documentation, and sometimes outright hostility.

If we want open source to thrive, we need to invest in community architecture as deliberately as we invest in software architecture. That means codes of conduct with actual enforcement. It means dedicated community management roles, funded and valued. It means mentorship programs that are actively maintained. And it means creating genuine pathways for new contributors—not "good first issues" that have been sitting untouched for three years, but real, structured onboarding.

The projects that will thrive are the ones that treat community health as a first-class engineering concern.

**[SLIDE 4: The AI Question]**

Now. The elephant in the room. The elephant that's also writing code, opening pull requests, and generating documentation at three in the morning.

AI-generated code is already reshaping open source, and we are not ready for the conversation we need to have about it.

Let me break this into three dimensions: volume, quality, and ownership.

**Volume.** GitHub reported that AI-assisted pull requests on the platform increased by over forty percent year-over-year in 2024. This means more code is being generated, faster, by more people. In theory, wonderful. In practice, maintainers are now fielding pull requests they didn't ask for, generated by tools that don't understand project conventions, architectural decisions, or the subtle human context behind a codebase. We are adding volume without adding understanding.

Now, it's not all one-sided. Many maintainers report that AI tools help *them* review code faster, write tests, and triage issues. AI is simultaneously increasing the burden on maintainers *and* offering tools to manage that burden. The question is which effect dominates—and right now, for most under-resourced projects, the flood is winning.

**Quality.** AI-generated code is getting better—rapidly. But "better" is not "good enough for critical infrastructure." AI tools generate code that *looks* correct, passes surface-level review, and sometimes contains subtle bugs that a human reviewer might miss precisely because the code *looks* so polished. The cost of code review is going up, not down, because surface quality masks deeper issues. And this connects directly to security: what happens when AI-generated contributions—perfectly formatted, well-tested, seemingly benign—are submitted at scale across thousands of projects?

**Ownership.** Who owns AI-generated code? If a model trained on GPL-licensed code generates a function, is that function GPL-licensed? The Copilot class-action lawsuit is still working through the courts. The FSF has raised serious concerns. Legal scholarship is fractured. And until these questions are resolved, every AI-generated contribution to an open source project carries an asterisk of legal uncertainty that engineering leaders in this room need to be factoring into their adoption decisions.

But here's the dimension I think we're underestimating most: **what AI means for community.**

The traditional open source contribution path—you find a bug, you read the code, you struggle with the build system, you submit a patch, you get feedback, you learn—that path is how we *grow* maintainers. It's how a user becomes a contributor becomes a committer becomes a steward. If AI lets people skip that struggle, we might gain contributions while losing contributors. We might get more code and fewer people who understand it. And in ten years, we will feel that loss acutely—because the maintainers of 2035 are the struggling first-time contributors of today.

I don't want to be a doomer about this. AI tools are genuinely powerful force multipliers. Automated documentation, test generation, bug triage, translation, accessibility improvements—these are areas where AI can take real burden off maintainers. The key is intentionality. We need AI tools designed for the open source context, not just enterprise productivity tools that happen to interact with open source repositories. Imagine an AI assistant that doesn't just generate code but understands a project's contribution guidelines, respects its architectural patterns, and helps new contributors *learn* the codebase rather than bypassing the learning entirely. That's the future worth building toward.

**[SLIDE 5: A Vision for the Next Decade]**

So where does all of this leave us?

I don't want to simply restate the problems as aspirations. You've heard the diagnosis. What I want to offer is a picture of institutional forms that don't fully exist yet—but could.

What if we treated critical open source infrastructure the way we treat public utilities? Not metaphorically—structurally. The EU's Cyber Resilience Act is already beginning to classify certain open source projects as critical digital infrastructure. What if that logic extended to public funding? Governments fund roads, bridges, power grids. OpenSSL is no less essential. A public funding model for critical open source—with accountability, with governance, without corporate capture—is not utopian. It's pragmatic. And it's overdue.

What if we built cooperative ownership models for major open source projects? Not foundations in the traditional sense, but structures where maintainers hold genuine governance power, where the people doing the work have a real voice in how resources are allocated. Some projects are already experimenting with this. We should be watching them closely and learning fast.

And what if we reimagined AI not as a contribution machine but as a *community* tool? AI that pairs experienced maintainers with newcomers. AI that identifies when a maintainer is overwhelmed and flags the need for support. AI that serves the social infrastructure of open source, not just its codebase.

The projects that will define the next decade are the ones that treat community health, financial sustainability, and technological change not as separate problems but as one deeply interconnected challenge.

**[SLIDE 6: Closing]**

I'll leave you with this.

Open source is not just a development methodology. It's not just a licensing model. At its best, it is a statement of belief—that we build better things together than apart, that knowledge shared is knowledge multiplied, and that the commons is worth protecting.

But a commons requires stewardship. It requires investment. It requires people who show up not just to take, but to tend.

The code is open. The question is whether we are willing to bear the cost of keeping it that way—not just in dollars, but in attention, in gratitude, in the daily, unglamorous work of showing up for each other.

That's not a technical problem. It's a human one. And it's ours to solve.

Thank you.

---

*[END OF TALK — approximately 2,050 words, ~15 minutes at speaking pace]*

# The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question

**A Conference Talk**

---

**[SLIDE 1: Title]**

Good morning.

I want to start with a number. Two billion, four hundred million. That's the estimated number of open source components that were downloaded from npm alone last *week*. Not last year. Last week.

Now here's another number: one.

That's how many maintainers are behind some of the packages your production systems depend on right now. One person. Probably mass-handling GitHub issues at eleven PM, probably mass-ignoring GitHub issues at eleven PM, probably mass-debating whether to mass-ignore GitHub issues at eleven PM. One person who didn't sign up to be your unpaid vendor.

We have built the entire modern software economy on a foundation that we have systematically refused to sustain. And now, just as we're starting to reckon with that, a new force has entered the picture — AI-generated code — and it is about to reshape what open source means, how it works, and who it's for.

That's what I want to talk about today. Not doom. Not hype. A clear-eyed look at where we are, what's changing, and what we need to build next.

---

**[SLIDE 2: The Sustainability Crisis Is Not New. It's Just Getting Worse.]**

Let's be honest with each other. The sustainability problem in open source isn't a secret. We've been talking about it for a decade. Nadia Eghbal wrote the book on it — literally — back in 2020. And yet here we are.

The pattern is painfully familiar. A developer builds something useful. Other developers adopt it. Companies adopt it. It becomes critical infrastructure. The maintainer burns out. And then one of two things happens: the project slowly decays, or there's a crisis — a security vulnerability, a supply chain attack — and suddenly everyone is asking, "Wait, who's in charge of this?"

Remember left-pad? That was 2016. Remember Log4Shell? That was 2021. Remember xz Utils? That was *last year*. We keep getting these wake-up calls, and we keep hitting snooze.

The economics are brutal. A 2024 survey by Tidelift found that 60% of maintainers are unpaid volunteers. Among those who do receive compensation, the median is well below what their skills would command in industry. Meanwhile, the companies extracting the most value from open source — and I say this with love, because I work at one — those companies are posting record revenues.

There's a term for this in economics. It's called a free-rider problem. And the conventional solutions — sponsorships, foundations, open core business models — they help, but they haven't solved it. GitHub Sponsors is wonderful. It is not a systemic fix. It's a tip jar.

So what does a systemic fix look like? I'll come back to that. But first, we need to talk about the elephant in the room. The elephant that writes code now, apparently.

---

**[SLIDE 3: The AI Question]**

Here's the thing about AI-generated code and open source: it's not one question. It's about seven questions tangled together, and we're pretending it's simple because the alternative is uncomfortable.

Let me untangle a few of them.

**Question one: Training data.** Large language models that generate code were trained on open source repositories. Copilot was trained on GitHub. The legal and ethical implications of this are still being litigated — literally, in courtrooms — but let's set aside the legal question for a moment and ask the moral one. Open source licenses grant permissions for use, modification, and distribution of code. They were written in a world where the "user" was a human being making conscious choices. Nobody anticipated that "use" might mean "ingest the entire corpus to build a commercial product that competes with the people who wrote the code." The social contract of open source assumed reciprocity. Train-and-commercialize breaks that assumption.

**Question two: Contribution quality.** We're already seeing it. Maintainers are reporting a surge in low-quality pull requests that are clearly AI-generated. Drive-by contributions from people who prompted a model, got some output, and submitted it without understanding the codebase, the conventions, or the context. One maintainer I spoke with called it "the Hacktoberfest problem on steroids." It's not that AI-assisted contributions are inherently bad. Some are excellent. But the signal-to-noise ratio is shifting, and the burden of filtering falls on — you guessed it — the already-overwhelmed maintainer.

**Question three: The contribution pipeline.** This is the one that keeps me up at night. Open source has always been a pipeline. Junior developers contribute small fixes. They learn the codebase. They learn the norms. They become senior contributors. They become maintainers. It's an apprenticeship model, and it works. But if AI handles the small fixes — if the entry-level contributions are automated away — where do the next maintainers come from? We might be optimizing for short-term efficiency while destroying the long-term pipeline of human expertise that open source depends on.

Now — and I want to be careful here — I am not an AI doomer. I use AI tools every day. They make me faster. They help me explore unfamiliar codebases. They're genuinely useful. The question isn't whether AI is good or bad for open source. The question is: are we being intentional about how we integrate it, or are we just letting it happen to us?

Because "letting it happen to us" is kind of our default mode.

---

**[SLIDE 4: What Thriving Looks Like]**

Okay. I promised this wouldn't be all doom. So let me paint a picture of what I think thriving open source communities could look like in the next decade — if we make deliberate choices starting now.

I don't mean bureaucratize it. I mean we need to treat maintenance as the skilled, essential work that it is, and fund it accordingly. The model I find most promising is what I'd call "institutional stewardship." Companies that depend on open source infrastructure should fund dedicated maintenance teams — not as charity, not as sponsorship, but as a line item in their engineering budget, the same way they budget for cloud services and security audits. Some companies are starting to do this. Sovereign Tech Fund in Germany is funding critical open source infrastructure with government money. This should be the norm, not the exception.

Imagine a world where the top 500 most critical open source projects all have at least two funded full-time maintainers. That's not utopian. That's, what, the cost of a few hundred senior engineering salaries? Distributed across the companies that depend on this software, it's a rounding error. We can afford this. We just have to decide it matters.

**Second: We need to rethink contribution models for the AI era.**

Instead of fighting AI-assisted contributions, we should design for them. That means better tooling for maintainers to triage and evaluate contributions — AI-powered review tools that can flag likely-generated PRs, assess test coverage, check for style consistency. It means establishing clear contribution guidelines that set expectations: "We welcome AI-assisted contributions, but we expect contributors to be able to explain their changes and respond to review feedback." And it means creating new pathways for human contributors to add value in ways that AI can't easily replicate — architecture decisions, community building, documentation that requires deep contextual understanding, mentorship.

The projects that will thrive are the ones that figure out how to make AI a force multiplier for their human contributors rather than a replacement for them.

**Third: We need to update the social contract.**

The open source licenses we have were designed for a different era. I'm not saying we need to throw them out. But we need to have an honest conversation about whether the existing frameworks adequately address AI training, AI-generated derivative works, and the concentration of value in a small number of companies that have the compute resources to train foundation models.

Some people are experimenting with new approaches. The Functional Source License. The Server Side Public License. Fair Source. These aren't perfect, and purists will argue they aren't "real" open source. Fine. But the purist position — that the four freedoms as defined in 1986 are sufficient for 2025 — that position is increasingly disconnected from reality. We need to evolve the frameworks while preserving the principles. Freedom, transparency, collaboration. Those don't change. But the mechanisms that protect them might need to.

**Fourth — and this is the one I care about most — we need to reinvest in community.**

The best open source projects have always been more than code. They're communities of practice. They're places where people learn, where they build relationships, where they develop shared understanding of hard problems. That human layer is what makes open source resilient. Code can be generated. Trust can't. Judgment can't. Shared context can't.

I think the projects that will thrive in the next decade are the ones that deliberately cultivate what I'll call "thick community" — not just a Discord server and a GitHub repo, but genuine relationships, mentorship structures, governance that gives contributors a voice, and a culture that values the people, not just the code they produce.

This is, frankly, harder than writing software. It's emotional labor. It's conflict resolution. It's showing up consistently. And it's exactly the kind of work that we chronically undervalue in engineering culture.

We need to fix that.

---

**[SLIDE 5: The Choice]**

So here's where we are. Open source is at an inflection point. The sustainability crisis is real and worsening. AI is reshaping the landscape in ways we're only beginning to understand. And the decisions we make in the next few years will determine whether open source remains a vibrant commons or becomes a strip mine — a place where value is extracted by the powerful and the burden is borne by the passionate.

I don't think that outcome is inevitable. But avoiding it requires intentionality. It requires companies to fund what they depend on. It requires maintainers to be valued as the professionals they are. It requires communities to adapt their practices for a world where AI is a participant, not just a tool. And it requires all of us — every person in this room who has ever typed `npm install` or `pip install` or `apt-get` — to recognize that open source is not a natural resource. It is a garden. And gardens require tending.

---

**[SLIDE 6: Closing]**

I want to leave you with this.

Twenty-five years ago, people said open source was a fad. They said you couldn't build serious software without proprietary control. They were wrong, and they were wrong because they underestimated what communities of committed people could build together.

The question in front of us now is not whether open source will survive. It's too deeply embedded in the infrastructure of the world to disappear. The question is whether it will survive as something we're proud of — as a genuine commons, a place of shared ownership and mutual benefit — or whether it will survive in name only, hollowed out, a label slapped on code that serves the interests of the few.

That's our choice to make. And I'd argue it's the most important choice in software right now.

So here's my ask. Go back to your teams. Look at your dependency trees. Find the maintainers who are holding up your world. And then do something about it. Fund them. Contribute upstream. Show up in their issue trackers not with demands, but with gratitude and help.

Because the future of open source isn't something that happens to us. It's something we build. Together. The way we always have.

Thank you.

---

# The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question

**A Conference Talk**

---

**[SLIDE 1: Title]**

Good morning.

I want to start with a number. Two billion, four hundred million. That's the estimated number of open source packages downloaded from npm alone last *week*. Not last year. Last week.

Now here's another number: one.

That's how many maintainers are behind some of the most critical packages in that supply chain. One person. Often unpaid. Often burned out. Often one mass transit delay away from mass infrastructure failure.

We all know the famous xkcd comic—the one with the tiny block at the bottom of the tower labeled "a project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003." We laugh at it. We share it. And then we go right back to depending on it.

So today I want to talk about the future of open source. And I want to be honest with you: I'm not sure we deserve the future we're hoping for. Not yet. Not unless we change some fundamental things about how we build, fund, and think about the software commons.

I want to cover three things in the next fifteen minutes. First, the sustainability crisis that's already here. Second, the AI question—and it is a question, not an answer. And third, a vision for what thriving open source communities could look like in the next decade, if we make the right choices now.

---

**[SLIDE 2: The Sustainability Crisis]**

Let's start with sustainability, and let's be specific.

In 2024, the Linux Foundation and Harvard conducted a census of the most critical open source projects in the world. The findings were sobering but not surprising to anyone paying attention. A huge percentage of critical infrastructure depends on projects with minimal funding, minimal contributor diversity, and maintainers who are one bad month away from walking away.

We've seen what happens when they do. The `core-js` maintainer publicly documented his financial struggles while his library was used by virtually every major website on the internet. The `colors.js` and `faker.js` maintainer deliberately sabotaged his own packages in frustration. The Log4Shell vulnerability in Log4j exposed what happens when a volunteer-maintained project in a critical security path doesn't have the resources for rigorous review.

These aren't edge cases. These are symptoms of a structural problem.

Here's the structural problem: open source won the argument. It won so completely that we forgot it was ever an argument at all. Every Fortune 500 company runs on open source. Every startup is built on open source. The entire cloud computing industry—which generates hundreds of billions of dollars in annual revenue—is essentially a monetization layer on top of open source software. And yet the creators of that software are, in aggregate, dramatically under-resourced.

We have a tragedy of the commons, and we've been remarkably creative at ignoring it.

Now, there have been genuine efforts to address this. GitHub Sponsors. Open Collective. The Sovereign Tech Fund in Germany—which I think is one of the most important experiments happening in this space. Tidelift's model of paying maintainers for security and maintenance commitments. These matter. They're real. But they're not yet operating at the scale of the problem.

And the problem is about to get more complicated.

---

**[SLIDE 3: The AI Question]**

Which brings me to AI.

I chose the word "question" deliberately in this talk's title, because I think the honest answer right now is that we don't fully know what AI-generated code means for open source. But I think we can identify the fault lines.

Let's start with what's already happening. Large language models trained on open source code are generating code at an unprecedented scale. GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Cody, open models like Code Llama and StarCoder—these tools are changing how developers write software every single day. Many of you in this room are using them. I use them.

Here's the first tension: these models were trained on open source code, often without explicit consent from the authors, and they generate code that may be derived from copyleft or permissively licensed work without clear attribution. The legal questions are still being litigated. The ethical questions are still being debated. But the practical reality is already here. Code is being generated, committed, and deployed at scale, and the provenance chain is murky at best.

This isn't just a legal abstraction. It goes to the heart of the social contract that open source is built on. That contract has always been: I give you my code freely, and in return I get attribution, community, the knowledge that I'm contributing to a commons. If AI models can launder that contribution—absorb it, recombine it, and output it without any connection back to the original author—then we've broken something fundamental about why people contribute in the first place.

But here's the second tension, and it cuts the other way. AI tools are also lowering the barrier to contribution. They're helping new developers understand unfamiliar codebases. They're generating tests, documentation, boilerplate—the unglamorous work that maintainers desperately need help with. In theory, AI could be the greatest force multiplier open source has ever seen.

In theory.

In practice, I'm hearing something different from maintainers. I'm hearing about a flood of low-quality, AI-generated pull requests from people chasing Hacktoberfest t-shirts or LinkedIn clout. PRs that look plausible but don't actually work. PRs that introduce subtle bugs because the person submitting them didn't understand the code the AI wrote for them. PRs that shift the burden from the contributor to the maintainer, who now has to spend more time reviewing bad contributions than they would have spent just writing the code themselves.

This is the AI question for open source, and it's really two questions in one. Can AI help sustain open source? And will AI undermine the human relationships that make open source work?

I don't think these questions have inevitable answers. I think they have *chosen* answers. Which brings me to the future.

---

**[SLIDE 4: A Vision for the Next Decade]**

So what does thriving look like? Let me sketch a vision—not a prediction, but an aspiration.

**First: we need to treat open source infrastructure like actual infrastructure.**

When a bridge is structurally critical, we don't rely on a volunteer to inspect it on weekends. We fund it. We staff it. We create institutional accountability for its maintenance.

The Sovereign Tech Fund model—where a government directly funds the maintenance and security of critical open source projects—should be the norm, not the exception. The European Union's Cyber Resilience Act, for all its imperfections, at least acknowledges that open source is critical infrastructure deserving of institutional support. I'd like to see every G20 nation funding open source maintenance the way they fund roads and bridges. Because at this point, open source *is* roads and bridges.

On the private sector side, I think we need to move beyond sponsorship and toward something more like *membership in the commons*. Companies that derive billions from open source should be contributing a meaningful, measurable percentage back—not as charity, but as an operational cost of doing business. Some already do. Most don't. And I think the industry needs to develop norms and, frankly, social pressure around this. We should be able to look at a company's open source contribution the way we look at their carbon footprint. It should be visible, measurable, and expected.

**Second: we need to evolve our community models.**

The single-maintainer model is a failure mode, not a feature. We need to build projects that are institutionally resilient—that can survive the departure of any single person. This means governance structures, contributor pipelines, documentation that doesn't live in one person's head, and succession planning.

I know that sounds bureaucratic. I know many of you started contributing to open source precisely because it *wasn't* bureaucratic. But there's a difference between a weekend project and critical infrastructure, and we need different models for each. Not every project needs a foundation. But every project that other people depend on needs a bus factor greater than one.

This also means rethinking what contribution means. Code is important, but so is documentation, triage, mentorship, community management, and security review. The projects that will thrive in the next decade are the ones that value and recognize the full spectrum of contribution, not just the git log.

**Third: we need to be intentional about AI integration.**

Here's what I'd propose. Open source communities should develop clear, explicit norms around AI-generated contributions. Not bans—I don't think bans are practical or desirable. But norms. Disclose when code is AI-generated. Take responsibility for understanding what you submit. Maintainers should feel empowered to reject contributions that don't meet quality standards, regardless of how they were produced.

On the training side, I'd like to see AI companies and open source communities negotiate something that looks like a new social contract. If you train on open source code, you contribute back—financially, through tooling, through infrastructure support. Some companies are starting to do this. It needs to become universal.

And I think we should be building AI tools *specifically designed* to support maintainers, not just code generators for individual developers. Imagine AI that helps with issue triage, that identifies security vulnerabilities in pull requests, that generates test cases for edge conditions, that helps maintainers manage the cognitive load of running a project. The AI tools we build should serve the community, not just the individual.

**Fourth, and finally: we need to protect the culture.**

This is the one I care about most, and it's the hardest to operationalize.

Open source is not just a licensing model. It's not just a development methodology. It's a culture—a set of values about collaboration, transparency, shared ownership, and the belief that knowledge should be free. That culture is what attracted most of us to this work in the first place.

And that culture is fragile. It can be diluted by corporate capture, where companies dominate project governance to serve their own interests. It can be eroded by burnout, when the people who carry the culture leave and aren't replaced. It can be hollowed out by AI, if contribution becomes a mechanical act disconnected from understanding and community.

Protecting the culture means investing in people. It means mentoring new contributors not just in how to write code, but in *why* open source matters. It means creating spaces—conferences like this one, online communities, local meetups—where the values are transmitted and reinforced. It means telling the story of open source not as a supply chain optimization strategy, but as one of the most remarkable experiments in human cooperation in the history of technology.

Because that's what it is. Millions of people, across every country, every language, every timezone, choosing to build something together that no one owns and everyone benefits from. That's extraordinary. And it's worth fighting for.

---

**[SLIDE 5: Closing]**

Let me leave you with this.

Twenty-five years ago, open source was a radical idea. Ten years ago, it was a winning strategy. Today, it's the foundation of the digital world.

But foundations crack if you don't maintain them. And right now, we're standing on a foundation that's more fragile than most people realize, at the exact moment when AI is about to reshape every assumption we have about how software gets written.

We have a choice. We can let open source become a strip mine—a place where value is extracted by the powerful and the cost is borne by the passionate. Or we can build something better. We can fund the commons. We can strengthen our communities. We can shape AI into a tool that serves maintainers, not just consumers. We can protect the culture that made all of this possible in the first place.

The future of open source is not a technical problem. It's a human one. And the answer isn't in the code. It's in the choices we make about who we value, what we fund, and what kind of world we want to build together.

Open source gave us the modern internet. The question now is whether we're willing to give something back.

Thank you.

---

*[END — Approximate runtime: 15 minutes at conversational pace]*

# The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question

### A 15-Minute Conference Talk

---

**[SLIDE: A blank screen. Then, one line of text: `$ git log --all --oneline | wc -l`]**

Let me start with a number.

Four billion.

That's a rough estimate of the number of commits that exist across all public repositories on GitHub today. Four billion discrete acts of someone sitting down, writing something, and saying: *here, take this, it's yours.*

No invoice. No contract. No guarantee of support.

Just: *here.*

That is the foundation everything in this room runs on. Your CI pipeline, your container runtime, your observability stack, your machine learning framework — all of it resting on this enormous, improbable, voluntary act of collective generosity that has been compounding for thirty years.

And here's what keeps me up at night: **we have never figured out how to sustain it.**

---

## Part One: The Sustainability Crisis Nobody Wants to Talk About

We talk a lot in this industry about technical debt. We talk about scalability, about incident response, about developer experience. What we don't talk about enough is the human debt we've accumulated in open source — the weight we've placed on individuals and small communities who never signed up to be critical infrastructure.

Consider this: the average npm package has 1.3 maintainers. The average PyPI package has fewer than two. A significant portion of the internet's security posture depends on people doing this work in their spare time, on nights and weekends, fielding bug reports from Fortune 500 companies who have never sent them so much as a thank-you email.

You remember Log4Shell? The Log4j vulnerability in late 2021 that sent every security team on the planet into emergency mode? The maintainers of that project — a library embedded in thousands of enterprise systems generating billions in revenue — were volunteers. When the crisis hit, they worked around the clock to patch it. One of them, Volkan Yazıcı, tweeted something I think about constantly. He said the library had been developed and maintained by volunteers in their free time, and asked: *"How about donating to the project?"*

The response was largely silence.

This is the paradox at the heart of open source: the more successful a project becomes, the more it is exploited, and often the less its maintainers are compensated for that success. We've built a $500 billion cloud computing industry on top of a volunteer fire department.

The burnout numbers are staggering. A 2021 GitHub survey found that 46% of open source maintainers reported feeling overwhelmed. Projects get abandoned not because the software stopped being useful, but because the human beings behind them ran out of energy, ran out of time, or simply decided their labor deserved better treatment.

And we've seen what happens when that occurs. The left-pad incident. The colors.js sabotage. The xz utils backdoor — where a lone maintainer, exhausted and under social pressure, nearly accepted a malicious contribution that would have compromised SSH servers worldwide. These aren't aberrations. They're symptoms.

We have a structural problem, and we need structural solutions.

The good news is that some of them are starting to emerge. GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective, Tidelift, the Sovereign Tech Fund — these are experiments worth watching and worth supporting. The FOSS Contributor Fund model, where companies allocate a budget for their employees to direct toward open source dependencies, is genuinely promising. Some companies — Shopify, Automattic, Google through its OSPO — are doing meaningful work here.

But these are patches, not architecture. We need to redesign the system.

---

## Part Two: The AI Question

Now let's talk about the thing everyone in this room has an opinion on, and most of us are still figuring out.

Artificial intelligence is changing open source. Full stop. The question is whether it changes it for better or worse — and I think the honest answer right now is: both, simultaneously, in ways we're still untangling.

Let's start with what's real. AI coding assistants are generating an enormous volume of code. Estimates suggest that by the end of 2024, somewhere between 20 and 40 percent of new code being committed in some organizations was AI-assisted. That number is going up, not down. We are entering an era of code abundance.

And here's the first tension: **AI models were trained on open source code.** Billions of lines of it. Code written by the same maintainers who can't pay their rent doing this work. The models ingested that code, learned from it, and are now being used to generate commercial products — without, in most cases, any compensation flowing back to the humans whose creative labor made those models possible.

This is not a hypothetical ethical concern. It is a live legal and moral question that the industry has not resolved. The Copilot litigation is ongoing. The debate about whether AI-generated code constitutes a derivative work is unresolved. We are, once again, building on a foundation before we've checked whether it can bear the weight.

But here's where I want to push back on simple narratives — in both directions.

The argument that AI will kill open source contribution is, I think, overstated. What AI is doing is changing *who* can contribute and *what* kinds of contributions are easy. It is dramatically lowering the barrier to entry for certain kinds of work — writing boilerplate, generating tests, drafting documentation. In the right hands, these are tools that let a solo maintainer punch above their weight class.

I've spoken with maintainers who say AI assistance has made their projects more sustainable, not less. They're reviewing AI-generated PRs that handle the tedious work, freeing them to focus on architecture and community. That's a real benefit.

But there's a darker side, and we need to name it clearly.

AI is also generating a tsunami of low-quality contributions. Maintainers are already reporting a dramatic increase in AI-generated pull requests — PRs that look plausible, pass surface-level inspection, but contain subtle bugs, miss context, or simply restate existing functionality. The *review burden* on maintainers is increasing even as the *apparent* contributor count goes up.

We are, in some projects, creating a situation where AI generates the work and humans pay the cost of evaluating it. That is not sustainability. That is a new form of exploitation wearing a different mask.

And then there is the deeper question: **what happens to the culture of open source when code becomes cheap?**

Open source was never just about the code. It was about learning in public. It was about the graduate student who submits a nervous first patch and gets a thoughtful review that shapes their entire career. It was about the community that forms around shared problems, shared values, shared craft. It was about the README that teaches you something, the issue thread where a hard design question gets debated across three continents.

If we're not careful, we will optimize for code volume and lose the thing that made open source worth defending in the first place.

---

## Part Three: A Vision for the Next Decade

So where do we go from here? I don't have a roadmap — anyone who tells you they do is selling something. But I have a set of principles I believe should guide us.

**First: Treat maintainers like the infrastructure they are.**

If a library is in your dependency tree, it is your infrastructure. Act like it. Fund it. Audit it. Engage with it. The companies in this room that have not yet established an Open Source Program Office, that have not yet created a budget for upstream contribution — that work is overdue. Not as charity. As risk management. As basic engineering hygiene.

The Sovereign Tech Fund model — where governments invest in open source the way they invest in roads and bridges — deserves more attention and more replication. Digital infrastructure is infrastructure. It should be funded like it.

**Second: Build AI policies that give back, not just take.**

If your organization is building products on top of AI models trained on open source code, you have an obligation to contribute back to the ecosystem those models learned from. This means funding. It means contributing engineering time upstream. It means advocating for licensing frameworks that acknowledge the labor that made these models possible.

The open source community needs to be at the table where AI policy is being written — not as an afterthought, but as a primary stakeholder. Organizations like the Open Source Initiative, the Linux Foundation, and the Apache Software Foundation need our support and our voices right now.

**Third: Defend the culture, not just the code.**

We need to make deliberate choices about what we value in open source communities. If we value learning, we need to protect space for imperfect, human contributions. If we value diversity, we need to recognize that AI-generated contributions can mask who is actually in the room. If we value mentorship, we need maintainers who have bandwidth to mentor — which means reducing the review burden, not increasing it.

Some projects are already experimenting with AI-contribution policies. Some require disclosure. Some restrict AI-generated code to specific types of contributions. These are healthy experiments. We should share what we learn from them.

**Fourth: Invest in the next generation of maintainers.**

The average age of a critical open source maintainer is going up, not down. We are not doing enough to bring new people into positions of real responsibility in these projects. Outreachy, Google Summer of Code, and similar programs are valuable — but they need more support, more companies willing to hire their graduates, more senior engineers willing to mentor.

The next decade of open source will be built by people who are, right now, maybe in college, maybe writing their first Python script, maybe reading a README and wondering if they could ever contribute something. Our job is to make sure that path is still open to them. That the door isn't locked by complexity, by gatekeeping, or by a flood of AI-generated noise that makes human contribution feel pointless.

**Finally: Remember what open source is actually for.**

It is not a business model. It is not a talent pipeline. It is not training data.

Open source is a philosophy. It is the radical, still-not-fully-realized idea that knowledge should be shared, that software should be auditable, that the tools we build our world with should belong to the people who use them. That idea is worth protecting. It is worth fighting for. It is worth funding.

---

## Closing

I want to leave you with one thought.

There's a concept in ecology called a keystone species — an organism whose presence is disproportionately important to the health of the entire ecosystem. Remove it, and the system collapses in ways that are hard to predict and harder to reverse.

Open source maintainers are keystone species in our digital ecosystem. And right now, we are watching them disappear under the weight of our collective indifference, while simultaneously flooding their habitat with machine-generated noise.

We can do better. We have done better — every time this community has faced an existential challenge, it has found a way to evolve. From the browser wars to the cloud transition to the mobile revolution, open source has adapted and, ultimately, prevailed.

But adaptation requires intention. It requires people in rooms like this one deciding that the foundation matters — not just what you build on top of it.

So here is my ask, and my closing thought:

**The next commit that changes the world will be written by a human being who believed their work was worth sharing. Our job is to make sure that person still exists.**

Thank you.

---

*[SLIDE: `$ git commit -m "the future is still ours to write"`]*

---

**[END — 15 minutes]**

It was about the README that teaches you something, the issue thread where a hard design question gets debated across three continents.

If we're not careful, we will optimize for code volume and lose the thing that made open source worth defending in the first place.

So that's the landscape: structural underfunding, a new technology that simultaneously helps and exploits the people doing the work, and a culture under pressure. What do we do about it?

## Part Three: A Vision for the Next Decade

I have a set of principles I'd stake my career on. Not a complete roadmap — but a direction. Three things, at three different scales, that I believe have to happen.

Across all three of these levels, we need to make deliberate choices about what we value in open source communities — not just what we produce. And here's the technical problem beneath the ethical one: we don't know what licenses those billions of lines were under. We don't know if they were secure. We're building AI foundations on uninspected fill dirt, and the liability question hasn't been resolved — it's just been deferred. The Copilot litigation is ongoing. Whether AI-generated code constitutes a derivative work is unresolved. We are, once again, building on a foundation before we've checked whether it can bear the weight.

But I want to push back on simple narratives in both directions.

The argument that AI will kill open source contribution is overstated. What AI is doing is changing *who* can contribute and *what* kinds of contributions are easy. It dramatically lowers the barrier to entry for certain kinds of work — writing boilerplate, generating tests, drafting documentation. I've spoken with maintainers who say AI assistance has made their projects more sustainable, not less. They're reviewing AI-generated PRs that handle tedious work, freeing them to focus on architecture and community. That's a real benefit.

Some also predict AI will make open source obsolete entirely — why share a logging library when you can generate one on demand? I think that's wrong. But we need to be able to articulate why, because "it's always worked before" is not an argument.

Here's why it's wrong: **the value of open source was never primarily in the artifact.** It was in the process. It was in the auditability — the ability to inspect what your infrastructure actually does. It was in the collective intelligence that emerges when thousands of people examine the same code from different angles, with different threat models, different use cases, different failure modes. A generated library that no one has read is not open source. It's a black box with a permissive license.

But there's a darker side to the AI question that we need to name directly.

AI is generating a tsunami of low-quality contributions. Maintainers are already reporting dramatic increases in AI-generated pull requests — PRs that look plausible, pass surface-level inspection, but contain subtle bugs, miss context, or simply restate existing functionality. The *review burden* on maintainers is increasing even as the *apparent* contributor count goes up.

We are creating situations where AI generates the work and humans pay the cost of evaluating it. That is not sustainability. That is a new form of extraction wearing a different mask.

And then there's the deeper question — the one that keeps me up more than the economics: **what happens to the culture of open source when code becomes cheap?**

Open source was never just about the code. It was about learning in public. It was about the graduate student who submits a nervous first patch and gets a thoughtful review that shapes their entire career. It was about the community that forms around shared problems and shared craft. It was about the issue thread where a hard design question gets debated across three continents, and everyone comes out understanding something they didn't before.

If we optimize for code volume and ignore that — we will have won the wrong argument.

---

## Part Three: A Vision for the Next Decade

I have principles, not predictions. The future is contingent on choices we haven't made yet. Here's how I think we should make them.

**First: Treat maintainers like the infrastructure they are.**

If a library is in your dependency tree, it is your infrastructure. Act like it. Fund it. Audit it. Engage with it. The companies in this room that have not established an Open Source Program Office, that have not created a budget for upstream contribution — that work is overdue. Not as charity. As risk management. As basic engineering hygiene. The Sovereign Tech Fund model — where governments invest in open source the way they invest in roads and bridges — deserves replication at every level, public and private.

**Second: Build AI policies that give back.**

If your organization is building products on AI models trained on open source code, you have an obligation to the ecosystem those models learned from. Here's a concrete place to start: match your AI tooling spend with direct funding to the projects in your dependency tree. Not proportionally. Not symbolically. Meaningfully. And advocate for licensing frameworks that acknowledge the labor that made these models possible — because the open source community needs to be at the table where AI policy is written, not handed the outcome afterward.

**Third: Defend the culture and the next generation simultaneously.**

We need to make deliberate choices about what we value in open source communities — and then protect the conditions that make those values possible. If we value learning, we need space for imperfect, human contributions. If we value mentorship, we need maintainers who have bandwidth to mentor, which means reducing review burden rather than compounding it with AI-generated noise.

The average age of a critical open source maintainer is going up. We are not doing enough to bring new people into positions of real responsibility. Programs like Outreachy and Google Summer of Code are valuable — but they need more companies willing to hire their graduates, more senior engineers willing to mentor, and more maintainers who have enough breathing room to do that work thoughtfully.

The next decade of open source will be built by people who are, right now, maybe writing their first Python script, maybe reading a README and wondering if they could ever contribute something. Our job is to make sure that path is still open — that it isn't locked by gatekeeping, or buried under a flood of AI-generated noise that makes human contribution feel pointless.

**Finally: Remember what open source is actually for.**

It is not a business model. It is not a talent pipeline. It is not training data.

Open source is a philosophy. It is the radical, still-not-fully-realized idea that knowledge should be shared, that software should be auditable, that the tools we build our world with should belong to the people who use them. That idea is worth protecting. It is worth funding. It is worth fighting for — especially now, when the forces that would reduce it to a resource to be extracted are better organized than they've ever been.

---

## Closing

I want to leave you with one thought.

There's a concept in ecology called a keystone species — an organism whose presence is disproportionately important to the health of the entire ecosystem. Remove it, and the system collapses in ways that are hard to predict and harder to reverse.

Open source maintainers are keystone species in our digital ecosystem. And right now, we are watching them disappear under the weight of our collective indifference — while simultaneously flooding their habitat with machine-generated noise and calling it contribution.

We can do better. We have done better — every time this community has faced an existential challenge, it has found a way to evolve. From the browser wars to the cloud transition, open source has adapted and prevailed. But adaptation requires intention. It requires people in rooms like this one deciding that the foundation matters — not just what you build on top of it.

Four billion commits. The next one matters.

The human who writes it matters more.

**Our job is to make sure that person still exists — and still believes their work is worth sharing.**

Thank you.

---

*[SLIDE: `$ git commit -m "the future is still ours to write"`]*

---

**[END — 15 minutes]**

# The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question

*[Conference talk script — approximately 15 minutes at a measured speaking pace]*

---

## OPENING

Here's a number I want you to sit with for a moment.

**96%.**

That's the percentage of codebases that contain open source components, according to the 2023 Synopsys Open Source Security and Risk Analysis report. Ninety-six percent. If you work in software — and you do, you're here — your work almost certainly runs on a foundation that somebody built for free, maintained in their spare time, and gave to the world without asking for anything in return.

Now here's another number: **$8.8 trillion.**

That's the estimated value of open source software to the global economy. Eight point eight trillion dollars. The GDP of Germany and Japan combined.

And yet, if you go look at the GitHub profile of the person maintaining the library that sits three layers deep in your dependency tree — the one your entire authentication system relies on — there's a decent chance you'll find a pinned post that says something like: *"This project is maintained by one person in their evenings. If you use it in production, please consider sponsoring."*

Those two realities living side by side — the incomprehensible value and the precarious human labor — that tension is what I want to talk about today. Because open source is not just a licensing model. It's one of humanity's most remarkable collaborative experiments. And right now, it's at an inflection point.

---

## PART ONE: THE SUSTAINABILITY PROBLEM IS REAL, AND IT'S GETTING WORSE

Let me be direct: open source has a sustainability crisis, and we have been politely not talking about it for years.

The story we tell ourselves goes something like this: open source is the gift economy of software. Developers contribute because they love it, because it builds their reputation, because it scratches their own itch. Companies use the software, and in return, they contribute back. A virtuous cycle. The commons flourishes.

That story was always partially true. But it was also always partially a convenient fiction — convenient, especially, for companies whose entire business model runs on open source infrastructure while their legal teams carefully ensure they have no obligation to contribute anything back.

The reality is that most open source projects follow what researchers call a **"bus factor of one"** — one maintainer, one human being, who is the single point of failure for software that might be running in thousands of production systems. When that person burns out, gets sick, takes a new job, or simply decides they've given enough — the project goes dark. And sometimes nobody notices until there's a critical CVE and the security advisory goes out and everyone realizes they've been depending on something that hasn't had a commit in three years.

We saw this with Log4Shell. We saw it with the XZ Utils backdoor — where, notably, the attacker's strategy was to *become* the trusted maintainer by offering help to an exhausted solo developer. That's not just a security story. That's a human story about what happens when we ask individuals to carry weight that entire industries should be sharing.

The funding models we've developed — GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective, Tidelift, the various foundation models — are genuinely good. They've helped. But they remain voluntary, opt-in, and structurally insufficient at scale. We've essentially built a cathedral on a foundation of crowdfunding.

And here's what makes this moment different from every previous moment: the demands on open source are accelerating faster than the sustainability models are maturing. Because now we have AI.

---

## PART TWO: THE AI QUESTION

I want to be honest with you about something. When I started preparing this talk, I thought the AI section would be the easy part — the exciting, forward-looking bit. The future stuff. 

But the more I dug in, the more I realized that AI doesn't just add new complexity to open source. It fundamentally challenges some of the assumptions the whole ecosystem is built on.

Let's start with the obvious: AI coding assistants are extraordinary productivity tools. GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude, Gemini — these tools are changing how developers write code. Studies suggest they can increase developer velocity by 20 to 55 percent on certain tasks. That's real. That's significant.

But here's the question nobody has fully answered yet: **What does it mean for a community when the primary unit of participation — the pull request — can be generated in seconds by a machine?**

Open source has always been more than code. It's been a social contract. When you submit a patch, you're entering a conversation. You're saying: I understand this project well enough to improve it. I've read the contributing guidelines. I've thought about the edge cases. I'm accountable for this change. The maintainer reviews it, asks questions, pushes back, approves. A relationship forms. Over time, contributors become reviewers become maintainers. That's how communities reproduce themselves.

Now consider what happens when AI can generate a plausible-looking pull request for any open source project in about forty-five seconds. We're already seeing it. Maintainers are already reporting floods of AI-generated issues and PRs — some helpful, many not, all requiring human attention to triage. The signal-to-noise ratio is collapsing.

There's also the licensing question, which is genuinely unresolved and genuinely important. The models that power these AI coding tools were trained on code. Much of that code was open source. The licenses under which that code was released — MIT, Apache, GPL — were written for a world where humans copy code, not for a world where machines ingest billions of lines and produce statistically related outputs. The legal frameworks haven't caught up. And depending on how courts eventually rule, we may find that the very openness that made open source training data available is now being used to erode the norms that made open source possible.

I'm not saying AI is bad for open source. I'm saying AI is *complicated* for open source, and anyone who gives you a clean, simple answer in either direction is selling something.

---

## PART THREE: A VISION FOR THE NEXT DECADE

So where do we go from here? I want to offer not a prediction, but a provocation — a vision of what open source could look like if we make the right choices in the next ten years.

**First: We need to treat open source infrastructure like public infrastructure.**

Roads don't get built by asking people to volunteer on weekends because they love asphalt. Critical digital infrastructure — the packages, libraries, and tools that underpin the global economy — should not be funded primarily by the goodwill of individuals. 

The EU's Cyber Resilience Act is a start. The White House's open source security initiatives are a start. But we need something more structural: a sustained, coordinated commitment from both governments and large enterprises to fund the maintenance of critical open source components. Not as charity. Not as PR. As the cost of doing business on infrastructure you depend on.

Some companies already do this well. Google, Microsoft, and others have open source program offices with real headcount and real budgets. But this needs to be the norm, not the exception. If your company's revenue depends on open source — and it does, see that 96% figure — then your company has an obligation to invest in its health.

**Second: We need to redesign contribution for the AI age.**

If AI is going to change the nature of contribution, communities need to actively shape what that looks like rather than just reacting to it.

That might mean contribution frameworks that explicitly value non-code work more highly — documentation, mentorship, community moderation, issue triage. These are the things AI cannot genuinely replace, and they're the things that have always been undervalued relative to code.

It might mean new contributor verification systems — not to exclude AI assistance, but to ensure human accountability. When you submit a contribution, you're still the human who is accountable for it. AI is your tool, not your proxy.

It might mean rethinking what "good" open source governance looks like at scale. Some projects are experimenting with AI-assisted triage — using models to help maintainers categorize issues and identify duplicates — which actually *reduces* maintainer burden rather than increasing it. That's the right direction: AI as a force multiplier for human maintainers, not a flood that drowns them.

**Third: We need to protect the social fabric of open source communities.**

This is the one that I think gets least attention, and it's the one I care most about.

Open source communities are not just code repositories. They are places where junior developers become senior developers. Where people from everywhere in the world — different countries, different backgrounds, different economic circumstances — collaborate on equal footing. Where someone in Lagos or Lahore or Lima can contribute to software that runs on servers in London and Los Angeles and their contribution is judged on its merits, not their credentials.

That is genuinely radical. That is one of the most egalitarian structures that exists in the technology industry, and we should fight to preserve it.

The risk in the AI age is that we optimize for output and lose the process. That we get more code, faster, and fewer communities. Fewer relationships. Fewer people who feel the deep ownership and pride of having built something together.

The communities that will thrive in the next decade are the ones that double down on the human elements — on mentorship programs, on welcoming first-time contributors, on documentation written for people not for machines, on codes of conduct enforced with care, on maintainers who see themselves not just as gatekeepers of code quality but as cultivators of human potential.

**Fourth: We need new licensing frameworks for the AI era.**

The open source community gave the world the GPL, the MIT license, the Apache license — legal innovations that shaped how software is shared. We need that same creativity applied to the new questions AI raises.

What does attribution mean when a model has ingested your code? What does copyleft mean when the "derivative work" is a statistical artifact? Organizations like the Open Source Initiative are already grappling with these questions. They need more voices — especially from practitioners, from the people who actually build and maintain open source software, not just the lawyers and the lobbyists.

This is a moment for the open source community to assert its values, not just react to commercial pressures.

---

## CONCLUSION

I started with numbers. Let me end with something harder to quantify.

Open source is, at its core, an act of faith. Faith that if you build something useful and share it openly, others will build on it. Faith that the community will be more than the sum of its parts. Faith that software — this strange, abstract, endlessly malleable thing we spend our lives making — can be a commons, not just a commodity.

That faith has been rewarded, over and over, in ways the early pioneers could never have imagined. Linux running the world's servers. Apache powering the web. Python becoming the lingua franca of science and AI. Kubernetes orchestrating the cloud. All of it built on the accumulated labor of millions of people who chose to share.

The challenges ahead are real. The sustainability gap is real. The AI disruption is real. The licensing uncertainty is real. I'm not asking you to be naive about any of that.

But I am asking you to remember that every hard problem in open source has ultimately been a human problem, and humans have solved it by doing what open source communities have always done: showing up, talking to each other, disagreeing productively, and building something together.

The future of open source will be determined not by the models we train or the licenses we write, but by the choices we make about what we value and who we include.

So here's what I want to leave you with — something you can take back to your teams, your companies, your communities:

**Open source didn't survive this long because it was efficient. It survived because it was meaningful. And in the decade ahead, meaning is exactly what we need to protect.**

Thank you.

---

*[End of talk — Q&A to follow]*
