**(Slide change: An image of a campfire at night. People are sitting around it. It’s warm, inviting, and human.)**

I want to close with this thought.

There is a concept in architecture called the "spandrel." It’s the space between two arches. Originally, it was just a byproduct of building the structure. But over time, artists realized that this empty space was the perfect place to paint, to carve, to create art.

AI is going to automate the arches. It’s going to build the heavy, structural, repetitive parts of coding. It will do the boilerplate. It will do the refactoring.

But that leaves the spandrels. It leaves the spaces in between. That is where we will live.

That is where open source thrives. In the creative, messy, human deliberation of how to build something beautiful together.

We need to stop competing with the machine on speed and volume. We will lose. We need to compete on quality, on trust, and on humanity.

So, here is my challenge to you.

Go back to your companies. Audit your dependencies. Find that library that saves you a thousand hours a year. Find out who maintains it. Send them money. Send them a thank you note. Ask them what they need.

And when you open your next Pull Request, don't just paste what the bot gave you. Read it. Understand it. Own it.

The future of open source isn't written by algorithms. It is written by us. It is written by the people who show up, who care, and who keep the flame lit when the night gets dark.

Let’s make sure that ten years from now, when a new developer raises their hand to say they shipped code, they aren't just thanking a machine. Let’s ensure they are thanking a community that we fought to protect.

Thank you.

**(Blackout. End of talk.)**

ZRR3V7mCMJMsDOYmCfv-g.text:
**Title:** The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question
**Speaker:** [Your Name/Persona]
**Duration:** ~15 Minutes
**Target Audience:** Developers, Engineering Managers, CTOs.

***

**(The stage is dark. A single spotlight hits the center. The speaker walks out, casual but focused. No slides yet. Just the speaker.)**

**Introduction: The Invisible Load**

Good morning.

I want to take you back to a specific date. March 29th, 2024. A Friday.

For most of the world, it was just the start of a weekend. But for us—for the people in this room, for the people watching the commit logs—it was the day the world almost caught fire.

That was the day Andres Freund, a developer at Microsoft, noticed that SSH logins on a Debian system were taking 500 milliseconds longer than usual. Not five seconds. Five hundred milliseconds. Half a heartbeat.

Because of that half-heartbeat, he pulled a thread that unraveled the `xz-utils` backdoor.

We all know the technical details by now. But I don’t want to talk about the code. I want to talk about *why* it happened. It didn’t happen because of a buffer overflow or a zero-day exploit in the traditional sense. It happened because of a tired human being.

It happened because a maintainer, who had been lovingly tending to a thankless, invisible piece of infrastructure for years, was burned out. He was overwhelmed. And when a "helpful" stranger offered to share the load, he said yes.

That is the state of Open Source today.

We have won the war. Open Source is no longer a fringe movement of hobbyists; it is the concrete foundation of the modern world. Every bank, every hospital, every rocket launch, and every social media feed runs on code that was given away for free.

But while we won the war for adoption, we are losing the peace.

We are standing at a fork in the road. To our left, we have the sustainability crisis—the human limits of volunteerism. To our right, we have the rise of Generative AI—a force that promises to write code faster than we can read it.

Today, I want to talk about how these two forces—human burnout and machine acceleration—are colliding. And I want to propose a vision for how we survive it.

**(Lights come up slightly. The first slide appears behind the speaker: A simple line graph showing "Code Volume" skyrocketing while "Maintainer Count" remains flat.)**

**Part 1: The Sustainability Paradox**

Let’s be honest with ourselves. The current social contract of Open Source is broken.

For twenty years, we have operated on a model that I call "The Infinite Free Lunch." Corporations—some worth trillions of dollars—build their empires on top of libraries maintained by a guy in Nebraska named Dave, who works on it on Tuesday nights after his kids go to sleep.

We all know the XKCD comic. We laugh at it because it’s true. But it’s not funny anymore.

The problem isn't just money. If it were just money, we could throw cash at it. The problem is *attention* and *entitlement*.

If you are a maintainer today, you know the feeling. You push a library to GitHub because you solved a problem for yourself. It’s useful. You feel good.

Then, the issues start rolling in.
"Hey, this breaks on Windows 7."
"Hey, when are you adding TypeScript support?"
"Hey, your library caused a security vulnerability in my enterprise app, fix it NOW."

We have confused "Free as in Speech" with "Free as in Labor."

We treat maintainers like unpaid employees. We demand SLAs from volunteers. And when those volunteers burn out, we act surprised when the project is abandoned—or worse, handed over to a bad actor.

This is the Sustainability Paradox: The more successful your open source project becomes, the more likely it is to fail you personally.

We have optimized for *consumption*. `npm install`. `pip install`. `cargo add`. It is frictionless to consume. But it is incredibly high-friction to maintain.

And now, into this fragile ecosystem of overworked humans, we are introducing a new variable. A variable that doesn’t sleep, doesn’t get tired, and can generate a million lines of code in the time it takes Dave in Nebraska to drink his coffee.

**(Slide change: A chaotic, beautiful fractal image generated by AI.)**

**Part 2: The AI Event Horizon**

Let’s talk about the AI question.

I am not here to be a Luddite. I use Copilot. I use ChatGPT. These are incredible tools. But we need to talk about what they do to the *topology* of Open Source.

For decades, the limiting factor in software development was the speed at which a human could think and type. That friction was actually a feature, not a bug. It meant that code was generally read at least once as it was being written. It meant there was intention.

AI removes the friction of creation.

We are about to see a tsunami of synthetic code hitting our repositories. We are already seeing it. Pull requests generated entirely by LLMs, often submitted by people who don't understand what the code does, hoping to farm contribution credits or just "help" without the requisite context.

This creates three massive existential risks for Open Source.

**First: The Pollution of the Commons.**
If Open Source is a garden, AI is an invasive species. It grows fast, it looks like the real plants, but it doesn't have the roots. If a maintainer receives 50 PRs a day, and 45 of them are subtly broken AI-generated code that looks correct at a glance ("LGTM"), the maintainer will drown. The trust model collapses. We shift from a high-trust society to a zero-trust society within our own teams.

**Second: The Junior Developer Gap.**
Open Source has traditionally been the training ground for new engineers. You fix a typo. Then you fix a bug. Then you add a feature. You learn by doing.
If the "easy" code is written by AI, how does the junior developer learn? If we automate away the bottom rung of the ladder, how does anyone climb to the top to become the senior architect who understands *why* the system works? We risk creating a generation of "editors" who can prompt, but cannot build.

**Third, and most dangerously: The Ouroboros Effect.**
LLMs are trained on public code. They are trained on Open Source. They ingest the GPL, the MIT, the Apache licensed code. They mix it up in a statistical blender and spit it out.
But now, we are filling GitHub with AI-generated code. The next generation of models will be trained on code written by the previous generation of models. We risk a feedback loop of mediocrity—a degradation of quality where the unique, brilliant, human spark is averaged out into a beige shade of "statistically probable" syntax.

Furthermore, there is the legal elephant in the room. If an AI generates code based on GPL libraries, and I put that in my proprietary product, have I violated a license? We don’t know yet. And until we do, Open Source is in a state of quantum uncertainty.

**(Slide change: A picture of a barn raising. Old school. People lifting a wooden frame together.)**

**Part 3: A Vision for the Next Decade**

Okay. That’s the doom and gloom. The burnout and the bots.

But I am an optimist. I believe in us. I believe in this community.

So, how do we thrive in the next decade? I believe we need a fundamental shift in how we view Open Source. We need to move from an era of *Creation* to an era of *Curation and Community*.

Here is my three-point plan for the future of Open Source.

**1. Sponsorship as Supply Chain Security.**
We need to stop asking companies for "donations." Charity doesn't scale.
We need to speak the language of business. If you are a CTO, you don't "donate" to AWS to keep the servers on. You pay a bill.
We need to treat Open Source dependencies as part of the supply chain. Companies need to budget for "Dependency Maintenance" just like they budget for cloud costs.
If you use `curl` or `openssl` or `react` to power a billion-dollar product, you should be paying for the maintenance of that infrastructure. Not out of the goodness of your heart, but to ensure that Dave in Nebraska doesn't get tired and hand the keys to a hacker.
We need platforms that make this friction-free. A "tax" on `npm install` for enterprise users that flows directly to maintainers. It’s radical, yes. But the alternative is security collapse.

**2. The Rise of the "Maintainer-Editor."**
In an AI world, the value of *writing* code goes down. The value of *verifying* code goes up.
The maintainer of the future is not necessarily the person who writes every line. They are the Editor-in-Chief. They are the curator of taste, of architecture, and of security.
We need to build tools that help maintainers detect AI-generated spam. We need "Proof of Human" mechanisms in our contribution flows. We need to value the "No."
In the past, a successful project was defined by how many PRs it accepted. In the future, a successful project might be defined by how many it wisely rejects.

**3. Community as the Moat.**
AI can write code. AI cannot build a community.
AI cannot mentor a junior dev. AI cannot mediate a dispute between contributors. AI cannot feel the excitement of a release party.
The projects that will survive are the ones that double down on the *human* element.
If your project is just a code dump, AI will fork it, ingest it, and replace it.
But if your project is a place where people gather, learn, and belong? That is un-copyable.
We need to stop optimizing for "contributions" and start optimizing for "connections." We need to bring back the forums, the IRC feel, the mentorship.

**(The speaker steps forward, the slide fades to black.)**

**Conclusion**

The era of "Open Source" as just "free code" is ending.

We are entering the era of **"Open Sustainability."**

It is an era where we recognize that code is abundant, but human attention is scarce.
It is an era where we realize that you cannot automate trust.

There is a Japanese concept called *Tsukuroi*—repairing broken pottery with gold lacquer. The idea is that the break, and the repair, make the object more beautiful and valuable than it was before.

Our system is broken. The burnout is real. The AI disruption is real.
But if we fill those cracks with gold—if we fund our maintainers, if we mentor our juniors, if we insist on human intention in our code—we will build something stronger than what we had before.

We are the architects of the digital world.
Let’s stop building on sand.
Let’s start building on each other.

Thank you.

**(Blackout.)**

t7rblI3uJmS6Iwk8mYOYi.text:
**Title:** The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question
**Speaker Time:** Approx. 15 Minutes
**Target Audience:** Developers, Engineering Managers, CTOs
**Setting:** Main Stage, Tech Conference

---

**(Stage lights come up. The speaker walks to the center of the stage. Behind them, a massive screen displays a single, high-contrast image: A Jenga tower, impossibly high, swaying slightly.)**

**SPEAKER:**

Good morning.

I want you to think about the last piece of code you shipped. Maybe it was a microservice, a UI component, or a massive data pipeline. Now, mentally strip away the proprietary logic. Strip away your company’s branding. Strip away the specific business rules.

What’s left?

If you are like 99% of the industry, what’s left is about 80% of the codebase. You are left with the foundation. Linux. Kubernetes. React. Python. The unspoken, invisible substrate of the digital world.

We all know the famous XKCD comic. You know the one. The massive, complex digital infrastructure of modern civilization, all resting precariously on a tiny pillar labeled: *"A project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003."*

**(Audience chuckles. Slide changes to the XKCD comic #2347.)**

We laugh because it’s true. But that nervous laughter is the sound of an industry realizing that the social contract of Open Source—the very thing that allowed us to build the modern internet—is fraying.

We are standing at a massive inflection point. We are squeezed between two massive forces. On one side, we have a sustainability crisis of human burnout and supply chain fragility. On the other, we have the tidal wave of Generative AI, which is fundamentally rewriting what it means to write, share, and license code.

Today, I want to talk about how we keep this tower from falling. I want to talk about the future of Open Source not as a repository of free code, but as a community of humans.

**(Slide changes: "Part I: The Sustainability Paradox")**

Let’s start with the human element.

For the last twenty years, we have operated under a specific illusion. We treated Open Source like a natural resource. Like air or water. It was just *there*. If you needed an HTTP client, you `npm install` it. If you needed a logger, you added the dependency.

But Open Source isn't a natural resource. It is a labor resource.

The paradox we face today is that while the *usage* of Open Source has become professionalized, the *production* of it remains largely amateur. And I don’t mean amateur in skill—I mean amateur in the French sense of the word: *amator*, lover. People doing it for the love of the craft.

But love doesn't pay the mortgage. And love certainly doesn't help you when a zero-day vulnerability is discovered in your library at 4:00 PM on a Friday, and you have Fortune 500 companies demanding a patch for a product they have never paid you a dime for.

We saw this with Log4j. We saw this with OpenSSL.

The current model is extractionary. We have trillion-dollar valuations built on the backs of maintainers who are burning out, stepping down, or worse—sabotaging their own code in protest because they feel exploited.

This is the "Maintainer’s Dilemma." If your project is successful, you are punished with more work, more entitlement from users, and more scrutiny, often with zero additional resources.

If we want Open Source to survive the next decade, we have to stop treating it like "Free as in Beer" and start treating it like "Free as in Puppy." It requires care. It requires feeding. It requires a vet.

But just as we are grappling with how to fund and support these humans, a new challenger appears.

**(Slide changes: A striking image of a robot hand painting on a canvas, but the canvas is a computer screen. Title: "Part II: The Synthetic Flood")**

Enter Artificial Intelligence.

In the last two years, the landscape of coding has changed more than in the previous twenty. Tools like GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, and Claude have moved from novelties to daily drivers.

There is a utopian view here. The utopian view says: "AI will lower the barrier to entry. It will help maintainers write tests, generate documentation, and triage bugs. It will be the ultimate force multiplier."

And there is truth to that. I use these tools. You use these tools. They are miraculous.

But we need to have a hard conversation about what Generative AI means for the *ethos* of Open Source.

First, let’s talk about the "Pollution of the Commons."

Maintainers are already reporting a spike in low-quality contributions. We are seeing pull requests generated entirely by LLMs, submitted by users who don’t understand the code they are submitting, simply to farm "contribution points" or Hacktoberfest T-shirts.

This turns the maintainer from a mentor into a garbage collector. It takes seconds to generate a hallucinated fix, and hours for a human expert to debunk it. If the cost of generating code drops to zero, but the cost of reviewing it remains high, we break the economic model of collaboration.

Second, and more dangerously, let’s talk about the Ouroboros—the snake eating its own tail.

These AI models are trained on Open Source code. They are trained on your work. They are trained on GPL, MIT, and Apache licensed code. Yet, the output is often proprietary, or at least, the "ownership" is murky.

We are seeing a dynamic where the collective knowledge of the Open Source community is being vacuumed up, processed, and sold back to us as a subscription service.

If I spend ten years building a library, and an AI ingests it and allows a junior developer to bypass my documentation and my community, and simply generate snippets based on my hard work—without ever engaging with the project—what happens to the community?

Open Source is not just about the code. It is about the *context*. It is about the issues tab. It is about the debate over architecture. It is about the transfer of wisdom from one generation of engineers to the next.

If we replace that interaction with a chat bot, we might gain efficiency, but we risk losing the culture. We risk creating a "Dark Forest" of code where nobody truly understands how the system works because the machine wrote it, and the humans just nodded along.

**(Slide changes: "Part III: The Centaur and the Citizen")**

So, is this the end? Is the tower coming down?

No.

But we have to pivot. We have to change how we operate. The future of Open Source requires a new social contract, built on two pillars: **Sustainable Citizenship** and **Augmented Stewardship**.

Let’s look at the vision for the next ten years.

**First: The Era of Corporate Citizenship.**
To the engineering leaders in this room: The days of passive consumption are over. You cannot build a secure supply chain on charity.

We are seeing the rise of the OSPO—the Open Source Program Office. This needs to become standard. But more than that, we need to normalize "Upstream Engineering."

If your company relies on a library, you should be paying your engineers to contribute back to it *on company time*. Not as a weekend hobby. As part of their sprint. We need to move from "sponsorship" (which feels like a donation) to "procurement." You pay for your cloud provider. You pay for your SaaS tools. You must find a mechanism to pay for your dependencies, either through direct funding or allocated engineering hours.

**Second: Redefining "Contribution" in the Age of AI.**
As AI generates more boilerplate code, the value of *human* judgment skyrockets.

In the future, a "contribution" to Open Source shouldn't just be measured in lines of code. AI can write lines of code. Humans provide *intent*.

We need to value the people who write the architectural RFCs. The people who improve the governance models. The people who curate the datasets. The people who mentor the juniors.

We need to build "Trust Networks." If the public commons becomes flooded with synthetic noise, we will need verified webs of trust—maintainers vouching for contributors. We might see a move toward more "Gated Open Source," where the code is viewable by all, but contribution rights are earned through high-trust human interaction, to protect against bot-flooding.

**Third: The AI as a Steward, not a Creator.**
We need to harness AI to solve the burnout problem, not exacerbate it.

Imagine an Open Source ecosystem where every repository comes with an automated "Steward." An agent that doesn't just write code, but runs the triage.
*   "Hey, this issue looks like a duplicate of Issue #402."
*   "This PR lacks unit tests; here is a suggested test suite based on the project's existing patterns."
*   "This documentation is out of date with the code changes; here is a draft update."

We need to build AI tools that serve the *maintainer*, not just the *consumer*. We need to turn maintainers into "Centaurs"—half human, half AI—capable of managing massive projects without crushing mental load.

**(The speaker pauses. The stage lights dim slightly, focusing on the speaker.)**

**(Slide changes: A photo of a diverse group of people hacking together at a table, laughing. No screens visible, just faces.)**

I want to close with this thought.

Code is ephemeral.

I have been in this industry long enough to see languages rise and fall. I’ve seen frameworks that were supposed to change the world become legacy debt in three years. The code you write today will likely be rewritten by a bot or deprecated in five years.

But the *network of people* is durable.

The magic of Open Source was never really about the software license. The license was just the hack we used to enable the collaboration. The magic was the fact that a kid in Brazil could collaborate with a professor in Germany and an engineer in Silicon Valley to solve a problem that none of them could solve alone.

AI cannot replicate that shared sense of purpose. AI can output syntax, but it cannot output *meaning*.

The future of Open Source depends on us remembering that we are not just building software. We are building a digital civilization.

If we let the sustainability crisis fester, we lose the foundation.
If we let AI hollow out our communities, we lose the soul.

So, here is my challenge to you.

When you go back to your desks on Monday, don't just look at your `package.json` or your `requirements.txt` as a list of files. Look at it as a list of people.

Pick one. Just one.
Send them a thank you.
Sponsor them for five dollars.
Or better yet, convince your boss to let you spend four hours on Friday fixing a bug in *their* repo, not yours.

The future of Open Source isn't written by algorithms. It’s written by us. Let’s make sure it’s a future we actually want to live in.

Thank you.

**(Blackout. Applause.)**

y_c1jxTHitJm4vFfaQRIe.text:
**Title:** The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question
**Speaker:** [Your Name]
**Time:** ~15 Minutes
**Setting:** A large stage at a major tech conference. A massive screen behind the speaker.

---

**(00:00) INTRODUCTION: THE INVISIBLE FOUNDATION**

**(The stage is dark. A single spotlight hits the speaker. The screen behind is black.)**

**SPEAKER:**
Raise your hand if you pushed code to production this week.

**(Wait for hands.)**

Keep your hands up. Now, keep your hand up only if you personally wrote every single line of code in that deployment. I’m talking about the libraries, the frameworks, the runtime, the compiler, the kernel it runs on.

**(All hands will go down. Smile.)**

Exactly.

**(Lights come up fully. Screen displays a massive, complex dependency graph—a galaxy of dots and lines.)**

We live in the era of the "Digital Commons." We don’t build software anymore; we assemble it. We stand on the shoulders of giants, but more often, we stand on the shoulders of a guy named "Dave" in Nebraska who has been maintaining a critical XML parser since 2003 as a hobby.

For thirty years, the Open Source Definition has been our constitution. It promised us that if we shared our work, the world would be better. It promised that many eyes would make all bugs shallow. It promised a meritocracy of ideas.

And it worked. Open Source won. It is the default setting for human innovation.

But today, that victory feels pyrrhic. The ecosystem is showing cracks. The social contract—code for reputation, contribution for community—is fraying. And now, a new, synthetic force has entered the chat, threatening to upend the very definition of authorship.

Today, I want to talk about the three things that will define the next decade of our industry: The sustainability crisis of the humans who build our code, the disruption of Artificial Intelligence, and the new social contract we must write to survive them both.

**(00:03) PART 1: THE SUSTAINABILITY CRISIS**

**(Screen changes to an image of a crumbling Roman aqueduct.)**

Let’s start with the elephant in the room: Sustainability. And I don’t mean "Green IT." I mean human sustainability.

We have built a trillion-dollar global economy on the backs of volunteers.

For a long time, we treated Open Source like a natural resource—like air or sunlight. It was just *there*. Corporations extracted value, built proprietary empires on top of MIT and Apache licenses, and gave back... occasionally. Maybe a patch here, a conference sponsorship there.

But the math has stopped working.

We are seeing an epidemic of maintainer burnout. We see supply chain attacks—not because the code is bad, but because the maintainer was tired, overworked, and handed the keys to a bad actor just to get some relief. We saw it with `event-stream`. We saw the chaos of `log4j`.

The problem isn’t that we lack funding platforms. GitHub Sponsors and Open Collective exist. The problem is the asymmetry of scale.

When a Fortune 500 company builds a product on an open-source library, they aren't just using code; they are outsourcing their R&D, their security, and their maintenance to people who do not work for them.

**(Walk to the edge of the stage.)**

I talked to a maintainer recently—someone whose library is downloaded 50 million times a week. He told me, "I don't feel like a community leader anymore. I feel like unpaid support staff for the richest companies on earth."

This is the "extraction economy." If we treat Open Source as a free buffet, eventually the kitchen closes. If we don’t figure out how to fund the *maintenance*—not just the innovation, but the boring, unsexy work of keeping the lights on—the aqueduct crumbles.

But just as we were grappling with this human resource crisis, the game changed completely.

**(00:07) PART 2: THE AI QUESTION**

**(Screen goes black. Then, slowly, code begins to type itself across the screen at superhuman speed.)**

Enter the Generative AI. Copilot. ChatGPT. Llama.

This is the single greatest disruption to software engineering since the compiler. And for Open Source, it is an existential paradox.

Let’s look at the training data. These Large Language Models were trained on *us*. They were trained on the billions of lines of code we pushed to public repositories. They ingested the GPL, the MIT, the Apache 2.0.

And now, they regurgitate that logic, stripped of its license, stripped of its context, and stripped of its attribution.

**(Pause for effect.)**

This creates a massive legal and ethical gray area. If I write code under a copyleft license, intending it to remain free forever, and an AI launders that logic into a proprietary codebase for a bank... have we broken the license? Legally? Maybe not yet. Ethically? That’s the question.

But the threat goes deeper than licensing. It goes to the heart of "Community."

Open Source has always been about the *conversation*. You open a Pull Request. You get feedback. You iterate. A senior dev teaches a junior dev why that loop is inefficient. Relationships are formed. Trust is built.

What happens when the Pull Request comes from a bot?

What happens when the internet is flooded with AI-generated code that *looks* correct but contains subtle hallucinations? We are already seeing maintainers overwhelmed by "drive-by" contributions generated by AI—low-quality code spam that takes human energy to review and reject.

We risk turning Open Source into a garbage patch of synthetic noise.

Furthermore, if the AI does the coding, does the "Open Source" label even matter? In the past, we demanded access to the source code so we could study it, learn from it, and modify it. But if in five years we are all just prompting a black box to generate binaries, the "source" becomes irrelevant. The "prompt" becomes the source.

If the machine writes the code, the human connection—the very soul of the Open Source movement—is severed.

**(00:11) PART 3: THE VISION FOR THE NEXT DECADE**

**(Screen changes to an image of a hybrid landscape: Cybernetic roots intertwining with an organic tree.)**

So, is this the end? Is Open Source dead?

Absolutely not. But it must evolve. We need to move from "Open Source" to "Open Governance" and "Trusted Source."

Here is my vision for the next decade.

**First: A New Economic Model.**
We must move beyond the "tip jar" economy. We need to normalize the idea of "Upstream Tithing." Engineering leaders in this room: It should be a line item in your budget. If you use a library for commercial gain, you pay for it. Not as a charity, but as a supply chain insurance policy.

We will see the rise of "FOSS Foundations" acting as unions for projects, negotiating support contracts collectively, so individual maintainers aren't fighting alone.

**Second: provenance becomes the new Gold Standard.**
In a world of AI-generated content, *authenticity* is the premium asset. We will see a shift where "Signed by a Human" becomes a badge of quality.

Open Source communities will transform into "Trust Networks." The value won't just be the code—the AI can generate code. The value will be the *curation*. The value will be the rigorous, human-led review process that certifies: "This code is safe. This code is ethical. This code works."

We will stop being just code factories and start being code curators.

**Third: We must Open Source the AI.**
We cannot allow the future of software to be dictated by three or four closed-source models owned by mega-corporations. We need truly Open Source AI—open weights, open training data, open infrastructure.

If the AI is the new compiler, then the AI must be free. Otherwise, we are just tenant farmers on someone else's land.

**(00:13) CONCLUSION**

**(The screen turns white. A single word appears: HUMAN.)**

I want to leave you with this.

Technologists often make the mistake of thinking Open Source is about software. It never was.

Open Source is a sociology experiment. It is a philosophy about how humans collaborate to solve problems that are too big for any one person to solve alone.

AI can generate syntax. It can optimize algorithms. It can write unit tests. But AI cannot care.

AI cannot feel the frustration of a user and stay up until 3:00 AM fixing a bug because it’s the *right thing to do*. AI cannot mentor a student in Nigeria and help them land their first job. AI cannot build a community.

The future of Open Source isn't about competing with the machines on speed. It’s about doubling down on what the machines can’t do: Trust. Governance. And Connection.

So, to the developers and leaders in this room:

Don’t just consume. Contribute.
Don’t just prompt. Understand.
And don’t let the fire of community burn out.

Because in an age of artificial intelligence, being authentically, messily, collaboratively human is the most disruptive thing you can be.

Thank you.

**(Mic drop. Applause.)**

Denis wrote that he was broke. He was facing legal issues. He was burned out. He asked for help.

And the internet responded.

But it didn’t respond with money. It didn’t respond with support. It responded with hatred. People called him greedy. They told him that if he didn’t like it, he should stop coding. They told him that "open source" means "free," and that he owed them his labor.

**(Slide change: An image of the famous XKCD comic "Dependency"—the small block supporting the massive structure.)**

We all know this comic. We laugh at it because it’s true. But lately, the laughter has become a little nervous.

We are gathered here today because we love open source. It is the engine of the modern world. It is the Library of Alexandria of our time. But the social contract that built this library is fraying. And just as the foundation is cracking, a new weight has been dropped on top of the structure: Artificial Intelligence.

Today, I want to talk about the intersection of these three things: The sustainability crisis, the AI disruption, and the human community that holds it all together. I want to talk about how we survive the next decade.

**(Slide change: Title Slide - "The Future of Open Source")**

### Part 1: The Sustainability Crisis

Let’s start with the elephant in the room. The current model of open source is economically broken.

For thirty years, we have operated on a philosophy that conflated "Free as in Speech" with "Free as in Beer." And for a long time, that worked. It worked because the stakes were lower, and the complexity was manageable.

But today, we have trillion-dollar valuations built entirely on the backs of volunteer maintainers who are working nights and weekends.

We call this "Open Source," but an economist would call it "Extractivism."

Large corporations have become incredibly efficient at strip-mining the commons. They ingest open source code, wrap it in proprietary SaaS, and sell it back to the ecosystem without contributing upstream.

This has led to what I call the **"Maintainer’s Dilemma."**

If you are successful, you are punished. If your project becomes critical infrastructure, your inbox fills with demands. You get CVE reports at 3:00 AM. You get angry GitHub issues from developers at Fortune 500 companies demanding to know why you haven't fixed a bug that blocks their quarterly release.

And what do you get in return? A shiny GitHub badge? Maybe a T-shirt?

**(Slide change: Logos of Redis, Terraform/HashiCorp, Elastic, MongoDB with a question mark over them.)**

We are seeing the consequences of this right now. Look at the licensing wars. Redis, Terraform, Elastic, Mongo. One by one, companies that started as open source stewards are moving to "Source Available" or restrictive licenses.

The internet reacted with outrage, calling it a "rug pull." But we have to look at the cause. These companies looked at the landscape and realized: *We cannot compete with the cloud providers who are reselling our own code better than we can.*

If we do not solve the sustainability problem—if we do not find a way to pay for the plumbing of the internet—open source will cease to be a community and will simply become a "loss leader" marketing strategy for big tech.

### Part 2: The AI Question

But while we were worrying about funding, the ground shifted beneath our feet.

**(Slide change: A visualization of a Neural Network merging with a Git commit graph.)**

Enter Generative AI. Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude.

AI represents the greatest existential question open source has ever faced. And it cuts two ways: it is both a threat to the *spirit* of open source, and a threat to the *quality* of open source.

First, the spirit.

Open Source is built on a gift economy. I give you my code, you give me your patch. We learn from each other.

Generative AI models have scraped the entire history of open source—every license, every "do not use" warning, every GPL header—and ingested it into a black box. They have privatized the commons.

When an AI writes a function for you, it is laundering the intellectual property of thousands of open source developers, stripping away the attribution, and serving it up as a paid product.

This creates an **"Ouroboros Effect."** The snake eating its own tail.

If we stop writing open source because AI does it for us, what will the next version of AI train on? We risk polluting the well. We are already seeing the flood of AI-generated pull requests—low quality, hallucinated logic, spamming maintainers who are already on the brink of burnout.

But there is a deeper, more subtle danger.

**(Slide change: A photo of a junior developer looking confused at a screen.)**

Open source has traditionally been the apprenticeship model of our industry. You learn by reading code. You learn by submitting a PR, getting rejected, fixing it, and trying again.

If a junior developer relies entirely on AI to write code, they bypass the struggle. They bypass the understanding. They become "operators" rather than "authors."

If AI writes the code, who maintains it when it breaks? Who understands the architecture deep enough to refactor it?

If we aren't careful, the future of open source isn't a vibrant community of creators; it’s a wasteland of auto-generated boilerplate that no human actually understands, maintained by tired volunteers trying to clean up the mess left by bots.

### Part 3: A Vision for the Future

**(Slide change: A bright, clean image of a futuristic, collaborative workspace. Hopeful imagery.)**

I know. That sounds dystopian. But it doesn't have to be.

We are at an inflection point. We get to choose what the next decade looks like. I believe we can build a Golden Age of Open Source, but it requires us to renegotiate the social contract.

Here is my vision for how we thrive.

**First: We must normalize paying for code.**

We need to move from "Donation" to "Taxation." Not government taxes, but dependency taxes.

If you are an engineering leader in this room, look at your budget. You probably have a line item for AWS, for Slack, for Jira. Do you have a line item for the Open Source Collective? Do you have a line item for GitHub Sponsors?

We need to build tooling that automatically routes a fraction of our cloud spend back to the dependency tree. If your company relies on `curl`, or `openssl`, or `react`, you should be paying for it as a utility bill. It is not charity; it is supply chain security.

**Second: We must redefine the role of the Maintainer in the age of AI.**

We should not fear AI; we should weaponize it for the maintainer.

Imagine a future where AI doesn't just spam you with code. Imagine an AI agent, trained on *your* project’s specific style guide, that triages issues for you. An agent that attempts to reproduce bugs before you ever see them. An agent that updates your documentation automatically when you change an API.

We need to shift the maintainer's role from "Code Janitor" to "Architect and Editor."

AI can generate the bricks, but humans must draw the blueprints. The value of a human developer in 2030 will not be syntax; it will be *taste*. It will be judgment. It will be the ability to look at AI-generated output and say, "This works, but it is bad design."

**Third: We must protect the "Community of Practice."**

We need to carve out spaces where humans still write code for the joy of it. We need to encourage "Slow Code."

We must mentor junior developers not just on how to prompt a model, but on how to read the source. We need to treat open source contributions not as a way to "fix a bug," but as a way to connect with another human being.

**(Slide change: The word "Trust" on a black background.)**

Because ultimately, Open Source is not about software. It is about Trust.

You don't use Linux because it’s free. You use it because you trust the thousands of eyes that have looked at it. You trust the process.

AI cannot replicate trust. An LLM cannot sit on a panel and discuss the ethics of a feature. An LLM cannot promise you that it will be there in five years to patch a security vulnerability.

Only people can do that.

### Conclusion

**(The speaker steps forward. The screen goes dark.)**

We are standing on the edge of a new era. The days of the "hobbyist hacker" powering the global economy for free are over. That model is dead.

We can let it collapse into a corporate-controlled, AI-generated landscape where software is a black box that no one owns and no one understands.

Or, we can build something better.

We can build an ecosystem where maintainers are paid like the critical infrastructure engineers they are.

We can build a world where AI is a tool that serves us, rather than replacing us.

We can build a community that values the *human* connection behind the pull request.

The code of the future might be written by machines. But the *purpose* of the software—the soul of the software—must remain human.

So, when you go back to your desks on Monday, I have one request. Don’t just `npm install`. Look at the names in that `package.json`.

Those are people. Support them. Fund them. Thank them.

Because without them, the screen just goes black.

**(Slide change: A single command prompt blinking. `_`)**

Thank you.

**(Applause)**

**Title:** The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question

---

**(The stage lights dim. The screen displays a single, stark image: A photo of a modern skyscraper under construction, its steel skeleton exposed against the sky. The speaker walks to center stage, pauses, and looks at the audience.)**

**SPEAKER:**

Good morning.

I want you to think about the last piece of code you shipped. Maybe it was a microservice, a UI component, or a simple script to automate a backup. Now, I want you to mentally strip away every single library, framework, and dependency you didn’t write yourself.

Gone is React. Gone is Kubernetes. Gone is Linux. Gone are the compilers.

What are you left with?

**(Pause)**

Silence. A blank text editor.

We like to call ourselves "architects" and "engineers." But the truth is, we are standing on the shoulders of giants who are currently very tired, very underfunded, and increasingly, very worried about the future.

We are living through the golden age of software. But beneath the shiny surface of our trillion-dollar industry lies a paradox. The digital infrastructure that powers the global economy—banking, healthcare, defense, social media—relies on a commons that is maintained by a surprisingly small group of volunteers, hobbyists, and under-resourced teams.

And right now, that commons is facing a dual threat. On one side, we have the cracking foundation of human burnout and sustainability. On the other, we have the rising tide of Artificial Intelligence, which promises to revolutionize how we code, but threatens to dismantle the very community that makes open source possible.

Today, I want to talk about that intersection. I want to talk about how we keep the lights on without burning out the humans, and how we survive the age of the machine.

**(Slide change: The famous XKCD comic #2347 "Dependency", showing a complex structure held up by a tiny piece labeled "Project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003.")**

Let’s start with the elephant in the room: Sustainability.

We all know this comic. We laughed when we first saw it because it was funny. We stopped laughing when the Log4j vulnerability hit, and we realized it was a documentary.

For the last twenty years, the open source social contract was simple: *"I give you code; you give me nothing, but maybe I get reputation, or I solve my own problem, and that’s enough."*

That worked when open source was a fringe movement. It does not work when open source is the supply chain of the modern world.

We have created a system of extraction. Trillion-dollar corporations build proprietary empires on top of MIT and Apache-licensed code, often without contributing a cent back to the maintainers. We have "free riders" on an industrial scale.

But the currency of open source isn’t just money; it’s attention and mental health.

I want you to picture a maintainer. Let’s call her Sarah. Sarah wrote a JSON parser five years ago. It’s fast, it’s reliable, and it’s now used by 40% of the Fortune 500. Sarah has a day job. She has a family. She has a life.

But every morning, Sarah wakes up to GitHub notifications. Not "thank yous." But demands.
*"This broke in version 2.1."*
*"When is the patch coming?"*
*"Why don't you support this edge case?"*

Sarah is maintaining critical global infrastructure for free, during her nights and weekends, while being yelled at by strangers who are paid six figures to use her work.

This is not sustainable. We are seeing a mass exodus of maintainers who are simply... done. They are archiving their repos. They are changing licenses. In some extreme cases, they are sabotaging their own code in protest.

If we do not fix the economic and emotional model of open source, the foundation will crumble. We cannot rely on the "passion" of volunteers to secure the banking systems of the future. Passion burns out. Mortgages do not.

**(Slide change: A visualization of a neural network overlaying a wall of code. The text reads: "THE AI QUESTION.")**

And just as we are grappling with this human crisis, a new variable enters the equation.

AI. Generative Large Language Models. Copilot. ChatGPT.

We have to talk about the impact of AI on open source, and we have to be honest about it. It is complicated.

On one hand, AI is a miracle for productivity. It can write boilerplate, generate tests, and explain complex legacy code. For a lonely maintainer like Sarah, an AI assistant could be the difference between burnout and survival. It can help triage issues, summarize pull requests, and draft documentation.

But there is a darker side to this coin, and it touches on the very soul of the open source philosophy.

Open source is built on the concept of "Copyleft" and attribution. It is a gift economy. I give you my code, you acknowledge my contribution, and the cycle continues.

LLMs, as they stand today, break that cycle. They have been trained on petabytes of open source code—*our* code. They have ingested the GPL, the MIT, and the Apache codebases. And now, they regurgitate that logic without attribution, stripped of its license, repackaged as a commercial service.

Some call it "fair use." Others call it "license laundering."

Regardless of where you stand legally, the cultural impact is undeniable. If a junior developer prompts an AI to write a function, and that AI pulls from a training set built on open source work, but no one ever visits the repo, no one stars the project, and no one joins the community... does the community survive?

We are risking a future where the "Open Source Community" is replaced by the "AI Oracle."

Furthermore, we are facing a pollution problem. Maintainers are already reporting a flood of low-quality, AI-generated Pull Requests. People are using bots to spam repos with "fixes" to farm contribution points. The noise-to-signal ratio is exploding.

So, we have a burnout crisis, and now we have a machine that might cannibalize the ecosystem to train itself, while flooding us with synthetic code.

**(Slide change: A photo of a diverse group of people sitting in a circle, laptops open, talking. The text reads: "THE PATH FORWARD.")**

It sounds bleak. I know. But I am not here to be a doomer. I am here because I believe in the resilience of this culture. Open source has survived Microsoft calling it a cancer. It survived the dot-com crash. It will survive AI.

But we have to adapt. We need a new vision for the next decade.

Here is what that vision looks like. It stands on three pillars.

**Pillar One: The Economic Pivot.**

We must move beyond the "tip jar" model of funding. GitHub Sponsors is nice, but it won’t pay a mortgage for most. We need to normalize the idea that *using* open source in a commercial product implies a financial responsibility.

We are seeing the rise of "Supply Chain Security" contracts. Companies shouldn't just pay for features; they should pay for insurance. If you use a library in production, you should be paying a subscription to a foundation or a collective that ensures that library is maintained, audited, and secure. We need to treat open source dependencies like we treat cloud providers: essential infrastructure that appears on the budget sheet.

**Pillar Two: AI as a Steward, not a Replacement.**

We need to aggressively integrate AI into the *maintenance* side of open source, not just the *creation* side.

Imagine a future where, when you open a Pull Request, an open-source-tuned LLM automatically reviews it for style, checks for security vulnerabilities, and summarizes the changes for the human maintainer. Imagine AI that automatically updates documentation when code changes.

We need to build tools that amplify the human maintainer, allowing one person to do the work of ten, not by writing more code, but by managing the community more effectively. We must master the machine, or it will master us.

**Pillar Three: The Return to Community.**

This is the most important one. AI can generate code, but it cannot generate *context*. It cannot generate *mentorship*. It cannot generate *trust*.

The future of open source isn't just about dumping code onto GitHub. It’s about the human connections that happen around that code.

We need to value the "soft skills" of open source—triaging, debating architecture, mentoring new contributors—higher than the raw code itself. The AI can write the function. Only a human can decide *why* that function should exist and how it fits into the larger system.

We need to build "High-Trust" communities. If the internet is flooded with synthetic, AI-generated noise, then the verified, human-curated open source repository becomes the premium product. The "Human-Verified" badge will be the mark of quality in the AI age.

**(Slide change: A black screen with white text: "CODE IS PERISHABLE. COMMUNITY IS NOT.")**

**SPEAKER:**

We are at an inflection point. The era of "free code from nowhere" is ending.

We are moving into an era where open source must be professionalized, funded, and protected.

To the engineering leaders in this room: Look at your dependency tree. Pick the top five libraries that would sink your company if they vanished. Go find out who maintains them. Ask them what they need. Don't send them a t-shirt. Send them a contract. Hire them to work on their own projects.

To the developers: Use AI. It’s a powerful tool. But do not let it sever your connection to the source. Read the code it generates. Understand it. And when you can, go back to the repo it learned from and contribute back.

The machine can predict the next token. It can predict the next line of code.

But it cannot predict the future. That is up to us.

Open source is not a license. It is not a repository. Open source is a fragile, beautiful, defiant agreement between humans to build something greater than themselves.

Let’s make sure that ten years from now, when the next generation of developers opens a text editor, they aren’t just staring at a blinking cursor and a chatbot. Let's ensure they are stepping into a vibrant, funded, human community that is ready to help them build the world.

Thank you.

**(The speaker nods. The screen fades to black. Applause.)**

Down one path is a future where open source becomes a barren wasteland—a depleted mine of training data, abandoned by burned-out maintainers, polluted by AI spam, and dominated by proprietary models that take everything and give nothing back.

Down the other path is a future where open source matures. A future where corporations pay their fair share for the infrastructure they use. Where AI is harnessed to protect and empower maintainers rather than overwhelm them. And where communities thrive because they realize that human connection is their ultimate competitive advantage.

We did not win the software revolution because our compilers were faster. We won it because we shared. We won it because we believed that a rising tide lifts all boats, and that technology is at its best when it belongs to everyone. 

Let us not lose that spirit to the machines we built or the balance sheets we serve. 

Because at the end of the day, code is cheap. Context is expensive. But community—community is priceless. 

Thank you.

Let’s start with a hard truth: Open source won the software war. But the victory is incredibly fragile. 

For the last twenty years, the narrative of open source has been a triumphant underdog story. It was the hackers against the suits. The cathedral versus the bazaar. And the bazaar won. Today, open source is no longer a radical counter-culture; it is the default supply chain of the global digital economy. Over ninety percent of commercial applications contain open-source components. Trillion-dollar market caps are built on top of free, community-maintained code.

But here is the disconnect: While the *consumption* of open source is heavily funded, institutionalized, and corporate, the *production* of open source remains largely decentralized, underfunded, and reliant on volunteer labor. 

We have built sprawling corporate mansions on top of infrastructure we refuse to budget for. 

When we talk about the "sustainability crisis," it’s easy to just say "companies don't pay maintainers." But as engineering leaders, we need to understand the specific failure modes of this ecosystem. There are three primary ways this foundation cracks:

**Number one: The Bus Factor and Succession.** A critical package relies on one or two maintainers. They get a new job, have a kid, or simply lose interest. There is no handoff path, no succession planning, and the project quietly decays until it breaks a million builds.

**Number two: Support Overload.** Issue trackers have transformed from collaborative workspaces into hostile customer support queues. Maintainers are drowning in unpaid triage.

**Number three: The Security Burden.** Vulnerability disclosure, patching, backports, and the CVE process—this is grueling, high-stress work. And crucially, this work scales with *corporate adoption*, not with *contributor count*. 

A recent survey showed that over fifty percent of maintainers are completely unpaid, and of those who *do* receive funding, the median income from their open-source work is often less than a thousand dollars a year. Yet they secure trillions in market cap. It is a human ecosystem, and right now, the humans are exhausted.

But just as this sustainability crisis is reaching a boiling point, a massive new variable has entered the equation, multiplying the strain. 

Let’s talk about the AI question.

Over the past two years, generative AI has fundamentally altered the mechanics of writing software. Tools like GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, and Claude have transformed from novelties into indispensable daily drivers. 

Let me be clear: AI is a developer superpower. And it has the potential to be a massive boon for open source. If guided correctly, AI can help newcomers write better documentation, generate reproduction steps for bugs, and easily scaffold test suites. It lowers the barrier to entry.

But for the open-source *maintainer*, AI introduces two massive, systemic problems.

**The first is the Trust and Verification Problem.** 
AI makes it exponentially faster to write code, but it also makes it exponentially faster to generate technical debt. We are already seeing open-source repositories flooded with AI-generated pull requests. Not all of them are bad! But the core issue is the review-time asymmetry. 

If it takes an AI three seconds to generate a complex pull request, but it takes a human maintainer thirty minutes to properly verify it, test it, and ensure it doesn’t introduce subtle logic bugs, the math of open source breaks down. Code generation is cheap; confidence is expensive. Think back to the "Hacktoberfest" disaster a few years ago, where thousands of low-effort PRs overwhelmed maintainers. AI has the potential to make every single day Hacktoberfest. It creates a massive verification bottleneck.

**The second is the Provenance and Licensing Problem.**
The large language models that write our code today were trained on the collective, historical output of the open-source community. Millions of developers shared their code freely under the social contract that knowledge should be open. While the legal and ethical complexities of training on public data are still being debated in the courts, the practical reality for engineering leaders is a question of provenance: *Where did this code come from, and what license obligations might it carry?*

Furthermore, there is an existential risk to the community lifecycle. If a junior developer uses AI to instantly solve a problem instead of searching a project’s documentation or asking questions in a forum, do they ever learn the culture of that project? Do they ever become a contributor, and eventually, a maintainer? 

If we are not careful, AI threatens to turn a vibrant, collaborative community into a mere dataset—a static library of "ground truth" used only to train the next generation of proprietary machines.

So, where do we go from here? If the current model is unsustainable, and the trust pipeline is being strained by AI, how do we forge a path forward?

The next decade of open source requires a radical reimagining of how we fund, maintain, and interact with open code. We must move from a model of extraction to a model of symbiosis. Open source must be treated as maintained infrastructure, not accidental philanthropy.

Here is what that vision looks like, and what you can do about it on Monday morning.

**First, we must redefine corporate responsibility through pragmatic frameworks.** 
Funding open source can no longer be viewed as a charitable donation or a marketing expense. It is a critical infrastructure cost. If you are an engineering leader in this room, you do not think twice about paying your AWS bill. You do not think twice about paying for Datadog, or Jira. 

You need to start paying your open-source bill. 

How? By tiering your dependencies. Monday morning, start an audit. Identify your Tier 0 dependencies—the existential projects where, if they break, your business is offline. Identify your Tier 1 critical projects. You need to actively fund your Tier 0 and Tier 1 projects. 

But it’s not just about throwing money over the wall. It’s about allocating engineering time. Establish Open Source Program Offices (OSPOs)—not just to manage your own license compliance, but to set targets and incentives for your engineers to spend time contributing upstream to the projects you rely on. Participate in initiatives like the OpenSSF to help secure the broader supply chain.

**Second, we must flip the AI dynamic and build project-level mitigations.** 
Right now, AI is a tool for *contributors*, which is overwhelming the *maintainers*. We need to build and deploy AI tooling specifically designed to be the maintainer’s shield. 

Imagine an open-source ecosystem where AI acts as a triage nurse for issue trackers. Every new issue gets an auto-reproduction attempt and environment capture. Every pull request gets an AI-generated risk summary and blast-radius analysis before a human ever reviews it. 

At the project level, maintainers and organizations need to establish clear guardrails. Require PR templates with reproduction steps. Add strict CI gates that require minimal test coverage for acceptance. Consider adopting contributor attestations or signed commits to solve the provenance problem. We must use AI to automate the drudgery, reducing the cognitive load so maintainers can focus on what humans do best: architecture and governance.

**Which brings me to my third and most important point: We must re-center the human element.**

In a world where code can be generated for free by machines, the value of *just writing code* will plummet. The commodity of the future is not the code itself; it is the context, the trust, and the community around that code.

An AI can write a function, but an AI cannot decide the strategic direction of a framework. An AI cannot mentor a first-time contributor from an underrepresented background. An AI cannot mediate a heated debate over API design, and an AI cannot build the deep, human trust required to maintain a piece of software that runs the global banking system.

The open-source projects that survive the next decade will be the ones that lean into their humanity. 

We are standing at a crossroads. 

Down one path is a future where open source becomes a depleted mine of training data, abandoned by burned-out maintainers, overwhelmed by a verification bottleneck, and dominated by proprietary models that take everything and give nothing back.

Down the other path is a future where open source matures. A future where corporations pay their fair share for the infrastructure they use. Where AI is harnessed to protect and empower maintainers. And where communities thrive because they realize that human connection is their ultimate competitive advantage.

Look around this room. The people who will decide which path we take are sitting right here. 

For the developers in the audience: I challenge you to make one small upstream contribution a month. A test, a doc fix, a triage pass on a dependency you use every day. 

For the engineering managers and CTOs: Monday morning, pick your top ten critical dependencies, sponsor them, and assign upstream engineering time to them. Measure the reduction in your own security response times when you actively support the maintainers keeping you safe.

We did not win the software revolution because our compilers were faster. We won it because we shared. We won it because we believed that a rising tide lifts all boats, and that technology is at its best when it belongs to everyone. 

If open source vanished tomorrow, our companies would stop. So let’s stop treating it like it’s free.

Let us not lose our collaborative spirit to the machines we built or the balance sheets we serve. Because at the end of the day, code is cheap. Context is expensive. But community—community is priceless. 

Thank you. 

**(The speaker nods, taking in the applause, and walks off stage.)**

Let us not lose that spirit to the machines we built or the balance sheets we serve. 

Because at the end of the day, code is cheap. 
Context is expensive. 
But community—community is priceless. 

Thank you.

That is where we are. And today, I want to talk about what we are going to do about it. 

I want to talk about the foundation upon which every single one of our companies is built. I want to talk about open source. Specifically, I want to address the slow-motion collapse of the infrastructure we built our careers on, the incoming tsunami of AI-generated code, and the choices we must make today to ensure that the open-source ecosystem survives—and thrives—in the next decade.

Let’s start with a hard truth, and a moment of honesty. Every single one of us in this room has built a feature, shipped a product, or hit a quarterly OKR using code we didn't write, from a project we never funded, under a license we probably didn't read. I have. You have. 

We act this way because open source won the software war. But the victory is incredibly fragile. 

For the last twenty years, the narrative of open source has been a triumphant underdog story. It was the hackers against the suits. The cathedral versus the bazaar. But let's look at where we are now: the bazaar won, and then the cathedral bought the bazaar—just look at Microsoft and GitHub. Today, open source is no longer a radical counter-culture; it is the default supply chain of the global digital economy. Over ninety percent of commercial applications contain open-source components. Trillion-dollar market caps are built entirely on top of free, community-maintained code.

But here is the disconnect: While the *consumption* of open source is heavily funded, institutionalized, and corporate, the *production* of open source remains largely decentralized, underfunded, and reliant on volunteer labor. 

We have built sprawling corporate mansions on top of a foundation we refuse to pay for. And the cracks are showing.

This is the sustainability crisis. We are experiencing a profound tragedy of the commons. We saw it with Heartbleed. We saw it with Log4j. When the Log4j vulnerability hit, it was a global emergency. Cybersecurity teams at Fortune 500 companies worked around the clock. The Pentagon was scrambling. Apple, Amazon, and Google were exposed.

A handful of unpaid maintainers working on their weekends, getting yelled at on GitHub by highly paid engineers demanding immediate patches for a product they never paid a dime for. The emotional toll on maintainers is staggering. Issue trackers have transformed from collaborative workspaces into hostile customer support queues. Maintainers are burning out, stepping away, or simply archiving their repositories. 

Now, the picture isn't uniformly dire. We do have models that work. The Linux Foundation and the Apache Software Foundation have built robust, institutional backing for massive projects. Projects like curl have achieved incredible longevity through dedicated, sponsored maintainership. 

But these successes have not scaled to cover the full ecosystem. They protect the massive, load-bearing pillars, but they do nothing for the millions of tiny, critical dependencies—the single-maintainer libraries that hold the rest of the web together. 

Why? Because we are trapped in a massive collective action problem. Corporations are full of rational actors. The cost of *not* funding a tiny dependency is diffuse and delayed, while the cost of *funding* it is immediate and visible on a quarterly balance sheet. So, the infrastructure becomes brittle. A disproportionate share of our critical systems is maintained by a dangerously small number of people, concentrated in specific geographic and demographic clusters. Tools like GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, and Claude have transformed from novelties into indispensable daily drivers. They lower the barrier to entry, automate boilerplate, and can translate complex logic between languages in seconds. 

The optimists will tell you that AI is the ultimate democratizing force. They argue it lowers the barrier to entry, allowing anyone to write code. They point out—correctly—that AI is already helping maintainers by auto-generating changelogs, summarizing chaotic issue threads, and drafting documentation. And they might be right—for contributors. 

The problem is that the contribution pipeline was never the bottleneck. The bottleneck has always been review, maintenance, and governance. And AI, so far, is making that bottleneck exponentially worse.

For a developer, AI is a superpower. But for an open-source maintainer, AI is a double-edged sword swinging directly toward their necks. AI makes it exponentially faster to write code, but it also makes it exponentially faster to generate technical debt.

Tech giants scraped that code, trained proprietary models on it, and are now selling the ability to generate code back to us.

This threatens to break the very lifecycle of open-source contribution. If junior developers use AI to instantly solve a problem instead of searching Stack Overflow, reading a project’s documentation, or asking questions in a forum, they bypass the culture of the project entirely. They never transition from passive consumers to active contributors, and eventually, to maintainers. If we are not careful, we risk turning a vibrant, collaborative community into a mere dataset—a static library of "ground truth" used only to train the next generation of proprietary machines.

So, where do we go from here? If the current model is unsustainable, and AI is accelerating the strain, how do we forge a path forward?

I believe the next decade of open source will require a radical reimagining of how we fund, maintain, and interact with open code. We must move from a model of *extraction* to a model of *symbiosis*. 

Here is what that vision looks like.

**First, we must redefine corporate responsibility.** 

Funding open source can no longer be viewed as a charitable donation or a marketing expense. It must be categorized as a critical infrastructure cost. 

If you are an engineering leader in this room, you know that telling your CFO to "fund open source because it's the right thing to do" will get you nowhere. You need a different vocabulary. You need to frame this as *supply chain risk management*. Most companies have absolutely no idea how many critical dependencies they rely on that are maintained by a single person with no succession plan. When you audit your dependency tree and find those vulnerabilities, you aren't asking for a charity budget; you are mitigating catastrophic operational risk. 

You need to start paying your open-source bill. Whether that’s through GitHub Sponsors, the Linux Foundation, Open Collective, or direct grants. But it’s not just about throwing money over the wall. It’s about allocating engineering time. It means establishing Open Source Program Offices (OSPOs)—not just as legal hurdles to manage license compliance, but as strategic hubs that mandate a percentage of your engineers' time is spent contributing upstream to the projects you rely on.

**Second, we must flip the AI dynamic.** 

Right now, AI is a tool for *contributors*, which is overwhelming the *maintainers*. We need to build and deploy AI tooling specifically designed to be the maintainer’s shield. 

Imagine an open-source ecosystem where AI acts as a triage nurse for issue trackers—automatically categorizing bugs, reproducing errors, and filtering out synthetic spam before a human ever sees it. Imagine AI agents that run continuous security audits on pull requests, explaining the potential blast radius of a change in plain English to the maintainer. 

We need to use AI to reduce the cognitive load of maintaining software, automating the drudgery so that maintainers can focus on what humans do best: architecture, governance, and community building.

**Which brings me to my third and most important point: We must re-center the human element.**

In a world where code can be generated for free by machines, the value of *just writing code* will plummet. The commodity of the future is not the code itself; it is the context, the trust, and the community around that code.

An AI can write a function, but an AI cannot decide the strategic direction of a framework. An AI cannot mentor a first-time contributor from an underrepresented background. An AI cannot mediate a heated debate over API design, and an AI cannot build the deep, human trust required to maintain a piece of software that runs the global banking system.

The open-source projects that survive the next decade will be the ones that lean into their humanity. They will prioritize clear governance, inclusive cultures, and mentorship. They will recognize that their greatest asset is not their codebase, but their people.

In version control, when a project forks, both paths represent possible futures. Right now, the open-source ecosystem is forking. And unlike a git branch, we cannot simply merge these two futures back together later.

Down one branch is a future where open source becomes a barren wasteland—a depleted mine of training data, abandoned by burned-out maintainers, polluted by AI spam, and dominated by proprietary models that take everything and give nothing back.

Down the other branch is a future where open source matures. A future where corporations treat dependencies as critical supply chains and pay their fair share. Where AI is harnessed to protect and empower maintainers rather than overwhelm them. And where communities thrive because they realize that human connection is their ultimate competitive advantage.

Look around this room. The people who will decide which branch becomes the main line are sitting right here. You are the developers opening the pull requests. You are the engineering managers allocating the budgets. You are the CTOs setting the strategic direction.

We did not win the software revolution because our compilers were faster. We won it because we shared. We won it because we believed that a rising tide lifts all boats, and that technology is at its best when it belongs to everyone. 

Let us not lose that spirit to the machines we built or the balance sheets we serve. 

Because at the end of the day, code is cheap. Context is expensive. But community—community is priceless. 

Thank you. 

**(The speaker nods, taking in the applause, and walks off stage.)**
