**Time:** 15 Minutes
**Estimated Word Count:** ~2,000 words

***

**(Stage direction: The speaker walks to the center of the stage. The lighting is warm but focused. No slides yet. Just a microphone and a conversational, yet urgent, demeanor.)**

I want to start with a statement that might surprise you.

The biggest threat to Open Source today isn’t Microsoft. It isn’t Oracle. It isn’t a hostile takeover or a proprietary competitor.

The biggest threat to Open Source is our own success.

Let me prove it to you with a quick experiment. Don’t raise your hands; just do this mentally.

Think about the application you deployed most recently. Or the backend service that kept your coffee hot and your data flowing this morning.

Now, strip away the open source code.

Remove the Linux kernel. Remove the SSL libraries. Remove the web servers, the container runtimes, the logging frameworks, and the database drivers. Remove React, remove TensorFlow, remove the dependency trees that stretch down into the earth like roots.

What is left?

If you are honest with yourself, the answer is usually: nothing. A blank screen. A blinking cursor.

But it’s not just a blank screen. That blank screen represents about $20 trillion in global market value evaporating. It represents hospital systems going offline, global banking halting, and the power grid shutting down.

We live in an era where the digital equivalent of a skyscraper is built on a foundation of magic. And that magic is Open Source. But today, I want to talk about why that magic is fragile. I want to talk about the silent crisis threatening the foundation we stand on, the tidal wave of AI that is reshaping how we build, and ultimately, how we save the soul of software development.

My name is [Name], and this is "The Future of Open Source."

***

**(Stage direction: The first slide appears behind the speaker. It’s a simple, stark graph showing a steep upward trend in software usage, contrasted with a flatline in maintainer contribution. The title: "The Collapse of the Commons.")**

Let’s start with the elephant in the room: Sustainability.

For twenty years, we’ve operated on a "gift economy" model. Developers write code because they love it, because they need a specific feature, or because they want status. Companies use this code because it’s free—as in free beer. They build billion-dollar valuations on top of software maintained by a single person working from their home office on a Tuesday night.

This worked when the stakes were low. If the `left-pad` package went down in 2016, it was a nuisance. It broke a few builds, we laughed, we patched it, we moved on.

But the stakes are no longer low.

Today, open source runs the power grid. It processes medical records. It moves trillions of dollars in financial transactions. We have moved open source from "hobbyist projects" to "critical infrastructure," but our funding models have remained stuck in the hobbyist era.

We are seeing a phenomenon I call "The Collapse of the Commons." The usage of these projects is exponential, but the number of active maintainers is linear—or in many cases, declining.

I remember a weekend last year. I was supposed to be hiking with my kids. Instead, I spent 48 hours frantically patching a security vulnerability in a library my company relied on—a library maintained by one person who had announced they were stepping back due to burnout. I wasn't paid for that weekend. I was doing it to save my production environment.

We are asking individuals to perform the labor of multinational corporations. We are asking them to be architects, security auditors, legal counsel, and community managers, all for the price of a few GitHub stars.

Consider this: The OpenSSL project, which secures roughly two-thirds of the entire web server market, was for years operating on less than $2,000 in annual donations. We are trusting the encryption of the internet to a budget that wouldn’t cover a coffee bill for a mid-sized engineering team.

Burnout is no longer just an emotional crisis; it is a silent security vulnerability in our supply chain. If we treat open source maintenance as a charity, we will eventually run out of volunteers. And when the volunteers leave, the infrastructure rots.

***

**(Stage direction: Slide change. An image of a robot hand typing on a keyboard, but the keyboard is dissolving into digital sand. Text overlay: "The AI Question.")**

So, we have a problem with sustainability. And just as we start to grapple with that, a meteor hits the planet.

That meteor is Artificial Intelligence.

There is a fear circulating in our community right now. A fear that AI will make programmers obsolete. That if a machine can generate a function in seconds, the need for public, collaborative code repositories will disappear.

I don’t believe that. But I do believe we are standing on the precipice of the largest shift in how code is created since the invention of the compiler. AI presents a double-edged sword that cuts deeper than most people realize.

Let’s look at the sharp edge first.

AI models are trained on our work. They are trained on every line of code pushed to GitHub, every Stack Overflow answer, every documentation page. Open source code is the fuel for the AI revolution.

The tension here is palpable. We have permissive licenses like MIT and Apache that were designed for humans to share code with humans. They were not written for machines to ingest code, learn the patterns of the authors, and then regurgitate that knowledge to sell as a proprietary service.

We are seeing a new form of "strip-mining." Giant tech corporations are training their models on the open source ecosystem—built by you and me—and then selling the output back to us behind a paywall.

Here is a concrete example: When GitHub Copilot suggests a code snippet that is clearly derived from a GPL-licensed library, who owns that output? Does the viral nature of the GPL apply to the AI's generation? We are building legal grey areas at the speed of light.

If AI companies consume the commons without replenishing it, they kill the very thing they feed on. We risk a future where the "open" in open source is just a training dataset for closed-source products.

But here is the other side of the sword. The hopeful side.

AI has the potential to solve the security vulnerability I mentioned earlier—the burnout problem.

Imagine a world where the tedious parts of maintenance are automated. Imagine an AI that can triage bug reports, automatically generate unit tests for edge cases, and even write documentation—something we all notoriously hate doing.

The promise of AI is not that it replaces the maintainer; it’s that it acts as a force multiplier. It gives a single maintainer the leverage of a team of ten. It handles the drudgery so the human can focus on the architecture, the vision, and the community health.

But this requires a shift in how we view the code. We are moving from being "writers" of code to being "editors" and "curators." And that changes the nature of the open source community.

***

**(Stage direction: Slide change. A diagram showing a diverse network of nodes, glowing and connecting. Some nodes are labeled with human faces, others with neural network icons. Title: "The New Community.")**

This brings us to the heart of the talk: Community.

For a long time, the open source community was defined by the "Commit." The prestige was in the lines of code you wrote. You were a core contributor if you had the green squares on your GitHub profile.

In an AI-driven world, the "Commit" matters less. The AI can write the function. The AI can write the test. The AI can even refactor the class.

So, what is left for us?

What is left is *intent*.

The AI doesn't care about the user. It doesn't care about the ethical implications of the code, or the inclusivity of the language used in the documentation, or the long-term roadmap of the project. It only cares about the next token.

The future of open source community is going to be defined by human connection. It’s going to be about stewardship.

We need to evolve from a community of "coders" to a community of "architects" and "shepherds."

In the next decade, the most successful open source projects won't be the ones with the most commits. They will be the ones with the strongest governance. We are already seeing this with projects like PostgreSQL or the Rust Foundation, which have robust community governance structures that outlast any single contributor.

We need to explore new models of collaboration. Consider the rise of DAOs—Decentralized Autonomous Organizations. Imagine a future where open source projects are funded not by donations, but by smart contracts that automatically pay maintainers whenever the software is used in production. It’s a radical shift, but it might be the necessary economic layer to save the commons.

In an AI world, code becomes a commodity. *Trust* becomes the currency.

If I download a library today, I trust it because I know who wrote it, or because the community around it is active and vigilant. In a world flooded with AI-generated code—some of which might be hallucinated or insecure—community reputation becomes the single most valuable asset we have.

We need to lower the barrier to entry for non-coders. We need to value the people who write the documentation, the people who manage the forums, the people who design the logos, and the people who organize the conferences.

***

**(Stage direction: Slide change. A stark, bold graphic. Title: "The Path Forward." Three vertical pillars rise up as the speaker speaks.)**

So, where do we go from here? How do we navigate the intersection of the sustainability crisis and the AI revolution?

I propose a three-part vision for the next decade of Open Source.

**First, we must professionalize the maintenance of critical infrastructure.**

We can no longer rely on the "gift economy" for the software that runs the world. This means a shift from "donations" to "sponsorships."

Companies that profit from open source must treat it as a line item in their supply chain budget, just like they treat electricity or server hosting.

I’m calling for a specific goal: By 2030, the top 100 critical infrastructure projects should have full-time, funded maintainers.

We are seeing the start of this with "Open Source Funds," but we need to go further. We need standardized ways to fund projects. Imagine a "Netflix" model for open source libraries—a subscription fee that your company pays to ensure the health of the top 50 packages in your dependency tree.

If you are an engineering leader here in the room: Go back to your office on Monday. Look at your `package-lock` or `go.mod` file. Find the top ten libraries you use. If you aren't paying for them, you are outsourcing your risk to a volunteer. Fix that.

**Second, we need a new social contract for AI.**

We need to establish norms where AI training acknowledges the source. We need to push for models that are "open source" themselves—transparent about how they were trained, and ideally, open source in their weights.

We should advocate for a "reciprocal license" for AI. If an AI model learns from our code, it should ideally contribute back to that ecosystem. We need to ensure that the AI tools we use to build our software are as open as the software we are building.

Don't let the AI layer become the new proprietary stack. We must insist on the right to repair, the right to inspect, and the right to modify the models that generate our code.

**Third, we must double down on "Human-Centric" open source.**

As AI makes code generation cheap, the value of human judgment goes up.

We need to build communities that prioritize mentorship over optimization. We need to focus on "Documentation-Driven Development" because if the AI is going to help us, the AI needs to understand *why* we are building something, not just *how*.

The future of open source isn't a lonely genius hacking in a basement. The future is a collaborative ecosystem where humans set the direction, and AI handles the implementation. The humans provide the soul; the machines provide the muscle.

***

**(Stage direction: The lights dim slightly. The speaker walks closer to the edge of the stage. The final slide is simply the word "Stewardship.")**

I want to leave you with a final thought.

Remember that blank screen we started with at the beginning of this talk? That void where the digital world used to be.

We are standing on the edge of that void. On one side is the collapse of the commons—the burnout, the lack of funding, the security vulnerabilities. On the other side is a future where AI strips the value out of our work and leaves us with nothing but walled gardens.

But I believe there is a third way.

I believe that as code becomes easier to generate, the *importance* of the code we choose to keep becomes greater.

Open source is not just a production methodology. It is a statement about how we want to live in a digital society. It is the belief that knowledge should be shared, that transparency is safer than secrecy, and that we are smarter together than we are alone.

The challenges of sustainability and the disruption of AI are not the death knell of open source. They are the growing pains. They are the transition from a hobbyist movement to a professional, global public utility.

The future is open. But it will only remain open if we fight for it.

It requires you to pay for the tools you use.
It requires you to train the AI on your terms.
And it requires you to remember that in a world of artificial intelligence, the human connection is the only thing that cannot be automated.

Go back to work on Monday. Look at your dependencies. Look at your communities. And don't just be a consumer. Be a steward.

Thank you.

**(Stage direction: Speaker nods, smiles warmly, and walks off stage as the screen fades to black.)**

We have a handful of mega-corporations—worth trillions of dollars—built entirely on top of free, volunteer-maintained infrastructure. Amazon, Google, Meta—they consume open source like oxygen. It is the substrate of their cloud services. But the exchange is asymmetric.

We have a situation where a single maintainer of a critical logging library is supporting the traffic of the entire Fortune 500, working in their spare time, while the companies profiting from that work treat it as a tax-free infinite resource.

You know that seal means a human being looked at the diff. You know that a human being debated the memory allocation strategy. You choose the seal. We need to shift the prestige of open source from "who has the most stars" to "who has the best stewardship."

The AI can write the `for` loop. The AI can write the boilerplate. The AI can write the unit tests. But the AI cannot care.

The AI can optimize. The AI can compile. But the AI cannot care. Care is a human resource, and it is currently depleted.

The code is open. The choice is yours.

Thank you.

**(Applause. Speaker nods, smiles, and exits.)**

**Title:** The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question
**Speaker:** [Your Name]
**Time:** 15 Minutes
**Setting:** A main stage at a major tech conference. The lights are dimmed, a single spotlight hits the center stage.

---

**(The speaker walks to the center of the stage. They don’t start with a "Hello." They start with a command.)**

**Speaker:**
Type `npm install`.

Go ahead. Mouth it if you want. Or just think about that muscle memory you have. You open your terminal, you type that command, and you summon the collective work of thousands of strangers into your project.

Now, raise your hand if you know exactly who wrote the last library you imported. Raise your hand if you know who paid their rent, or if they were paid at all.

I see a few hands. Mostly, I see uncertainty.

We live in a miracle age of software. We are building cathedrals of code on top of a foundation that we assume is solid bedrock. The sheer acceleration of technological progress in the last decade is staggering. But today, I want to talk to you about the cracks in that bedrock. I want to talk about the three forces that are colliding right now: the economic fragility of our ecosystem, the existential disruption of Artificial Intelligence, and the one thing that might actually save us: you.

I’m calling this talk: "The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question."

**(Slide change: A black and white photo of a tired person at a keyboard, late at night. A coffee cup sits precariously near the edge.)**

Let’s start with the uncomfortable truth: The economic model of open source is broken.

We like to tell ourselves a story. We like to say that Open Source is a meritocracy where the best code wins, and developers contribute because they love to code. And that’s partially true. It is a meritocracy of passion. But passion doesn’t pay the mortgage. Passion doesn’t put food on the table.

We have created a "Tragedy of the Commons" in digital form. A handful of mega-corporations—worth trillions of dollars—are built entirely on top of free, volunteer-maintained infrastructure. Amazon, Google, Meta—they consume open source like oxygen. It is the substrate of their cloud services. It is the invisible mortar holding the brickwork of the internet together.

But the exchange is asymmetric. We have a situation where a single maintainer of a critical logging library is supporting the traffic of the entire Fortune 500, working in their spare time, while the companies profiting from that work treat it as a tax-free infinite resource.

We saw the cracks widen with the Log4j incident. We saw it again, more recently, with the XZ Utils backdoor attempt. Did you follow that story?

For those who missed it: A lone maintainer of a compression utility, burned out, under pressure, and perhaps a bit too lonely, was manipulated by a sophisticated attacker using social engineering to introduce a backdoor. We were days away from a potential catastrophic compromise of SSH servers across the internet.

That wasn’t a technical failure. It was a human failure. It was a failure of sustainability. When one person is carrying the weight of the world’s digital infrastructure, they become a single point of failure. When they burn out, we all burn out.

And let's be clear: burnout isn't just about being tired. It's about the erosion of spirit. It is the realization that you are working a second job, for free, for people who view your labor as a line item in a spreadsheet they don't even have to pay. This model is not just unfair; it is unsustainable. We are consuming the seed corn because we are too hungry to plant for the next season.

**(Slide change: A graph showing the meteoric rise of "AI" search trends overlapping with the steady, slower growth of "Open Source.")**

Now, enter the AI elephant in the room.

Just when we were trying to figure out how to pay maintainers, Generative AI arrived and completely changed the physics of the internet.

Yes, these tools are incredible levers for productivity today. They write boilerplate faster than we can think. They autocomplete our thoughts. But we must ask: at what cost to the source material?

Suddenly, we have GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude, and a dozen other tools that can write code faster than any human. And where did these AIs learn to write code? They learned from us. They were trained on GitHub.

This creates a paradox. Open source is the fuel for the AI revolution. The permissive licenses—MIT, Apache 2.0—that allowed us to share code freely also allowed tech giants to scrape that code, train multi-billion dollar models on it, and sell the output back to us as a subscription.

We are effectively strip-mining the public commons to build private walled gardens.

But this brings us to the messy, legal, and ethical question: What is AI-generated code?

If I ask an AI to write a Python script, and it produces code that looks suspiciously like a function I wrote five years ago and put on GitHub under an MIT license... do I own that? Does the AI own that? Does the user own that?

And more importantly for the sustainability question: If AI is trained on open source, but the AI itself is closed source... is that fair use? Or is that the greatest act of "open washing" in history?

We are seeing a shift where the value of code is being decoupled from the creation of code. The AI aggregates the value of millions of commits, distills it, and sells it. The original contributors—the humans who wrote the bugs, fixed the bugs, and documented the edge cases—see zero return on that investment.

**(Slide change: A graphic showing a "Feedback Loop." Open Source -> AI Training -> AI Code -> Dilution of Open Source.)**

Here is the danger I see: The "Gray Goo" scenario.

Imagine a future where 90% of new code is AI-generated. That code is pushed back to GitHub. It’s buggy. It’s hallucinatory. It’s full of subtle security vulnerabilities that only look correct because they statistically resemble correct code. Then, the next generation of AI is trained on *that* code.

We are creating a feedback loop of mediocrity. We risk polluting the very reservoirs of knowledge we rely on. If open source becomes a dumping ground for auto-generated sludge, the value of "open source" as a badge of quality evaporates.

And for maintainers, this is a nightmare. They are already drowning in pull requests and issues. Now imagine being a maintainer and receiving a hundred PRs a day from bots, each one slightly wrong, each one requiring you to debug the AI’s homework. It will drive the last of our maintainers into the private sector or out of the industry entirely.

So, that’s the grim reality. We have an economic model that doesn't pay, and a new technology that extracts value without permission. It feels like a perfect storm.

**(Slide change: A bright, stark white slide with the word: "EVOLVE.")**

But I didn’t come here to bury open source. I came here to talk about how we save it.

The future is not about fighting AI. The future is not about demanding Microsoft pay every maintainer a million dollars—though that would be nice. The future is about evolving our social contract. We need to move from a passive consumption model to an active stewardship model.

Here is my vision for the next decade of Open Source.

**Number One: We must move from Charity to Structural Support.**

We need to stop relying on the "donation button" model. It is undignified and it doesn't work. It creates a power dynamic where the maintainer is a beggar and the corporation is the benefactor. That needs to flip.

Engineering leaders in this room: you need to change how you buy. When you procure software, do you ask about the open source supply chain? Do you require that your vendors contribute back to the dependencies they use?

We need to normalize "Support Contracts." Not for features, but for existence. If your company depends on a library with two maintainers, you should have a contract to pay those two maintainers to keep the lights on. It’s risk management. It’s insurance. You are paying for the guarantee that when a critical vulnerability is found, someone will be there to fix it.

We need to treat open source maintenance not as a hobby, but as critical infrastructure. Just as we pay for electricity and bandwidth, we must pay for the software that binds our systems together.

**Number Two: The Rise of "Human-Centric" Standards.**

In an age of AI, the scarcest resource is not compute. It is human intent and verification.

We need a new tier of open source projects. A tier that certifies "Human Maintained." A badge that says, "This code is reviewed, curated, and stewarded by actual people who understand the trade-offs."

This will become a premium brand. Just as we buy "organic" or "fair trade" food because we care about the supply chain, enterprises will eventually pay for "Human Verified" code because they won't trust the black-box hallucinations of a model to run their banking systems.

We need to shift the prestige of open source from "who has the most stars" to "who has the best stewardship." We need to value the boring work: documentation, security auditing, and triage. These are things AI struggles to do with empathy and context.

**Number Three: A New Licensing Paradigm.**

We need to fix the legal asymmetry of AI.

We are seeing the emergence of licenses like the "Functional Source License" or specific AI-use clauses that say, "You can use this code to build apps, but you cannot use this code to train a model that competes with me."

This is controversial. The Free Software Foundation will tell you this isn't "open." They will argue that restrictions violate the four freedoms. But I think we need to be pragmatic. If the definition of "open" allows a trillion-dollar company to extract all value and give nothing back, the definition is broken. We need licenses that protect the commons from being strip-mined by algorithms.

This doesn't mean closing the source. It means closing the loop on value extraction. If you profit from the commons, you must contribute back to the commons.

**(Slide change: A photo of a diverse group of people sitting around a table, laughing, with laptops open.)**

And finally, the most important part: Community.

The AI can write the `for` loop. The AI can write the boilerplate. The AI can write the unit tests. But the AI cannot care.

The AI cannot mentor a junior developer at 2 AM when they’re stuck on a deployment error. The AI cannot debate the philosophy of software architecture with empathy. The AI cannot look at a feature request and say, "No, that’s going to hurt our users in the long run," because the AI has no long term.

The future of open source is not the code. The code is just the artifact. The future is the connection between people.

We need to rebuild the social infrastructure of our communities. We need to make our communities welcoming, not just for the code, but for the humans. We need to lower the barrier to entry for new contributors so they aren't just submitting typo fixes, but are learning how to be stewards.

The AI is a tool. It is a lever. If we use it right, it frees the maintainers from the drudgery of bug fixing so they can focus on governance, vision, and mentorship.

Imagine a world where a maintainer uses an AI agent to triage 500 issues automatically, leaving them with mental energy to actually guide the roadmap. That is the promise. That is the utopia. But we only get there if we own the tool, rather than letting the tool own us.

**(Speaker walks to the edge of the stage, speaking directly to the front row. The tone softens, becomes personal.)**

So, I ask you again. You are going to go back to your desks. You’re going to open your terminals. You’re going to type `npm install` or `cargo build`.

When you do that, I want you to think about the people on the other side of that wire.

**If you are a leader, this is your mandate:** Go find the top five dependencies your company relies on. Find the maintainers. Give them money. Give them time. Treat that contribution as risk management, not charity. Build a relationship with them. Ensure that the foundation you are building upon is stable.

**If you are a developer, this is your imperative:** Don’t just be a consumer. Be a contributor. Not just with code, but with empathy. Review a PR. Answer a question. Help someone who is struggling where you once struggled. Be the human connection that the AI cannot replace.

We are standing at a crossroads. One path leads to a wasteland of auto-generated code, maintained by bots, devoid of soul, fragile and brittle. The other path leads to a renaissance. A future where AI handles the syntax, and we handle the meaning. A future where open source is sustainable, where maintainers are valued, and where technology serves humanity, not the other way around.

Open source won the war for how we build software. Now, we have to win the peace for how we sustain it.

The code is open. But the future? The future is up to us to write.

Thank you.

**(Applause. Speaker nods, smiles, and exits.)**

And more importantly for the sustainability question: If AI is trained on open source, but the AI itself is closed source... is that fair use? Or is that the greatest act of "open washing" in history? Courts are deciding this right now, but we cannot wait for judges to save us.

**(Slide change: A graphic showing a "Feedback Loop." Open Source -> AI Training -> AI Code -> Dilution of Open Source.)**

Here is the danger I see: The "Gray Goo" scenario.

For those who aren't sci-fi nerds: Gray Goo is a hypothetical end-of-the-world scenario where self-replicating nanobots consume all matter on Earth, turning everything into sludge.

Imagine a digital version of that. Imagine a future where 90% of new code is AI-generated. That code is pushed back to GitHub. It’s buggy. It’s hallucinatory. It’s full of subtle security vulnerabilities that look correct but aren't. Then, the next generation of AI is trained on *that* code.

We are creating a feedback loop of mediocrity. We risk polluting the very reservoirs of knowledge we rely on. If open source becomes a dumping ground for auto-generated sludge, the value of "open source" as a badge of quality evaporates.

And for maintainers, this is a nightmare. They are already drowning in pull requests. Now imagine being a maintainer and receiving a hundred PRs a day from bots, each one slightly wrong, each one requiring you to debug the AI’s homework. It will drive the last of our maintainers into the private sector or out of the industry entirely.

So, that’s the grim reality. We have an economic model that doesn't pay, and a new technology that extracts value without permission. We are staring into the abyss.

But I’ve seen enough of the abyss. Let me tell you how we step back from the edge.

**(Slide change: A slide showing a simple diagram: Money flowing from Corporate User -> Maintainer, bypassing the "Tragedy of the Commons" box.)**

The future is not about fighting AI. The future is not about demanding Microsoft pay every maintainer a million dollars—though that would be nice. The future is about evolving our social contract.

Here is my vision for the next decade of Open Source.

**Number One: We must move from Charity to Structural Support.**

Engineering leaders in this room: you need to change how you buy. When you procure software, do you ask about the open source supply chain? Do you require that your vendors contribute back to the dependencies they use?

We need to normalize "Support Contracts." Not for features, but for existence. If your company depends on a library with two maintainers, you should have a contract to pay those two maintainers to keep the lights on. It’s risk management. It’s insurance.

And we won't be doing this alone. Regulators in Brussels and Washington are about to make software liability real. The EU Cyber Resilience Act and NIS2 Directive are shifting the landscape. When "free as in beer" becomes "free as in lawsuit," those support contracts I mentioned? They'll become mandatory. We need to shape that transition, not resist it.

**Number Two: The Rise of "Human-Centric" Standards.**

In an age of AI, the scarcest resource is not compute. It is human intent and verification.

We need a new tier of open source projects. A tier that certifies "Human Maintained." A badge that says, "This code is reviewed, curated, and stewarded by actual people who understand the trade-offs."

This will become a premium brand. Just as we buy "organic" or "fair trade" food because we care about the supply chain, enterprises will eventually pay for "Human Verified" code because they won't trust the black-box hallucinations of a model to run their banking systems.

We need to shift the prestige of open source from "who has the most stars" to "who has the best stewardship."

**Number Three: A New Licensing Paradigm.**

We need to fix the legal asymmetry of AI.

We are seeing the emergence of licenses like the "Functional Source License" or specific AI-use clauses that say, "You can use this code to build apps, but you cannot use this code to train a model that competes with me."

This is controversial. The Free Software Foundation will tell you this isn't "open." But I think we need to be pragmatic. If the definition of "open" allows a trillion-dollar company to extract all value and give nothing back, the definition is broken. We need licenses that protect the commons from being strip-mined by algorithms.

**(Slide change: A photo of a real community event—a sprint room full of diverse developers collaborating, screens glowing.)**

And finally, the most important part: Community.

The AI can write the `for` loop. The AI can write the boilerplate. The AI can write the unit tests. But the AI cannot care.

The AI cannot mentor a junior developer at 2 AM when they’re stuck on a deployment error. The AI cannot debate the philosophy of software architecture with empathy. The AI cannot look at a feature request and say, "No, that’s going to hurt our users in the long run," because the AI has no long term.

The future of open source is not the code. The code is just the artifact. The future is the connection between people.

We need to rebuild the social infrastructure of our communities. We need to make our communities welcoming, not just for the code, but for the humans. We need to lower the barrier to entry for new contributors so they aren't just submitting typo fixes, but are learning how to be stewards.

The AI is a tool. It is a lever. If we use it right, it frees the maintainers from the drudgery of bug fixing so they can focus on governance, vision, and mentorship.

Imagine a world where a maintainer uses an AI agent to triage 500 issues automatically, leaving them with mental energy to actually guide the roadmap. That is the promise. That is the utopia. But we only get there if we own the tool, rather than letting the tool own us.

**(Speaker walks to the edge of the stage, speaking directly to the front row.)**

So, I ask you again. You are going to go back to your desks. You’re going to open your terminals. You’re going to type `npm install` or `cargo build`.

When you do that, I want you to think about the people on the other side of that wire.

But don't just think about it. I want to give you homework. Before you leave this conference today, I want you to open your `package.json`, your `Cargo.toml`, or your `go.mod`. I want you to pick the three dependencies with the fewest GitHub stars that you couldn't live without.

Then I want you to email your procurement team. Ask them one simple question: "Do we have a support contract for these?"

If the answer is no, that is your budget request for Q3. That is how we save the ecosystem.

If you are a developer, don't just be a consumer. Be a contributor. Not just with code, but with empathy. Review a PR. Answer a question. Help someone who is struggling where you once struggled.

We are standing at a crossroads. One path leads to a wasteland of auto-generated code, maintained by bots, devoid of soul, fragile and brittle. The other path leads to a renaissance. A future where AI handles the syntax, and we handle the meaning. A future where open source is sustainable, where maintainers are valued, and where technology serves humanity, not the other way around.

Open source won the war for how we build software. Now, we have to win the peace for how we sustain it.

The code is open. But the future? The future is up to us to write.

Thank you.

**(Applause. Speaker nods, smiles, and exits.)**

**Title:** The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question
**Speaker:** [Your Name]
**Time:** Approx. 15 Minutes
**Setting:** Main Stage at a major tech conference

---

**(The speaker walks to the center of the stage. Behind them, the screen is black, displaying a single, blinking cursor.)**

**SPEAKER:**

Raise your hand if you have run `npm install`, `pip install`, or `cargo add` in the last seven days.

**(The speaker pauses, looking out at the sea of hands.)**

Keep your hand up if you knew exactly who wrote the code you just pulled down, or how that person is paying their rent this month.

**(Most hands go down. A few remain up, perhaps belonging to the maintainers in the room.)**

That. That right there. That is the magic and the fragility of our entire industry.

We build the future of the world on the shoulders of strangers. We ship products worth billions of dollars built on top of libraries maintained by a single person in their spare time, working out of a home office in Helsinki, or a coffee shop in Sao Paulo, or a basement in Ohio.

Good morning. I want to talk to you today about the invisible backbone of the digital age. We are going to talk about the economics of love and labor, the existential threat and the miraculous promise of Artificial Intelligence, and how we save the thing that gives us the most power: Open Source.

**(Slide changes: A split screen. On the left, a graph showing the explosive growth of open source usage over the last 20 years. On the right, a flatline showing the diversity and funding of maintainers.)**

Let’s start with the uncomfortable truth: Open source is winning, but open source maintainers are losing.

We have created a "tragedy of the commons" at a global scale. The value extraction in open source is asymmetric. Companies consume the code, package it into products, generate revenue, and yet, the flow of capital back to the creators is often a trickle.

We all know the stories. The maintainer who burns out after a 14-hour day fixing a critical security vulnerability for free. The "bus factor" of one—the fear that if one person gets hit by a bus, a critical piece of the internet’s infrastructure goes dark. We saw it with Log4j. We saw it with the XZ Utils backdoor attempt, which was really just a cry for help from a maintainer pushed to the brink.

The model is broken. We are treating community maintenance as a charity, when it is actually critical infrastructure.

If you are an engineering leader in this room, I am looking at you. We need to stop asking "How do we get more code for free?" and start asking "How do we pay for the stability we depend on?" Sustainability isn't just about keeping the lights on; it’s about cognitive load. It’s about the mental health of the people building our tools. If we want the software to be sustainable, the humans writing it must be sustainable too.

**(Slide changes: An artistic rendering of a robotic hand typing on a keyboard, merging with a human hand.)**

But just as we start to grapple with the economics of open source, a new variable has entered the equation. A variable that changes the math entirely.

Artificial Intelligence.

In the last eighteen months, we have seen a Cambrian explosion of AI-generated code. GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, Anthropic Claude—these tools are no longer novelties. They are integrated into our IDEs. They are the pair programmers we didn't ask for but can't live without.

This brings us to the central tension of our time. AI is, fundamentally, a remix engine. It learns from the past to predict the future. And where did it learn from? It learned from us.

Open source is the training data for the brain of the internet.

This creates a massive, ethical, and legal gray area. We have AI models trained on permissively licensed code—MIT, Apache—that are now generating proprietary code for corporations. We have models trained on copyleft code—GPL—where the legal requirements of sharing and attribution are effectively being washed away by the opacity of the neural network.

This is the "AI Question" for open source: If a machine learns from my code, generates a solution for you, and neither of us pays me, have I been open-sourced, or have I been strip-mined?

**(The speaker walks to the other side of the stage.)**

Now, I don’t want to be a Luddite here. The potential is undeniable. Imagine an AI that acts as a universal translator for documentation. Imagine an AI that can triage bug reports, identifying the duplicates and the noise, leaving maintainers with only the signal. Imagine lowering the barrier to entry so that a teenager in a developing nation can contribute to a global project without needing a PhD in Computer Science first.

That is the promise.

But the peril is the degradation of the "commons." If we flood the ecosystem with AI-generated code, we risk lowering the signal-to-noise ratio. We risk filling GitHub with "spam code"—functional, perhaps, but devoid of intent, devoid of the human context that makes code maintainable.

And there is a deeper, more philosophical risk. If we rely on AI to write our code, and we rely on AI to review our code, do we eventually lose the ability to understand the systems we built? Do we become the operators of a black box we no longer know how to open?

This is the crossroads.

**(Slide changes: A bright, clean graphic showing a network of nodes, glowing and connecting.)**

So, where do we go from here? How do we navigate a future where our code is sustainable, our communities are vibrant, and our artificial intelligence serves us rather than replaces us?

I believe the answer lies in a renaissance of "Intentional Community."

For the last decade, we treated open source like a content economy—more code, more stars, more commits. Quantity was the metric. In the AI era, quantity is free. If you need a thousand lines of boilerplate, an AI can give it to you in a second.

Therefore, the value of open source is shifting from *volume* to *trust*.

In the next decade, the most successful open source projects will not be the ones with the most downloads. They will be the ones with the strongest provenance. They will be the projects where you know exactly who wrote the code, why they wrote it, and that they were fairly compensated for their time.

We need to move from "Open Source" to "Open Ecosystems."

**(Slide changes: Three pillars: Economic, Social, Technical.)**

**First, the Economic Shift.**
We need to normalize paying for open source, not as a donation, but as a subscription to stability. Companies, you need to budget for open source like you budget for electricity or cloud hosting. It is not optional. And we need better tools to facilitate this. We need to move beyond the "Sponsor" button and into integrated, frictionless payment streams for dependencies.

**Second, the Social Shift.**
We must protect the human in the loop. AI should handle the drudgery—the formatting, the test generation, the documentation updates. But humans must handle the architecture, the ethics, and the "why." We need to double down on mentorship. The next generation of developers needs to learn the *craft* of coding, not just the syntax. They need to understand that code is a conversation between humans, facilitated by a machine.

**Third, the Technical Shift.**
We need new licenses. The current open source licenses were written for a world of copy-paste. They are not equipped for a world of machine learning. We need a framework—perhaps a "Human Use License" or a "Generative Source License"—that ensures that AI models trained on community code give back to that community. If an AI learns from my project, my project should have free, unlimited access to that AI. We need reciprocity.

**(The speaker steps forward, dropping the notes, speaking more directly and passionately.)**

I want to leave you with a thought about the soul of our work.

There is a fear that AI will make the developer obsolete. That we will just become "prompt engineers" supervising a code-generating oracle.

I don't believe that.

I believe that the rise of AI elevates the role of the developer from a mason to an architect. It frees us from the tyranny of the semicolon. It allows us to focus on the *problems*, not just the *syntax*.

But for this to work, we need the underlying substrate—the open source libraries, the frameworks, the operating systems—to be healthy. We need the maintainers to be empowered.

We are on the verge of the greatest acceleration of software development in human history. But speed without direction is just a crash.

Open source is our compass. It is the mechanism by which we ensure that the future of technology is transparent, collaborative, and humane.

We must defend it. We must fund it. We must participate in it.

Don't just be a consumer. Be a contributor. Don't just use the code. Understand the code. And when you see a maintainer struggling to keep the lights on, don't just send them a "thumbs up" emoji. Buy them a coffee. Better yet, buy them a salary.

**(Slide changes: A black screen with white text: "The future is open. The choice is ours.")**

Because in a world of artificial intelligence, open source is our guarantee of authentic intelligence. It is the proof that we are building this future together, not just having it built for us.

Thank you.

**(The speaker nods, smiles, and walks off stage as the lights fade.)**

# The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question

**A 15-Minute Conference Talk**

*[The speaker walks to center stage. No slides yet. Just silence for a moment.]*

---

## [OPENING]

Here's a number I want you to hold in your head: seventy-nine percent.

That's the percentage of codebases in modern enterprises that contain open source components. Seventy-nine percent. And if you work in infrastructure, devops, or backend systems, I'd wager the real number is closer to ninety—or higher.

Now here's another number: two thousand.

That's roughly how many dollars most critical open source maintainers have received, total, for work that your company—and I mean *your* company specifically—probably relies on every single day.

*[Slide: A blank screen with just these two numbers: 79% and $2,000]*

We have built the most sophisticated software infrastructure in human history on a foundation that we never actually agreed to pay for. And for twenty years, that worked. Passion and curiosity and the desire to build something useful—that was enough. It was enough when open source was the underdog. It was enough when it was hobbyists and academics and the occasional corporate contribution.

But we are not the underdog anymore. Open source won. And now we have to figure out what comes after winning.

*[Pause]*

I want to talk to you today about three things: the sustainability crisis that we've been pretending isn't happening, the AI revolution that's about to make everything weirder, and what I think a thriving open source ecosystem actually looks like in the next decade. Because I believe open source has a future—but only if we're honest about its present.

---

## [PART I: THE SUSTAINABILITY CRISIS]

*[Slide: A GitHub issue page. The title reads: "Critical security vulnerability." The timestamp shows it was opened 847 days ago. The last comment is from the maintainer, six months ago: "I don't have time to fix this. If someone wants to submit a PR, please do."]*

This is a real issue. I won't name the project because this isn't about calling anyone out—this is about recognizing a pattern. The maintainer is not lazy. They're not irresponsible. They're exhausted.

The average npm package has 1.2 maintainers. That's not a statistic I made up—that's from a 2023 study of over a million packages. 1.2 maintainers. Which means that for the package your production application depends on, there's a 20% chance that the person maintaining it is doing so alone. And a much higher chance that they're doing it in their spare time, for free, while working a full-time job, raising kids, managing a life.

*[Slide: A graph showing "Maintainer Burnout Timeline"—a line that starts moderate in 2015 and curves sharply upward starting in 2020]*

The pandemic accelerated everything. More software demand. More dependency chains. More security scrutiny after Log4j. More everything—except more maintainers.

Here's what burnout looks like from the inside. You maintain a library that gets 50,000 downloads a week. You get maybe two thank-you emails a year. You get fifty issues filed monthly. Half of them are people asking when you'll add a feature they need. A quarter are entitled demands for support. The rest are genuine bugs that you feel guilty about not fixing.

You used to love this work. Now you dread opening GitHub.

And the funding conversation? It's stuck in a weird place. We have GitHub Sponsors, we have Open Collective, we have Tidelift, we have companies that will absolutely put "we support open source" in their marketing materials while their engineering teams file issues on projects they've never donated to.

*[Slide: A quote from a maintainer interview: "I don't want money. I want people to stop yelling at me in my own issue tracker."]*

The sustainability problem isn't just financial. It's emotional. It's social. We built a system that rewards the creation of open source but punishes its maintenance. We celebrate the initial commit and ignore the ten years of thankless work that follows.

And now we're adding AI to this already fragile system.

---

## [PART II: THE AI QUESTION]

*[Slide: A simple question: "Where does training data come from?"]*

I want to be precise here, because AI is a loaded term and everyone's exhausted of the hype. When I say AI, I mean large language models trained on code. GitHub Copilot. CodeWhisperer. StarCoder. The growing ecosystem of models that can generate functional code on demand.

These models work because they were trained on billions of lines of open source code. Your code. My code. Code that was shared under licenses that grant certain permissions—use, modification, distribution—but that were written before anyone imagined that "use" might include "ingest into a massive statistical model that will eventually compete with the humans who wrote the training data."

*[Pause]*

I'm not here to tell you whether this is legal. Courts are figuring that out. I'm not even here to tell you whether it's ethical—reasonable people disagree, and the conversation is still evolving.

I'm here to tell you what it's doing to open source communities.

*[Slide: Three bullet points]*

- **The attribution problem**: When Copilot suggests a function that's recognizably from a specific project, who gets credit? The answer right now is: no one. The model doesn't cite sources. It doesn't link back. It doesn't drive traffic or recognition to the original creators.

- **The contribution problem**: Junior developers are learning to code by accepting AI suggestions. Some of that code is good. Some of it is subtly wrong. And increasingly, those developers are less likely to seek out the original documentation, the original community, the original source. Why would they? The answer just appeared in their editor.

- **The sustainability problem**: If AI makes it easier to write code without understanding open source libraries, if it reduces the friction that used to lead people to discover projects and become contributors, then we're accelerating the exact dynamic that's already burning maintainers out. More usage, fewer contributors, more demand, less community.

*[Slide: A screenshot of a GitHub issue where someone has pasted AI-generated code that doesn't work, asking for help fixing it. The maintainer's response is patient but tired: "This code wasn't written for our library. It's hallucinated API calls. I can't help you debug AI's imagination."]*

This is happening now. Today. Maintainers are spending time debugging code that was never meant to work—code generated by models that learned the syntax but not the semantics, the patterns but not the purpose.

And I want to be clear: I'm not anti-AI. I use these tools. They're genuinely useful for certain tasks. But we have to recognize that they're fundamentally changing the relationship between code consumers and code creators in ways that our current open source model wasn't designed to handle.

The social contract of open source was always a little implicit: I share this code freely, and in exchange, you maybe contribute back, or at least you acknowledge where it came from, and we all build something together. That contract assumed that using code meant engaging with the community that created it.

AI severs that connection. And we haven't figured out what replaces it.

---

## [PART III: A VISION FOR THE FUTURE]

*[Slide: The year 2034. A question mark.]*

So let me tell you what I think a healthy open source ecosystem looks like in ten years. Not a utopian vision—just a plausible, achievable version of better.

**First, we get explicit about sustainability.**

The projects that survive will be the ones that institutionalize their maintenance. That means funding models that don't depend on a single person's availability. It means governance structures that distribute responsibility. It means treating critical infrastructure projects like... critical infrastructure.

We're already seeing this. The OpenJS Foundation. The Apache Software Foundation's incubation process. The European Union's funding for critical open source security audits. These are early signals of a maturing ecosystem that recognizes: if the internet depends on this code, then we need to treat it like the infrastructure it is.

*[Slide: A diagram showing "Sustainability Layers"—individual maintainers at the bottom, foundation support in the middle, corporate funding at the top, government/public funding as a fourth pillar]*

I believe by 2034, we'll have a tiered system. Small libraries and tools will continue to be maintained by individuals, but with better tools for accepting contributions and clearer expectations. Medium-criticality projects will have foundation support that provides administrative backing, security auditing, and a bench of maintainers. And the truly critical infrastructure—the stuff that if it fails, the internet has a bad day—will have dedicated, paid maintainer teams, funded through a combination of corporate contributions and public interest funding.

**Second, we reinvent the contributor pipeline.**

The current model assumes that users become contributors through a natural progression: you use a library, you hit a bug, you file an issue, you eventually submit a pull request. AI disrupts this pipeline. But it doesn't have to eliminate it.

What if AI tools were designed to route people back to the communities they're learning from? What if Copilot suggested code *and* linked to the documentation where it came from? What if models were trained only on code with compatible licenses, and those licenses were respected in the output?

*[Slide: "AI as Bridge, Not Barrier"]*

I can imagine a future where AI tools are the on-ramp to open source contribution. Where they help newcomers understand codebases faster, where they lower the barrier to that first meaningful contribution, where they amplify maintainer productivity instead of replacing maintainer judgment.

This isn't the default trajectory. The default trajectory is extraction: more code consumed, less community connection. But there's nothing inevitable about that. It's a choice. And open source communities can push back.

**Third, we get honest about governance.**

For too long, open source governance has meant "who has commit access." That's not governance. That's a security model.

Real governance means clear decision-making processes. It means documented ways to resolve disputes. It means succession planning—what happens when the founder gets a new job, has a health crisis, or just loses interest?

*[Slide: "Governance is not control. Governance is continuity."]*

The projects that survive the next decade will be the ones that figured out how to be bigger than any individual contributor. That doesn't mean they'll be corporate. Some of the best-run open source projects are unapologetically community-governed. But they're *governed*—not just maintained.

**Finally, we embrace a new relationship with AI-generated code.**

Here's what I think happens: AI-generated code becomes a new category of open source input. We'll develop licenses that specifically address training rights. We'll build tools that attribute AI suggestions to their sources. We'll create community norms around when AI assistance is appropriate and when human understanding is required.

And yes, some projects will struggle. Some maintainers will quit. Some beloved libraries will become unmaintained. That's already happening. The question isn't whether there will be disruption—there will be. The question is whether we build something better on the other side.

---

## [CLOSING]

*[Speaker moves closer to the audience. The slide goes dark.]*

I've been in open source for about fifteen years now. I've maintained projects that people relied on. I've been the exhausted person staring at an issue tracker that never stops growing. I've also been the contributor who showed up to help, and discovered that the best feeling in this entire profession is when someone tells you: "Your pull request saved my weekend."

That feeling—that connection—is what open source is actually about.

The licenses and the repositories and the foundation structures are all just infrastructure. They're necessary, but they're not sufficient. What makes open source work is the human relationships underneath. The mentorship that happens in pull request reviews. The trust that builds when someone fixes a bug you reported. The sense that we're all building something together that none of us could build alone.

AI can't replace that. It can accelerate code generation, but it can't generate trust. It can suggest solutions, but it can't build community. That still requires humans showing up for each other.

*[Pause]*

So here's what I want you to take from this talk.

If you're an engineering leader, look at your dependency tree. Find the ten projects you rely on most critically. And then actually support them—not just with money, though money helps, but with engineering time. Give your developers permission to contribute back. Make open source maintenance part of someone's job description. Stop treating the commons as a free resource and start treating it as shared infrastructure that you help maintain.

If you're an individual developer, the ask is simpler but not easier: be the community you want to find. Respond to that newbie's question with patience. Review that pull request with generosity. Thank the maintainers whose work you use. And when you're ready, become a maintainer yourself—because we need more of you.

*[Slide returns: The two numbers from the beginning—79% and $2,000]*
*[Then the numbers fade, replaced by text: "What if we made these numbers match?"]*

Open source won the war for relevance. We're everywhere now. The next decade isn't about winning—it's about learning to live with our own success.

The future of open source isn't something that happens to us. It's something we build. Together. The same way we've always built everything.

Thank you.

---

*[End of talk. Time: approximately 15 minutes at measured delivery pace.]*

We have GitHub Sponsors, we have Open Collective, we have Tidelift, we have companies that will absolutely put "we support open source" in their marketing materials while their engineering teams file issues on projects they've never donated to.

*[Slide: A quote from a maintainer interview: "I don't want money. I want people to stop yelling at me in my own issue tracker."]*

The sustainability problem isn't just financial. It's emotional. It's social. We built a system that rewards the creation of open source but punishes its maintenance. We celebrate the initial commit and ignore the ten years of thankless work that follows.

We need to move past the performative donation and start demanding that our teams treat open source contributions as billable engineering time, not a weekend hobby. Your company tracks billable hours meticulously for client work. Why isn't maintaining the infrastructure your product runs on treated with the same professional weight?

This is the fragile foundation we've built. And now, into this system of exhausted maintainers and neglected infrastructure, we are introducing the most disruptive technological force in a generation: AI.

---

## [PART II: THE AI QUESTION]

*[Slide: A simple question: "Where does training data come from?"]*

I want to be precise here, because AI is a loaded term and everyone's exhausted of the hype. When I say AI, I mean large language models trained on code. GitHub Copilot. CodeWhisperer. StarCoder. The growing ecosystem of models that can generate functional code on demand.

These models work because they were trained on billions of lines of open source code. Your code. My code. Code that was shared under licenses that grant certain permissions—use, modification, distribution—but that were written before anyone imagined that "use" might include "ingest into a massive statistical model that will eventually compete with the humans who wrote the training data."

*[Pause]*

Is ingestion "use"? Is the output a derivative work? The legal system is slow, but the community impact is immediate. I'm not here to tell you whether this is legal. Courts are figuring that out. I'm not even here to tell you whether it's ethical—reasonable people disagree, and the conversation is still evolving.

I'm here to tell you what it's doing to open source communities right now.

*[Slide: Three bullet points]*

- **The attribution problem**: When Copilot suggests a function that's recognizably from a specific project, who gets credit? The answer right now is: no one. The model doesn't cite sources. It doesn't link back. It doesn't drive traffic or recognition to the original creators.

- **The contribution problem**: Junior developers are learning to code by accepting AI suggestions. Some of that code is good. Some of it is subtly wrong. And increasingly, those developers are less likely to seek out the original documentation, the original community, the original source. Why would they? The answer just appeared in their editor.

- **The sustainability problem**: If AI makes it easier to write code without understanding open source libraries, if it reduces the friction that used to lead people to discover projects and become contributors, then we're accelerating the exact dynamic that's already burning maintainers out. More usage, fewer contributors, more demand, less community.

*[Slide: A screenshot of a GitHub issue where someone has pasted AI-generated code that doesn't work, asking for help fixing it. The maintainer's response is patient but tired: "This code wasn't written for our library. It's hallucinated API calls. I can't help you debug AI's imagination."]*

This is happening now. Today. Maintainers are spending time debugging code that was never meant to work—code generated by models that learned the syntax but not the semantics, the patterns but not the purpose.

And I want to be clear: I'm not anti-AI. I use these tools. They're genuinely useful for certain tasks. But we have to recognize that they're fundamentally changing the relationship between code consumers and code creators in ways that our current open source model wasn't designed to handle.

The social contract of open source was always a little implicit: I share this code freely, and in exchange, you maybe contribute back, or at least you acknowledge where it came from, and we all build something together. That contract assumed that using code meant engaging with the community that created it.

AI severs that connection. And we haven't figured out what replaces it.

---

## [PART III: A VISION FOR THE FUTURE]

*[Slide: The year 2034. A question mark.]*

So let me tell you what I think a healthy open source ecosystem looks like in ten years. Not a utopian vision—just a plausible, achievable version of better.

**First, we get explicit about sustainability.**

The projects that survive will be the ones that institutionalize their maintenance. That means funding models that don't depend on a single person's availability. It means governance structures that distribute responsibility. It means treating critical infrastructure projects like... critical infrastructure.

We're already seeing this. The OpenJS Foundation. The Apache Software Foundation's incubation process. The European Union's funding for critical open source security audits. These are early signals of a maturing ecosystem that recognizes: if the internet depends on this code, then we need to treat it like the infrastructure it is.

*[Slide: A diagram showing "Sustainability Layers"—individual maintainers at the bottom, foundation support in the middle, corporate funding at the top, government/public funding as a fourth pillar]*

I believe by 2034, we'll have a tiered system. Small libraries and tools will continue to be maintained by individuals, but with better tools for accepting contributions and clearer expectations. Medium-criticality projects will have foundation support that provides administrative backing, security auditing, and a bench of maintainers. And the truly critical infrastructure—the stuff that if it fails, the internet has a bad day—will have dedicated, paid maintainer teams, funded through a combination of corporate contributions and public interest funding.

**Second, we reinvent the contributor pipeline.**

The current model assumes that users become contributors through a natural progression: you use a library, you hit a bug, you file an issue, you eventually submit a pull request. AI disrupts this pipeline. But it doesn't have to eliminate it.

What if AI tools were designed to route people back to the communities they're learning from? What if Copilot suggested code *and* linked to the documentation where it came from? What if, when suggesting a function from an open source library, the tool also surfaced a relevant "Good First Issue" from that project's backlog—creating a direct on-ramp for contribution?

*[Slide: "AI as Bridge, Not Barrier"]*

I can imagine a future where AI tools are the on-ramp to open source contribution. Where they help newcomers understand codebases faster, where they lower the barrier to that first meaningful contribution, where they amplify maintainer productivity instead of replacing maintainer judgment.

This isn't the default trajectory. The default trajectory is extraction: more code consumed, less community connection. But there's nothing inevitable about that. It's a choice. And open source communities can push back.

**Third, we get honest about governance.**

For too long, open source governance has meant "who has commit access." That's not governance. That's a security model.

Real governance means clear decision-making processes. It means documented ways to resolve disputes. It means succession planning—what happens when the founder gets a new job, has a health crisis, or just loses interest?

*[Slide: "Governance is not control. Governance is continuity."]*

We have working models for this. The Linux kernel development process has survived multiple leadership transitions and continues to scale. The Rust Foundation's RFC process creates transparent decision-making that the entire community can understand and participate in. These aren't perfect systems, but they demonstrate that projects can become bigger than any individual contributor. That's the goal: continuity that outlasts burnout, life changes, and shifting interests.

The projects that survive the next decade will be the ones that figured this out. That doesn't mean they'll be corporate. Some of the best-run open source projects are unapologetically community-governed. But they're *governed*—not just maintained.

**Finally, we embrace a new relationship with AI-generated code.**

Here's what I think happens: AI-generated code becomes a new category of open source input. We'll develop licenses that specifically address training rights. We'll build tools that attribute AI suggestions to their sources. We'll create community norms around when AI assistance is appropriate and when human understanding is required.

And yes, some projects will struggle. Some maintainers will quit. Some beloved libraries will become unmaintained. That's already happening. The question isn't whether there will be disruption—there will be. The question is whether we build something better on the other side.

---

## [CLOSING]

*[Speaker moves closer to the audience. The slide goes dark.]*

I've been in open source for about fifteen years now. I've maintained projects that people relied on. I've been the exhausted person staring at an issue tracker that never stops growing. I've also been the contributor who showed up to help, and discovered that the best feeling in this entire profession is when someone tells you: "Your pull request saved my weekend."

That feeling—that connection—is what open source is actually about.

The licenses and the repositories and the foundation structures are all just infrastructure. They're necessary, but they're not sufficient. What makes open source work is the human relationships underneath. The mentorship that happens in pull request reviews. The trust that builds when someone fixes a bug you reported. The sense that we're all building something together that none of us could build alone.

AI can't replace that. It can accelerate code generation, but it can't generate trust. It can suggest solutions, but it can't build community. That still requires humans showing up for each other.

*[Pause]*

So here's what I want you to take from this talk.

If you're an engineering leader, look at your dependency tree. Find the ten projects you rely on most critically. And then actually support them—not just with money, though money helps, but with engineering time. Give your developers permission to contribute back. Make open source maintenance part of someone's job description. Stop treating the commons as a free resource and start treating it as shared infrastructure that you help maintain.

If you're an individual developer, the ask is simpler but not easier: be the community you want to find. Respond to that newbie's question with patience. Review that pull request with generosity. Thank the maintainers whose work you use. And when you're ready, become a maintainer yourself—because we need more of you.

*[Slide returns: The two numbers from the beginning—79% and $2,000]*

*[The numbers fade, replaced by text: "What if we made these numbers match?"]*

*[Pause. Three full seconds.]*

Open source won the war for relevance. We're everywhere now. The next decade isn't about winning—it's about learning to live with our own success.

The future of open source isn't something that happens to us. It's something we build. Together. The same way we've always built everything.

Thank you.

---

*[End of talk. Time: approximately 15 minutes at measured delivery pace.]*
