**The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question**

Two months ago, I got a Slack message at 2 AM. Not unusual—I'm a maintainer. But this one was different. It wasn't a bug report. It wasn't a feature request. It was from a developer at a Fortune 50 company, and it said: "Your library is down. We're losing $50K per minute. What are you going to do about it?"

I was sitting in my pajamas, in my apartment, having just spent my evening—my *unpaid* evening—reviewing pull requests from their employees.

That, my friends, is the open source paradox in a single message. The world runs on our code. The world assumes our code is a utility, like water or electricity—always there, always reliable, and somehow, magically, free. But behind every `npm install`, every `pip install`, every `docker pull`, there's a human being. A human being with a lifespan, with burnout, with rent to pay.

And right now, that human is being asked to compete with something that never sleeps, never burns out, and is being fed a diet of their own work: artificial intelligence.

---

**I. The Unsustainable Present**

Let's start with some uncomfortable math.

There are roughly 45 million developers on GitHub. About 3% of them are responsible for maintaining the packages that 90% of the industry depends on. That's about 1.3 million people holding up the digital infrastructure of the modern world.

The average maintainer spends 20 hours a week on their project. The median compensation? Zero dollars. The burnout rate? Over 50% annually.

We talk about open source as a meritocracy, but it's really a tragedy of the commons dressed up as a gift economy. We celebrate the individual hero—the lone maintainer in Nebraska whose library runs every Kubernetes cluster—but we never ask: why is it *one* person? Why is that person in Nebraska, and not in a room with a salary, a team, and a therapist?

The sustainability crisis isn't coming. It's here. It's been here. We've just been too busy typing `npm install` to notice.

I want you to think about Log4j. Not the vulnerability itself, but what it revealed. When that crisis hit, we discovered that a critical piece of internet infrastructure was maintained by three volunteers. Three. Their names weren't in any corporate org chart. They didn't have a vendor support contract. They had email addresses and a passion for logging.

The aftermath was predictable: panicked executives, emergency patches, and a brief moment of collective guilt. Then, right back to business as usual. The maintainers? They got t-shirts. Maybe a thank-you note. Definitely not a retirement plan.

This is the first sustainability challenge: the free-rider problem on steroids. Every Fortune 500 company profits from open source, but less than 5% meaningfully fund it. We've created a system where the most economically valuable work is the least economically rewarded.

But there's a second, deeper problem: the work itself is changing.

---

**II. The AI Question**

Six months ago, I accepted a pull request that I later discovered was 90% generated by Copilot. The code worked. It was fine. It passed tests. But it contained a subtle concurrency bug that only appeared under real-world load. It took me 12 hours to track it down—12 hours I could have spent on design, on documentation, on community building.

This is the AI question, and it's not about whether AI can write code. Of course it can. The question is: who owns the code? Who maintains it? Who understands it?

Right now, we're watching a massive transfer of value. Models trained on decades of open source contributions—a cathedral built by millions of hands—are now being used to generate code that may never be contributed back. The commons is being mined, refined, and sold back to us as a service.

The licensing questions are thorny and unresolved. If Copilot suggests a verbatim snippet from GPL'd code, does your entire project become GPL? If a model trains on MIT-licensed code, is the output truly "free"? We're in a legal gray area that makes the Oracle v. Google case look like a parking dispute.

But the bigger issue is sustainability at the human level. AI doesn't burn out, but it also doesn't care. It doesn't understand context. It doesn't feel the weight of a community depending on it. It doesn't know the difference between "this works" and "this is right."

We're seeing a flood of low-quality contributions. A maintainer I know recently received 47 pull requests in a single day, all generated by AI, all fixing the same trivial linting issue. The AI had found a pattern and executed it at scale, without understanding that 46 of those PRs were redundant.

We're shifting from a world where writing code was the scarce resource to a world where *understanding* code is the scarce resource. And understanding is a deeply human activity. It requires context, judgment, and care.

The irony is that AI could be our salvation. It could automate the tedious work—dependency updates, security patches, test generation. It could free maintainers to focus on the creative, human work of architecture and community. But only if we build the right social contract around it.

---

**III. A Vision for the Next Decade**

So what does thriving look like? Not surviving. Not "hanging on." Thriving.

I want to propose three shifts: in funding, in governance, and in our relationship with technology.

**First, funding must become a first-class concern, not an afterthought.**

We're seeing experiments: GitHub Sponsors, Tidelift, Open Collective. These are good, but they're band-aids on a hemorrhage. We need structural change.

Imagine if every software license included a 1% "infrastructure fee"—a tiny fraction of your AWS bill automatically distributed to the open source projects you depend on. Not a donation. A royalty. A recognition that value flows downhill.

Imagine if VC term sheets included line items for open source maintenance. If you're building a billion-dollar company on open source, you should be required to fund its foundation. Not out of charity. Out of self-interest.

We need to stop treating funding as a personal favor to a developer and start treating it as infrastructure investment. Like roads. Like the power grid. Like the internet itself.

**Second, governance must evolve from BDFL to "Benevolent Distributed Federated Labor."**

The "Benevolent Dictator for Life" model worked for the era of cathedral-building. But we're in the age of bazaards within bazaards. We need governance that scales with complexity.

I envision a future where projects have explicit governance tiers: contributors, maintainers, stewards, and sponsors. Each tier has rights and responsibilities. Sponsors get a voice, not a veto. Stewards get paid for the emotional labor of community management. Contributors get mentorship and clear paths to leadership.

We need to professionalize the parts of open source that are already professional. The Linux Foundation has a $100M budget. Why does Linus still merge patches at 3 AM? We can do better.

**Third, we must treat AI as a community member, not a replacement.**

Here's my controversial take: we should require AI-generated contributions to be explicitly labeled, and we should treat them like contributions from a junior developer. They need review. They need mentorship. They need to earn trust.

But we should also use AI to amplify human maintainers. Imagine an AI that doesn't write code, but writes the first draft of a release note. That triages issues. That identifies contributors who are burning out based on their commit patterns. That flags when a new contributor hasn't been welcomed.

The future isn't human *or* AI. It's human *with* AI, but with clear boundaries. AI is the bicycle for the mind, not the rider.

---

**IV. The Work Ahead**

This vision requires us to change our culture. To stop celebrating the martyr and start celebrating the sustainable. To stop asking "What can I get for free?" and start asking "What does it cost to keep this free?"

We need to build new institutions. A maintainer's union, perhaps. A standardized "open source maturity model" that evaluates not just code quality, but community health and maintainer sustainability. We need conferences like this one to have tracks not on new frameworks, but on governance and mental health.

And we need to act individually. If you're a developer, sponsor your dependencies. If you're a leader, fund the projects your business relies on. If you're a VC, make sustainability a condition of investment.

The next decade will define whether open source remains a public good or becomes a tragedy. The variables are in our hands.

---

**V. The Last Commit**

I'll leave you with this.

The future of open source isn't about code. It never was. It's about the social contract we write in the spaces between the code. It's about the recognition that every commit is an act of generosity, and generosity untended eventually becomes exhaustion.

We have a choice. We can continue to treat open source as a magical fountain of free labor, and watch it dry up. Or we can build the civic infrastructure it deserves—funding, governance, and a humane relationship with our tools.

The AI question isn't whether machines will replace developers. It's whether we'll use machines to finally value the humans who taught them how to code.

So when you go back to your teams, to your companies, to your own projects, I want you to remember that 2 AM Slack message. Remember the maintainer in pajamas, holding up your production stack.

Then open your wallet, open your governance model, and open your mind.

Because the future of open source isn't written by AI. It's written by us.

**And commit messages, as we all know, are forever.**

Thank you.

---

*[The speaker pauses, then steps back. The lights fade to black.]*

---

**I. The Unsustainable Present**

Let's start with some uncomfortable math.

There are roughly 45 million developers on GitHub. About 3% of them are responsible for maintaining the packages that 90% of the industry depends on. That's about 1.3 million people holding up the digital infrastructure of the modern world.

The average maintainer spends 20 hours a week on their project. The median compensation? Zero dollars. The burnout rate? Over 50% annually.

We talk about open source as a meritocracy, but it's really a tragedy of the commons dressed up as a gift economy. We celebrate the individual hero—the lone maintainer in Nebraska whose library runs every Kubernetes cluster—but we never ask: why is it *one* person? Why is that person in Nebraska, and not in a room with a salary, a team, and a therapist?

The sustainability crisis isn't coming. It's here. It's been here. We've just been too busy typing `npm install` to notice.

I want you to think about Log4j. Not the vulnerability itself, but what it revealed. When that crisis hit, we discovered that a critical piece of internet infrastructure was maintained by three volunteers. Three. Their names weren't in any corporate org chart. They didn't have a vendor support contract. They had email addresses and a passion for logging.

The aftermath was predictable: panicked executives, emergency patches, and a brief moment of collective guilt. Then, right back to business as usual. The maintainers? They got t-shirts. Maybe a thank-you note. Definitely not a retirement plan.

This is the first sustainability challenge: the free-rider problem on steroids. Every Fortune 500 company profits from open source, but less than 5% meaningfully fund it. We've created a system where the most economically valuable work is the least economically rewarded.

But there's a second, deeper problem: the work itself is changing. The humans are breaking under the load, just as a new kind of "contributor" arrives—one that doesn't need sleep, but also doesn't understand why the code matters.

---

**II. The AI Question**

Six months ago, I accepted a pull request that I later discovered was 90% generated by Copilot. The code worked. It was fine. It passed tests. But it contained a subtle concurrency bug that only appeared under real-world load. It took me 12 hours to track it down—12 hours I could have spent on design, on documentation, on community building.

This vision requires us to change our culture. To stop celebrating the martyr and start celebrating the sustainable. To stop asking "What can I get for free?" and start asking "What does it cost to keep this free?"

We need to build new institutions. A standardized "open source maturity model" that evaluates not just code quality, but community health and maintainer sustainability. We need conferences like this one to have tracks not on new frameworks, but on governance and mental health.

And we need to act individually. If you're a developer, sponsor your dependencies. If you're a leader, fund the projects your business relies on. If you're a VC, make sustainability a condition of investment.

The next decade will define whether open source remains a public good or becomes a tragedy. The variables are in our hands.

---

**V. The Last Commit**

I'll leave you with this.

The future of open source isn't about code. It never was. It's about the social contract we write in the spaces between the code. It's about the recognition that every commit is an act of generosity, and generosity untended eventually becomes exhaustion.

We have a choice. We can continue to treat open source as a magical fountain of free labor, and watch it dry up. Or we can build the civic infrastructure it deserves—funding, governance, and a humane relationship with our tools.

The AI question isn't whether machines will replace developers. It's whether we'll use machines to finally value the humans who taught them how to code.

So when you go back to your teams, to your companies, to your own projects, I want you to remember that 2 AM Slack message. Remember the maintainer in pajamas, holding up your production stack.

Then open your wallet, open your governance model, and open your mind.

Because the future of open source isn't written by AI. It's written by us.

**And commit messages, as we all know, are forever.**

Thank you.

---

*[The speaker pauses. A single slide appears behind them, white text on black: "Commit messages are forever." They step back. The lights fade to black.]*

**The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question**

Good morning. Let me tell you about the day the internet broke.

Not the dramatic, Hollywood-style breaking—no explosions, no cyberattacks. Just a quiet Tuesday in March 2016, when a developer in Oakland, frustrated by a trademark dispute, unpublished an 11-line JavaScript function called "left-pad" from the npm registry. Within minutes, builds failed across the planet. React wouldn’t install. Babel wouldn’t compile. Literally millions of projects—worth billions of dollars—ground to a halt because of 17 lines of code that removed whitespace from the beginning of strings.

That’s the paradox of open source in a nutshell: the most powerful companies on Earth, with their trillion-dollar market caps, are utterly dependent on software maintained by someone having a bad day.

[PAUSE]

I’m here today because that paradox has become a crisis. And AI has just poured gasoline on it.

**The Unsustainable Present**

Let’s start with some uncomfortable math. Open source runs the world. 96% of all applications contain open source components. The average project has 500 dependencies. Your Docker container probably has more volunteer labor in it than a small town’s worth of community service.

But here’s the distribution: less than 0.1% of open source contributors are responsible for more than 50% of the commits. We have a word for these people: maintainers. And they’re burning out.

[PAUSE]

I spoke with a maintainer last month who manages a logging library. It’s used by 40,000 other projects. Every day, she gets 50 notifications: bug reports, feature requests, demands for instant support. She does this after her day job, after putting her kids to bed, for approximately $0. Last year, a Fortune 500 company opened a critical security issue at 2 AM and complained when she didn’t respond within an hour. They were using her software to process $2 billion in daily transactions.

This is the sustainability crisis we don’t talk about. It’s not just about money—though that’s part of it. It’s about the structural violence of building a digital commons on unpaid emotional labor.

[PAUSE]

We’ve tried Band-Aids. GitHub Sponsors is wonderful, but it’s the equivalent of tipping your bus driver—it’s charity, not compensation. Tidelift tries to create a market for maintenance, but it’s a drop in the ocean. The Linux Foundation has a $100 million budget, but that’s for the kernel—one project. We have 30 million open source projects.

The current models fail because they treat symptoms, not the disease. The disease is that we’ve built a trillion-dollar infrastructure on a social contract that expects talented engineers to work for free because... passion? Because it’s good for their career? Because they’re supposed to be grateful for the privilege?

That social contract is collapsing under its own weight. Maintainer burnout is at an all-time high. The average tenure of a maintainer in a popular project is 18 months before they step away. And when they leave, they don’t just disappear—they take with them the institutional memory, the design philosophy, the subtle understanding of why that one weird bug hack exists.

**The AI Tsunami**

And now, AI has arrived. And it’s complicated everything.

GitHub Copilot writes 40% of the code in files where it’s enabled. Some developers report 2-3x productivity gains. But here’s what nobody’s talking about: the generated code has the same problems as Stack Overflow copy-paste, just at industrial scale.

[PAUSE]

I recently reviewed a pull request where an engineer had used Copilot to implement a crypto function. It looked perfect. It compiled. It passed tests. But it was subtly vulnerable to a timing attack that would have been obvious to anyone who’d actually read the OpenSSL source. The AI had copy-pasted a pattern from 2015 that was deprecated for a reason.

This is the AI code paradox: it increases velocity while decreasing comprehension. It’s like giving every developer a Formula 1 car without teaching them how to drive. Sure, you’ll go fast—until you hit the first corner.

But the more profound impact is on the social dynamics of open source itself. When AI can generate a plausible implementation of any feature request in seconds, what happens to the craft of contribution? When a bot can answer every beginner question on your issue tracker, what happens to mentorship? When code becomes cheap, what happens to the human connections that make open source resilient?

[PAUSE]

We’re already seeing the effects. Projects are drowning in low-quality AI-generated pull requests. Maintainers report spending more time closing spam PRs than reviewing genuine contributions. The signal-to-noise ratio is collapsing. It’s as if we’ve opened the gates to a city and said, “Anyone can contribute, but also we’ve built a machine that can generate infinite contributions at zero cost.”

And then there’s the licensing question. Copilot was trained on open source code, regardless of license. Was that fair use? Theft? Something in between? The courts will decide, but the community has already rendered its verdict: 30% of developers now say they’re less likely to contribute to open source because they don’t want their code used to train proprietary AI models.

We’ve gone from a world where open source was a gift economy to a world where open source is training data for someone else’s profit engine. That’s a fundamental breach of trust.

**A Vision for the Next Decade**

So what do we do? Do we retreat into gated communities? Do we give up and let AI commoditize software entirely? No. We evolve. We build something better.

Here’s my vision for open source in 2035: not more code, but better stewardship. Not replacing humans, but amplifying what makes us human.

**First, we professionalize maintenance.**

We need to stop treating maintainership as a hobby and start treating it as critical digital infrastructure. That means companies that depend on open source must pay for it—not through optional donations, but as a cost of doing business. I’m talking about a 1% tax on engineering payroll for every company that ships software. Not a tax to government, but a tax to the commons. Distributed directly to maintainers through something like a digital infrastructure fund.

Sound radical? Amazon Web Services alone could fund 10,000 full-time maintainers with 1% of their engineering budget and barely notice. The math works. The will doesn’t.

But we’re seeing seeds of this. The Sovereign Tech Fund in Germany is doing it at a national level. The OpenSSF is doing it for security-critical projects. We need to scale this to every company, every project.

**Second, we use AI to augment, not replace, human judgment.**

The future isn’t AI writing code alone. It’s AI acting as a senior engineer who never sleeps—reviewing PRs, catching bugs, writing documentation, onboarding new contributors. But always under human direction.

Imagine a world where every open source project has an AI assistant that’s been trained not just on code, but on the project’s history, its design philosophy, its social norms. A new contributor asks a question, and the AI responds with context: “We tried that approach in 2019, see issue #3421, but it broke this edge case. Here’s the maintainer who worked on it—she might have time to mentor you.”

The AI becomes a force multiplier for community health, not just code velocity. It handles the tedious triage so maintainers can focus on architecture and mentorship. It remembers everything, so when a veteran maintainer burns out, the institutional knowledge doesn’t disappear with them.

**Third, we redesign governance for a world of abundant code and scarce attention.**

We need new models that prioritize maintainer sustainability over contributor growth. That means:

- **Term limits for maintainers**—yes, really. Force rotation before burnout.
- **Contributor licensing agreements** that explicitly opt out of AI training unless consented.
- **Quality gates** that use AI to filter contributions before a human even sees them.
- **Community health metrics** that measure mentor-mentee relationships, not just commit counts.

The Apache Software Foundation has been doing some of this for decades. We need to take their lessons and apply them with modern tools.

**Fourth, we rebuild the social contract.**

The old contract was: “You write code for free, and you get reputation and experience.” The new contract must be: “You steward critical infrastructure, and society pays you for that labor—while AI handles the drudgework, and the community provides the meaning.”

Because here’s the truth: people don’t contribute to open source just for code. They contribute for belonging. For mastery. For purpose. AI can generate infinite code, but it cannot generate meaning. It cannot create the bond between a mentor and a mentee when they finally squash that impossible bug together. It cannot replicate the joy of a community that has your back when life falls apart.

**The Path Forward**

This transition won’t be easy. It requires us to challenge some deeply held beliefs: that open source must be volunteer-led, that more contributors is always better, that code is the primary output.

But necessity is a great motivator. And we are at an inflection point. The AI revolution has exposed the brittleness of our current system. We can either use this moment to patch the cracks, or we can rebuild the foundation.

I believe we’ll rebuild. Because the alternative is unthinkable: a world where our digital infrastructure is either abandoned or controlled by a handful of AI companies that never understood the philosophy that made open source powerful in the first place.

**The Conclusion**

So here’s my call to action, and I want you to remember this:

The future of open source isn’t about choosing between human and machine. It’s about choosing between extraction and stewardship. Between burnout and sustainability. Between infinite code and infinite care.

[PAUSE]

We have spent the last 30 years building a cathedral of code, stone by stone, gifted by millions of hands. AI will not build the next cathedral. AI is just a better crane. The question is: will we use it to build higher, faster, stronger? Or will we let it demolish the community that knows how to build at all?

The future of open source will be written by those who understand that the most important pull request isn’t the one that adds a feature—it’s the one that says, “I see you, maintainer. I’ve got your back. Take a break.”

[PAUSE]

Let’s stop optimizing for code velocity and start optimizing for community longevity. Let’s stop asking how AI can replace contributors and start asking how it can amplify compassion. Let’s stop treating maintainers as volunteers and start treating them as the critical infrastructure they are.

Because at the end of the day, the sustainability crisis in open source was never really about money. It was about whether we, as an industry, have the moral imagination to value care as much as we value code.

And that’s a question no AI can answer for us.

[The speaker holds the pause, then steps back from the podium]

Thank you.

[END]

It's 2:47 AM. Your pager just went off. Production is down. 

While you're frantically tracing the stack trace, you notice the culprit: a transitive dependency, six layers deep, maintained by one person in Nebraska. You've never heard of them. You've never paid them. But right now, your company's entire revenue stream depends on their code.

This is the invisible architecture of our digital world. And it's held together by duct tape, good intentions, and the sleep-deprived keystrokes of a handful of maintainers who've been screaming into the void for help.

I'm here today because that void is getting louder. And AI is about to change everything.

[Pause]

We call it "open source," but we should call it what it really is: the largest, most successful, and most fragile collaborative infrastructure project in human history. Four hundred million repositories. Forty million developers. Trillions of dollars of economic value built on top of code that is, by definition, free.

But free is not sustainable. And sustainable is not optional.

Let's talk about the three existential questions facing open source today: How do we keep the lights on? How do we keep our communities whole? And what do we do when the robots show up to help?

[Click to next slide: a graph showing maintainer burnout statistics]

The sustainability crisis isn't coming. It's here. A 2023 Tidelift survey found that 60% of open source maintainers are either burnt out or teetering on the edge. The average popular npm package has 1.3 maintainers. The average time to maintainership for a critical vulnerability? Six years. 

We saw this play out in real time with Log4j. A volunteer team, fielding calls from Fortune 500 CEOs, patching a zero-day that threatened the entire internet. They were heroes. They were also exhausted, unpaid, and largely anonymous until the crisis hit.

Or take the xz backdoor attempt earlier this year. A patient attacker spent years building trust, contributing to a compression library used everywhere. They nearly succeeded because the single maintainer was overwhelmed, overworked, and—this is the crucial part—alone.

This is the tragedy of the digital commons. We all graze on the green fields of open source, but nobody wants to pay for the fence. Companies consume maintainers' work at scale, bake it into products worth billions, and return the favor with a GitHub star and a Stack Overflow question.

We've built a gift economy where the gifts are priceless and the givers are going broke.

[Click to next slide: corporate usage vs. contribution data]

The economic model is broken. We've tried donation buttons—Patreon for programmers. It doesn't work at scale. GitHub Sponsors is a beautiful idea, but it's a rounding error compared to the value extracted. Tidelift and similar platforms are promising, but they've only scratched the surface.

Meanwhile, the problem compounds. The barrier to entry has never been lower, which means the volume of code has never been higher, which means the surface area for burnout has never been wider. We're drowning in pull requests, issues, and "quick questions" from developers who treat maintainers like Stack Overflow with a pulse.

And now, just as we need human connection and sustainable funding the most, AI walks through the door.

[Click to next slide: GitHub Copilot usage statistics]

AI is not just another tool. It's a phase shift. 

In 2023, GitHub reported that developers using Copilot accepted 30% of its suggestions. That number is climbing. In some languages, in some domains, we're approaching 50%. We're not writing code anymore. We're curating it.

This changes everything about open source.

First, the licensing apocalypse. If an AI model trained on GPL code generates a snippet, is that snippet GPL? What about MIT? What about proprietary code? Courts are wrestling with this, but developers can't wait for judges. They're already building products on AI-generated code with unknown provenance. We're sleepwalking into a legal minefield.

Second, the contribution economy is fracturing. Why spend an hour crafting a thoughtful pull request when you can spend five minutes prompting an AI to generate something that looks right? We've seen a 50% drop in Stack Overflow questions since ChatGPT launched. Not because people have fewer questions, but because they're asking robots instead of communities.

The problem? Robots don't mentor. They don't teach. They don't say, "Hey, I noticed you're new here—let me walk you through why we do things this way." They produce code, but they don't produce coders.

Third, the quality paradox. AI generates code that looks correct. It has the syntax of a senior developer and the judgment of a junior one. It doesn't understand context, deprecation, or the subtle tribal knowledge embedded in a decade-old codebase. It's like hiring a brilliant contractor who never reads the architecture docs.

I recently reviewed a PR where an AI had "modernized" error handling. It looked beautiful. It also introduced a subtle race condition that would have taken down our entire authentication system. The developer who submitted it trusted the machine more than their own understanding.

This is our new reality: a flood of plausible-looking code, written by no one, understood by fewer, and maintained by the same exhausted humans who were already drowning.

[Click to next slide: "The Ghost Contributor Problem"]

But here's the thing. AI isn't the villain. It's a mirror.

It's showing us what we valued: speed over understanding, output over craftsmanship, consumption over contribution. The machine learned from our behavior. If we don't like what we see, we need to change the inputs.

So what does a sustainable, human-centered, AI-compatible open source future look like? I want to propose three shifts.

**Shift One: From Consumption Tax to Stewardship Investment**

We need to stop thinking about funding open source as charity and start treating it as infrastructure. Companies don't donate to their cloud provider. They pay for reliability, support, and guarantees.

Imagine a world where every commercial software license includes a 1% "stewardship fee"—not a donation, but a mandatory investment in the commons you depend on. Not a button you click, but a line item you budget.

We're seeing glimpses of this. The Sovereign Tech Fund is directly funding critical projects. The Open Source Security Foundation is doing coordinated vulnerability response. But these are still exceptions.

The model should be: if you ship it, you support it. Automatically. At scale.

**Shift Two: From Lone Hero to Collective Governance**

The xz incident taught us that bus factor of one is a national security risk. We need to professionalize maintainership without killing the passion that makes open source special.

This means:
- Rotating maintainership models with built-in sabbaticals
- Paid contributor pipelines—companies giving employees 20% time to maintain upstream projects
- Mentorship-first contribution models where the goal isn't just merging code, but growing humans
- AI-assisted triage that reduces the burden without replacing the judgment

Imagine a maintainer's dashboard that uses AI to summarize issues, detect duplicate bugs, and suggest reviewers—but the human makes every call. The machine handles the noise so the human can focus on the nuance.

**Shift Third: From Code Contribution to Community Cultivation**

In an AI world, the scarce resource isn't code—it's trust. It's judgment. It's the human network that vouches for quality.

The future belongs to communities that treat humans as the essential infrastructure. That means:

- Recognizing mentorship as a first-class contribution, equal to commits
- Building onboarding paths that take six months, not six minutes
- Celebrating the developers who say "no" to bad code, not just the ones who ship fast
- Using AI to lower the barrier to *understanding*, not just the barrier to *producing*

We need to teach developers to be AI shepherds, not AI stenographers. To ask: "Why did you suggest this?" To demand: "Show me the test." To care about the lineage of their code like a chef cares about their ingredients.

[Click to final slide: a simple, bold statement]

This is the crux: **AI can write code, but it cannot build trust. It can optimize functions, but it cannot sustain communities. It can generate answers, but it cannot ask the right questions.**

The future of open source isn't human versus machine. It's human *with* machine, bound by a social contract that values the long-term over the immediate, the collective over the individual, the craft over the commodity.

[Speaker steps away from the podium, closer to the audience]

Ten years from now, I believe we'll look back at this moment as the inflection point. The moment we realized that free code has a cost, and that cost must be paid in dollars, in time, and in human connection.

We'll have professional maintainers with salaries and mental health support. We'll have AI tools that act as apprentices, not replacements. We'll have legal frameworks that protect the commons. And we'll have a generation of developers who understand that their most important skill isn't prompting—it's judgment.

But only if we build it. Only if we choose to.

The open source community has always been the immune system of the internet. We've found the bugs, patched the holes, and shouted truth to power. Now we need to heal ourselves.

So here's my ask: Stop treating open source like a free buffet. Start treating it like a public park that your children will play in. Pick up the trash. Pay the ranger. Teach the next generation where the trails are.

[Pause, then deliver the final lines slowly and deliberately]

The future of open source was never about licenses or repositories. It was about the radical idea that we build better things together than we ever could apart.

AI can write the next line of code. But only we can write the next chapter.

Let's make it one worth reading.

[Thank you. Hold for applause.]

**The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question**

[Stage: Center, conversational]

At 2:47 AM last Tuesday, while most of us were asleep, a software developer in Nebraska—let’s call him Dave—merged a pull request that patched a zero-day vulnerability. The library Dave maintains sits thirteen layers deep in the dependency tree of a payment processor you probably used yesterday. It has 4,200 dependent packages. It has three active maintainers. And it runs on a budget of roughly eighty dollars a month in Patreon pledges.

Dave merged the fix, closed his laptop, and stared at the ceiling until dawn. He has 847 unread GitHub notifications. He hasn’t taken a real vacation in three years. And last month, he seriously considered deleting his account and becoming a barista.

[Pause]

We are here today because we love the craft of building things together. But we need to talk about the fact that our entire digital civilization rests on the mental health of people like Dave. We need to talk about what happens when the machines start writing the code. And we need to talk about whether open source—real open source, not just code dumps with permissive licenses—can survive the next decade.

**The Sustainability Crisis**

Let’s start with the uncomfortable math. The modern software stack is a miracle of collective intelligence. A single npm install might pull in a thousand transitive dependencies, each one a gift from strangers. We have built a trillion-dollar industry on the invisible infrastructure of volunteer labor. And we are burning through that capital at an alarming rate.

We’ve all seen the XKCD comic—the one about the critical project maintained by a random person in Nebraska. It’s funny because it’s true. But the punchline isn’t just about geographic distribution. It’s about the tragedy of the commons. We treat open source like infrastructure—we depend on it absolutely—but we fund it like hobbycraft.

The symptoms are everywhere. Maintainer burnout isn’t just anecdotal anymore; it’s systemic. We’ve normalized a culture where Fortune 500 companies demand immediate security patches from individuals working on weekends, then complain when those patches break backward compatibility. We’ve created an entitlement economy where the maintainers feel guilty for needing sleep, and the users feel frustrated for needing stability.

And it’s not just about money. Yes, funding matters. The GitHub Sponsors and Open Collective pledges help. But sustainability is also about succession. It’s about governance. It’s about the fact that many critical projects are still “benevolent dictator” models where the bus factor is literally one. When that person burns out—or gets hit by a bus, or simply decides to go be a barista—the code doesn’t die immediately. It enters a slower, more insidious decay. Dependencies rot. Security holes fester. And the next generation of developers inherits technical debt they don’t understand.

We are living through the Great Maintenance Crisis. And we haven’t even talked about the robots yet.

**The AI Question**

For the last two years, we’ve been flooded with predictions that AI will replace programmers. Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude—these tools can now generate boilerplate faster than we can type, debug errors we’ve never seen, and even write documentation that’s almost accurate. For open source, this should be a golden age, right? Infinite contributors! Automated triage! No more “good first issue” tickets languishing for years!

But look closer. The reality is more complicated.

First, there’s the licensing entropy. These models were trained on billions of lines of open source code—much of it under copyleft licenses—and now they emit synthetic code that may or may not infringe on those licenses. We are sleepwalking into a legal gray zone where the provenance of our software becomes untraceable. When AI-generated code enters the commons, who owns it? Who maintains it? When it breaks, who do we blame?

Second, and more dangerously, AI is about to flood the zone with low-grade contributions. We’re already seeing it: pull requests opened by bots, documentation “improved” by LLMs that don’t understand context, issue comments generated by agents that haven’t read the thread. The bottleneck in open source was never code generation. It was code *review*. It was the cognitive load of maintaining context across thousands of conversations, of understanding architectural intent, of saying “no” to features that would break the philosophy of the project.

AI makes it trivial to create. It makes it exhausting to curate.

But here’s the twist that gives me hope: AI also exposes what actually matters in open source. For years, we confused open source with “free code.” But open source was never about the source code. It was about the social contract. It was about governance, trust, and the slow, messy work of building consensus among humans with different agendas.

AI can generate a sorting algorithm. It cannot generate the RFC process that decides whether that algorithm belongs in the standard library. It cannot mediate a conflict between two contributors who both think they’re right. It cannot write the empathy required to onboard a nervous first-time contributor. 

In other words, AI commoditizes the easy part—the syntax—and makes the hard part—the community—more valuable than ever.

**A Vision for the Next Decade**

So where do we go from here? How do we build an open source ecosystem that survives both the sustainability crisis and the AI disruption?

I believe we need three fundamental shifts.

**First, we must professionalize maintenance.** Not by killing the volunteer spirit, but by recognizing that critical digital infrastructure deserves institutional support. We need to move beyond the “heroic lone maintainer” model and toward consortium governance. Foundations like the Linux Foundation, the Python Software Foundation, and the Rust Foundation are proving that we can treat maintenance as infrastructure engineering, not as a side hustle. Companies that depend on open source need to stop thinking of sponsorship as charity and start thinking of it as a utility bill. You don’t donate to the electric company. You pay for power because you depend on it.

This means creating career paths for maintainers. We need “Staff Maintainer” roles at companies, where engineers are paid to work upstream. We need tenure tracks for open source governance. We need to teach computer science students not just how to write code, but how to read it, how to deprecate it, and how to hand it off.

**Second, we need to embrace AI as a maintainer’s assistant, not a replacement.** The future is hybrid. Imagine AI agents that handle the first-line triage—closing stale issues, requesting reproduction steps, suggesting documentation fixes—freeing up human maintainers to do the architectural thinking. Imagine tools that automatically generate migration guides when APIs change, or that summarize years of mailing list debates for new contributors.

But—and this is crucial—these tools must be governed by the community, not imposed by platforms. The danger is that AI becomes another extraction layer, where tech giants scrape open source code to train models, then sell those models back to us as “productivity tools,” while the original maintainers still can’t pay their rent. We need to flip that script. We need AI models that are trained transparently, licensed fairly, and whose economic benefits flow back to the commons they depend on.

**Third, and most importantly, we need to redesign open source for interdependence.** The next decade will be defined by climate change, geopolitical instability, and the consolidation of corporate power. Open source has always been political—it was born from the idea that knowledge should be free—but we’ve often pretended it’s neutral.

We need to build systems that assume fragility. That means better succession planning as a feature, not an afterthought. It means “maintainer health” metrics alongside code coverage. It means teaching organizations that using open source without contributing back is not “efficient”—it’s risky. It’s technical debt with interest rates that can spike overnight.

We need to celebrate the social code—the governance models, the codes of conduct, the decision logs—as much as we celebrate the source code. Because when the AI can write the functions, the value proposition of open source becomes the *process* by which we decide which functions matter.

**Conclusion**

[Pause, step forward]

Fifteen years ago, we thought open source was about licenses. Then we thought it was about GitHub stars. Then we thought it was about venture-backed “open core” business models.

We were wrong every time.

Open source is a commons of care. It is the radical, fragile idea that strangers can build things together without asking permission—and that those things can outlast any single contributor, any single company, any single technology trend.

The AI revolution will not kill open source. But it will force us to answer a harder question: If the code is free, and now the code writes itself, what are we actually building together?

The answer is trust. The answer is governance. The answer is the slow, expensive, deeply human work of maintaining relationships across time zones and ideologies.

So here is my charge to you: If you use open source, fund it like infrastructure. If you maintain open source, protect your boundaries like a professional. And if you’re building AI tools, remember that you are standing on the shoulders of giants—giants who are tired, who are underpaid, and who deserve better than to be scraped and forgotten.

The future of open source is not a repository of code generated by machines. It is a covenant between humans, mediated by machines, sustained by the recognition that software is made of people.

[Pause]

Code is easy. Community is hard. That’s why they can’t automate us away.

Thank you.

[Stage: Step back, applause]

The future of open source is not a repository of code generated by machines. It is a covenant between humans, mediated by machines, sustained by the recognition that software is made of people.

[Pause]

Code is easy. Community is hard. That’s why the community—the us—can’t be automated.

Thank you.

And we need to stop talking about the “bus factor” as if human beings were risk variables in a spreadsheet. We’ve built an entire vocabulary around maintainer replaceability while doing almost nothing to make maintainers *want to stay*. The problem isn’t that Dave might get hit by a bus. It’s that Dave is staring at the ceiling at 3 AM wondering why he’s sacrificing his health for companies that won’t pay him enough to fix their own security holes.

This is increasingly a Global South story, too. Some of the most critical infrastructure in our stack is maintained by developers in Nigeria, India, and Brazil—places where eighty dollars in Patreon pledges goes further, but where access to corporate sponsorship, healthcare, and conference networks is severely limited. We talk about open source as a global commons, but we fund it like a Western hobby.

Yes, money matters. But sustainability is also about succession. It’s about governance. It’s about the fact that many critical projects are still “benevolent dictator” models where the technical debt includes a single human psyche. **The AI Question**

For the last two years, we’ve been flooded with predictions about AI. The interesting question was never whether Copilot or ChatGPT would replace programmers. It’s whether AI changes the *economics* of open source contribution in ways that destabilize the ecosystem.

First, there’s the licensing entropy. These models were trained on billions of lines of open source code—much of it under copyleft licenses—and now they emit synthetic code that may or may not infringe on those licenses. We are sleepwalking into a legal gray zone where the provenance of software becomes untraceable. When AI-generated code enters the commons, who owns it? Who maintains it? When it breaks, who do we blame? These aren’t abstract questions; they’re being tested right now in cases like *Doe v. GitHub*, and in emerging corporate policies requiring AI-assisted code disclosure. The law is five years behind the technology, and we’re building our infrastructure in that gap.

Second, and more dangerously, AI is about to flood the zone with low-grade contributions. We’re already seeing it: remember the 2023 Gentoo spam incident, where automated tools generated hundreds of nonsensical pull requests? Or the Hacktoberfest chaos of a few years back, where t-shirt hunters drowned maintainers in trivial changes? That was the dress rehearsal. Now imagine every casual user armed with an agent that can generate plausible-looking documentation “improvements” that subtly break technical accuracy, or issue comments that haven’t read the thread but sound authoritative.

The bottleneck in open source was never code generation. It was code *review*. It was the cognitive load of maintaining context across thousands of conversations, of understanding architectural intent, of saying “no” to features that would break the philosophy of the project.

AI makes it trivial to create. It makes it exhausting to curate.

Here’s the asymmetry nobody’s talking about: AI tooling benefits platforms and drive-by contributors far more than it benefits maintainers. The same technology that could help Dave triage issues can also generate fifty new low-quality issues for him to triage. The cost of opening a PR approaches zero, while the cost of reviewing it remains constant. We are about to see a collapse in the signal-to-noise ratio of contribution, and we have not built the filtration systems to handle it.

It was about the social contract. It was about governance, trust, and the slow, messy work of building consensus among humans with different agendas.

It cannot mediate a conflict between two contributors who both think they’re right. It cannot write the empathy required to onboard a nervous first-time contributor in a timezone twelve hours away.

**A Vision for the Next Decade**

So where do we go from here? How do we build an open source ecosystem that survives both the sustainability crisis and the AI disruption?

We need to move beyond the “heroic lone maintainer” model and toward consortium governance. Foundations like the Linux Foundation, the Python Software Foundation, and the Rust Foundation are proving that we can treat maintenance as infrastructure engineering, not as a side hustle. Companies that depend on open source need to stop thinking of sponsorship as charity and start thinking of it as a utility bill. You don’t donate to the electric company. You pay for power because you depend on it.

This means creating career paths for maintainers. We need “Staff Maintainer” roles at companies, where engineers are paid to work upstream. We need tenure tracks for open source governance. We need to teach computer science students not just how to write code, but how to read it, how to deprecate it, and how to hand it off.

Some will argue that professionalization kills the volunteer ethos—that the magic of open source comes from passionate amateurs working outside corporate structures. There’s truth there. Imagine tools that automatically generate migration guides when APIs change, or that summarize years of mailing list debates for new contributors.

The danger is that AI becomes another extraction layer, where tech giants scrape open source code to train models, then sell those models back to us as “productivity tools,” while the original maintainers still can’t pay their rent. We need to flip that script. We need AI models that are trained transparently, licensed fairly, and whose economic benefits flow back to the commons they depend on.

We need concrete mechanisms, not just aspirations. I propose we adopt “maintainer transition protocols”—standardized, documented procedures for how a project transfers leadership, modeled on corporate succession planning but adapted for volunteer communities. We need “sustainability scores” displayed alongside package metadata, measuring not just code coverage but maintainer health, documentation freshness, and governance maturity.

Open source has always been political. It was born from Stallman’s radical proposition that “free” meant freedom, not price—the idea that knowledge should be liberated from proprietary control. But we’ve spent two decades pretending it’s neutral, apolitical infrastructure. It’s not. It’s a battleground between extraction and cooperation. The next decade will be defined by whether we can defend the commons against enclosure.

**Conclusion**

[Pause, step forward]

Fifteen years ago, we thought open source was about licenses. Then we thought it was about GitHub stars. Then we thought it was about venture-backed “open core” business models.

We were wrong every time.

Open source is a commons of care. It is the radical, fragile idea that strangers can build things together without asking permission—and that those things can outlast any single contributor, any single company, any single technology trend.

The AI revolution will not kill open source. But it will force us to answer a harder question: If the code is free, and now the code writes itself, what are we actually building together?

The answer is trust. The answer is governance. The answer is the slow, expensive, deeply human work of maintaining relationships across time zones and ideologies.

So what does this mean for Monday morning? If you use open source, fund it like infrastructure. If you maintain open source, protect your boundaries like a professional. And if you’re building AI tools, remember that you are standing on the shoulders of giants—giants who are tired, who are underpaid, and who deserve better than to be scraped and forgotten.

The future of open source is not a repository of code generated by machines. It is a covenant between humans, mediated by machines, sustained by the recognition that software is made of people.

[Pause]

Code is easy. Community is hard. That’s why they can’t automate us away.

Thank you.

AI integration is measured by adoption of transparent, community-governed tools and reduction in maintainer burnout. Interdependence is measured by cross-project collaboration agreements and shared governance policies.

[Pause, step forward]

Open source isn’t just code; it’s a covenant.

AI will change the pace, not the purpose.

If the code is free, let the governance be brave.

Fund it like infrastructure. Protect it like a boundary. Build it as a community.

[Pause]

Code is easy. Community is hard. That’s why they can’t automate us away.

Thank you.

Thank you.

*[Pause for emphasis]*

This creates three existential risks to open source that we’re not talking about enough.

First: the licensing gray zone. When an AI model ingests copyleft code and outputs synthetic code, is that a derivative work? Projects like License Zero and the AI Model Openness Framework are experimenting with new licenses and training opt-outs, but courts will take years to decide. In the meantime, we’re normalizing a world where the legal frameworks that protect copyleft—those carefully crafted licenses that ensured freedom—are being dissolved by statistical models that don’t understand intent.

*[Pause]*

We’re creating a generation of developers who can prompt but cannot comprehend.

*[Pause]*

The irony is almost too perfect. We extract value from maintainers for twenty years without paying them, use that value to train models that automate their work, and then wonder why no one wants to maintain open source anymore.

*[Step to side]*

But let’s be fair—AI is also democratizing contribution. A student in Lagos can now get meaningful help understanding the Linux kernel. The question isn’t whether AI is good or bad. It’s: who controls the loop?

And while we’re fighting over Copilot, a new commons is emerging: open-source AI models like Llama and Mistral. The battle for the next decade won’t just be about code—it’ll be about whether the *means of production* for AI itself remain open.

Here’s the thing. I’m not here to declare that AI is the enemy. Because I actually think—if we’re very careful, and very intentional—AI could be the thing that saves open source. But only if we stop thinking about AI as a replacement for community and start thinking about it as infrastructure for community.

So what does thriving look like in 2034?

First, we implement the Stewardship Model at scale. Imagine a world where every major tech company has Open Source Engineers who spend their time maintaining the dependencies they rely on. Not as a side project, but as a core job function.

I want to see a Fortune 500 company lose a SOC 2 audit because they *don’t* have upstream maintainers on staff. That’s the incentive shift we need.

Second, we need to reimagine AI as a maintainer’s assistant, not a replacement. Picture this: an AI that triages issues, writes documentation, handles the “good first issue” onboarding for new contributors, and automates the bureaucratic toil that burns maintainers out. The human maintainer focuses on architecture, community building, and vision. The AI handles the drudgery.

This isn’t science fiction. We can build this. But it requires that we train these models transparently, with consent, and with revenue sharing. If your AI was trained on my code, I should get a slice of the pie. Not as charity—as justice.

Third, we need to protect the craft. We need to teach the next generation not just to prompt, but to understand. We need “read the source” to be a rite of passage again. AI should lower the barrier to entry, not the barrier to comprehension. We need interfaces that explain code, not just generate it. We need AI that teaches, not just performs.

Finally, we need to embrace what I call **The Commons 2.0**—a federated ecosystem where projects aren’t isolated fiefdoms but part of a resilient network. Where maintainers have health insurance, where burnout is recognized as an occupational hazard, and where we’ve replaced the hero’s journey with sustainable, team-based stewardship.

*[Move to center]*

If you’re an engineering leader wondering where to start, here’s your first 90 days: conduct a dependency audit. Identify your top 10 critical open-source packages. Then fund them directly, with a 3-year commitment. No strings attached.

This future is possible. But it requires us to make a choice. We can let AI accelerate the extraction economy—automating creation while ignoring care. Or we can use this technological inflection point to redesign the incentives that govern our digital world.

**Conclusion**

*[Pause, slow down]*

I started with the xz utils backdoor. Let me end with something else.

Last year, I watched a maintainer—someone who’d kept a critical Python library alive for eight years—announce they were stepping down. Not because they stopped caring, but because they couldn’t afford to care anymore. The comments filled with heart emojis and “thank you for your service.” Three weeks later, a corporation that had built a billion-dollar product on that library posted a job opening: “AI Infrastructure Engineer, $400K.”

That’s the world we’re leaving behind if we don’t change course.

*[Step forward, voice rising slightly]*

But here’s what I believe: code is temporary. Algorithms decay. Languages go extinct. But community—the relationships we build, the standards we uphold, the care we show for the commons—that’s the only technology that endures.

*[Pause]*

The future of open source isn’t artificial intelligence. It’s human wisdom—funded, federated, and finally, sustainable.

*[Speaker steps back, applause]*

# The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question

## A 15-Minute Conference Talk

---

**[SLIDE: Black screen. Single line of code appears:]**

```
import { future } from 'open-source';
```

**[SPEAKER walks to center stage, pauses]**

In 1991, a Finnish graduate student announced he was working on "just a hobby, won't be big and professional." Thirty-three years later, that hobby—Linux—runs on every smartphone, most of the world's servers, and increasingly, the infrastructure of our daily lives.

But here's what keeps me up at night: **the open source that built our world is running on fumes.**

**[SLIDE: Graph showing maintainer burnout, funding gaps, security incidents]**

I'm not here to deliver another eulogy for open source. We've heard those. I'm here because I believe we can still choose a different future—but only if we confront three forces that are colliding right now: the sustainability crisis, the transformation of community, and what I call "the AI question."

Let me take you through each, and then I'll share what I think thriving open source actually looks like in 2035.

---

**[SLIDE: "The Sustainability Crisis: By the Numbers"]**

First, the crisis we don't talk about enough.

The `log4j` vulnerability in 2021 affected three billion devices. It was maintained by—let me check my notes—three unpaid volunteers, one of whom had stepped back due to burnout. When the crisis hit, they worked through holidays while Fortune 500 companies demanded fixes on Twitter.

This isn't an edge case. It's the model.

Research from Tidelift and the Linux Foundation shows that the average open source maintainer spends fewer than five hours per week on their projects. Not because they lack passion, but because they're fitting critical infrastructure maintenance between full-time jobs, family obligations, and sleep.

**[SLIDE: Quote from maintainer survey]**

One maintainer wrote: *"I feel like I'm operating a nuclear power plant in my spare time, and the only compensation is angry GitHub issues."*

The economics are broken. We've built a trillion-dollar industry on volunteer labor and goodwill, and we've convinced ourselves this is sustainable because... it always has been? That's not strategy. That's denial.

But here's where it gets interesting. The funding solutions we've tried—corporate sponsorships, Tidelift, GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective—are necessary but insufficient. They're treating symptoms. The deeper problem is that **we've industrialized open source consumption without industrializing its production.**

Every company has an open source strategy for *using* code. Few have strategies for *maintaining* the code they depend on. We've created a massive free-rider problem, and we keep hoping moral suasion will solve it.

It won't.

---

**[SLIDE: "Enter AI: The Disruption We Didn't Ask For"]**

Now let's talk about the elephant in the room. Or rather, the elephant generating code in the room.

GitHub Copilot launched in 2021. Two years later, it's generating 35% of code on GitHub. Other estimates suggest AI-assisted development is now standard across major tech companies. And we're just getting started.

**[SPEAKER pauses]**

I want to be careful here. I'm not an AI skeptic. I use these tools daily. They've made me faster, helped me explore unfamiliar languages, caught bugs I would have missed.

But I want to ask a question that I think we're not asking enough: **What happens to open source when the primary mode of contribution changes from human craft to AI generation?**

Consider three scenarios.

**[SLIDE: Three panels]**

**First: The dilution problem.** If AI makes it trivial to generate code, we may see an explosion of low-quality contributions—PRs that compile but don't fit the project's philosophy, documentation that reads like... well, like AI wrote it. Maintainers, already stretched thin, now become curators of machine output. The signal-to-noise ratio degrades.

**Second: The attribution crisis.** Current AI systems are trained on open source code—often without clear licensing compliance, almost always without compensation to the original authors. We're watching the largest uncompensated transfer of intellectual labor in history. The legal frameworks are struggling to catch up, but the ethical question is immediate: **Is open source becoming a commons that we all exploit while AI companies privatize the gains?**

**Third—and this is where I get genuinely uncertain—the transformation of expertise.** Open source has always been, in part, a credentialing system. You contribute to significant projects, you demonstrate skill, you build reputation, you advance your career. If AI intermediates this—if the path from "interested developer" to "respected contributor" becomes opaque or automated—what happens to the talent pipeline that sustains projects?

I don't have definitive answers to these questions. I don't think anyone does yet. But I know this: **treating AI as just another tool, without considering how it reshapes the social and economic fabric of open source, is a category error.**

---

**[SLIDE: "Community: The Variable We Can't Optimize Away"]**

Let me pivot to something I think we *can* influence, and must.

At its core, open source has never been about code. It's about **community as coordination mechanism.** The license is the legal framework, but the community is the living organism that makes decisions, resolves conflicts, allocates attention, and sustains motivation through difficulty.

This is where I'm most optimistic, and most concerned.

Optimistic because we've learned a tremendous amount about building healthy technical communities. The work of Nadia Eghbal, the CHAOSS project, the evolution of codes of conduct, the growing recognition that maintainership is a skill to be developed—these represent genuine progress. We know more about sustainable open source governance than ever before.

**[SLIDE: Principles of healthy communities]**

Concerned because the pressures are intensifying. The sustainability crisis creates burnout, which hollows out communities. The AI transformation risks replacing collaborative learning with transactional code generation. And geopolitically, we're seeing fragmentation—sanctions affecting open source participation, national regulations diverging, the ideal of a global commons under strain.

But here's my core conviction: **The communities that thrive in the next decade will be those that treat themselves as primary assets, not incidental byproducts.**

What does this look like in practice?

It means explicit succession planning—treating maintainership as a role with defined responsibilities, support structures, and off-ramps. It means investment in contributor experience, not just user experience. It means recognizing that documentation, onboarding, and conflict resolution are technical skills worthy of recognition and compensation.

It also means rethinking scale. We've celebrated projects with thousands of contributors, but some of the most sustainable models I've seen are intentionally small—communities of 10-50 people with strong relationships, clear boundaries, and realistic scope.

---

**[SLIDE: "A Vision for 2035: Thriving Open Source"]**

So let me sketch what I think thriving open source looks like in ten years. Not prediction—aspiration. The future we could build if we make deliberate choices.

**First: Sustainable funding as infrastructure, not charity.**

By 2035, I hope we've normalized the idea that critical open source deserves institutional funding as a matter of economic rationality, not generosity. This means companies treating open source maintenance as a line item, like cloud infrastructure or security. It means public funding recognizing open source as digital public infrastructure. It means new models—perhaps something like a "public benefit corporation" structure for essential projects—that align incentives without capturing value.

**Second: AI as amplifier, not replacement, of human judgment.**

I imagine AI systems that are explicitly designed to support open source communities—tools that help maintainers review code, that assist with documentation, that lower barriers to contribution without eliminating the learning that comes from struggle. The key is **augmentation that preserves agency.** The maintainer remains the decision-maker. The contributor still grows through engagement.

This requires intentional design. The default path—AI systems trained on open source to replace open source contributors—is not inevitable. We can build differently.

**Third: Governance models that match scale and impact.**

Not every project needs the same structure. A utility library used by millions might need professional maintainers with institutional backing. A specialized tool for a niche community might thrive with volunteer governance. A project at the intersection of commercial interests might need explicit conflict-of-interest policies.

By 2035, I hope we've developed a richer vocabulary for these choices—moving beyond "BDFL" or "foundation" to a spectrum of models with documented tradeoffs.

**Fourth: Global participation that reflects global impact.**

Open source has always been more diverse than tech generally, but power still concentrates. The maintainers of critical infrastructure, the voices in governance, the recipients of funding—these remain skewed. Thriving open source means genuine global participation, which requires addressing barriers of language, timezone, visa policy, and economic access that we've too often treated as intractable.

---

**[SLIDE: Return to single line of code]**

I opened with a line of code. Let me close with a story.

Last year, I spoke with a maintainer who's kept a project alive for fifteen years. It's not famous. It doesn't have a corporate sponsor. But thousands of developers depend on it daily. I asked how he's sustained the work.

He said: **"I stopped trying to be a hero. I started treating it like gardening."**

Gardening. Not architecture, with its grand designs and finished products. Not manufacturing, with its efficiency metrics. Gardening—ongoing, seasonal, responsive to conditions, requiring patience and attention and the acceptance that some things will fail.

I think this is the mindset we need. Open source was never a finished achievement. It's a continuous practice of cultivation. And like any garden, it can thrive or wither depending on whether we show up, whether we invest, whether we adapt to changing conditions.

**[SPEAKER steps forward]**

The AI question, the sustainability crisis, the transformation of community—these are not threats to be survived. They're invitations to evolve. The open source that built our world was created by people who imagined that collaboration could outcompete control, that transparency could outperform secrecy, that gift economies could coexist with market economies.

Those people were right. And their successors—we—now face the task of proving that this vision can renew itself.

**[SLIDE: Final quote]**

So here's my closing thought, the line I hope you remember:

**"Open source doesn't need saving. It needs gardeners who are willing to get their hands dirty in soil that AI can't yet touch—relationships, judgment, and the stubborn belief that code is better when we build it together."**

Thank you.

**[SPEAKER exits]**

---

*[END OF TALK]*

# The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question

The library was faker.js. The maintainer was Marak Squires. And what happened next became a watershed moment for our entire industry.

It laid bare a fundamental truth we've been dancing around for years: **the infrastructure of the modern software economy runs on volunteer time and personal burnout.**

[Pause]

Now, I know this audience. I know many of you build your entire careers on open source. You've contributed to projects, maybe even maintain one. You understand the romance of it—the idea that code should be free, collaborative, universal.

But I'm here today to tell you that romance is under threat. Not from outside forces. Not from some grand conspiracy. But from a perfect storm of economic pressures, shifting technology, and hard truths about what sustainability actually means.

And yes—I'll get to the AI question. Because that's the elephant in every room these days.

[Transition]

---

[SECTION 1: SUSTAINABILITY CHALLENGES]

Let me give you some numbers. Stripe research found that the average large company uses over 600 open source dependencies. Six hundred. Think about the attack surface there. Now think about who maintains those dependencies.

Here's the uncomfortable reality: **most open source maintainers are working essentially for free.** Not because they're naive or don't understand their value—but because the funding mechanisms we've built are broken.

Let's look at what actually sustains projects today. Sponsorships? A handful of companies have stepped up—Google, Microsoft, Red Hat. Their contributions matter. But they're the exception, not the rule. GitHub Sponsors has helped many individual maintainers, but let's be honest: the distribution is brutal. A few projects get meaningful funding. Most get almost nothing.

And then there's the hidden cost we don't talk about enough: **the maintenance burden doesn't scale linearly.** As a project grows, so do issues, pull requests, security vulnerabilities, and community management demands. One person handling 500 issues isn't sustainable. It's not a job—it's a lifestyle that consumes everything else.

I've talked to maintainers who describe themselves as "on call" for their spare time. Who check GitHub before bed, worried about security disclosures. Who haven't taken a real vacation in years because there's no backup.

[Emphatic]

This isn't noble. This is a structural failure.

The companies building billion-dollar businesses on open source code have a responsibility here. And I'm not just pointing fingers—I'm including myself, including my own organization. We all benefit from this ecosystem. We all have skin in the game.

[Pause]

---

[SECTION 2: AI AND THE LANDSCAPE SHIFT]

Now let's talk about what everyone wants to discuss. AI. Specifically, AI-generated code.

[Shift in tone—acknowledge the complexity]

Here's my honest take: I'm not afraid of AI replacing developers. I've been in this industry long enough to know that every "developer-killing" technology has instead made us more productive. The compiler didn't kill assembly programmers. High-level languages didn't kill C programmers. And AI won't kill us either.

But here's what does concern me: **AI is changing the nature of open source contribution itself.**

Think about it. When someone submits a pull request to your project today, there's an implicit assumption—a social contract, really—that a human being read the codebase, understood the architecture, and made a thoughtful change. We review code assuming a human wrote it with care.

Now imagine a future where 30% of your pull requests are AI-generated. Not necessarily wrong, but generated without deep understanding of your project's context, conventions, or long-term direction. Generated because someone wanted a quick fix and an AI assistant made it easy.

[Rhetorical question]

What happens to the quality bar of open source when code production becomes frictionless?

We already see this happening. Maintainers report an uptick in low-quality contributions. PRs that look right but don't actually solve the problem. Issues opened that are really just prompts for AI to answer. The volunteer time that was already scarce is now being consumed by triaging work that has less signal and more noise.

And there's another dimension we need to consider: **the training data question.**

Large language models are trained on publicly available code—much of it open source. The people who wrote that code didn't consent to having it used as fuel for models that may eventually replace the value of writing code itself. There's a legitimate argument here about reciprocity, about whether the open source community should benefit from the value being extracted from it.

This isn't a solved problem. And anyone who tells you they have all the answers about AI and open source is selling something.

[Transition]

---

[SECTION 3: A VISION FOR THE NEXT DECADE]

So where does this leave us? Feeling doomed?

[Turn the corner—toward hope and actionable vision]

No. I'm actually optimistic. But my optimism isn't naive. It's grounded in what I see as possible when we make deliberate choices.

Here's what I believe needs to happen in the next decade:

**One: We need to professionalize maintenance, not romanticize burnout.**

The volunteer model got us here, but it can't get us to the next level. That means companies need to fund maintainers as legitimate roles—not as side projects, not as hobbies, but as real jobs with real compensation. It means foundations need to step up with sustainable grant funding. It means we need to treat open source sustainability as infrastructure investment, not charity.

**Two: We need to build community, not just code.**

The projects that will thrive are the ones that invest in human connection. Not just contributors, but stewards. Mentors. People who onboard new maintainers and build succession plans. The projects that treat their community as an asset—not a resource to be mined—will outlast the ones that don't.

[Strong statement]

**The code is the artifact. The community is the organism.**

**Three: We need to shape AI as a tool, not a takeover.**

[Pause]

---

[CONCLUSION - Bring it home with a quotable, memorable ending]

I'll leave you with this.

[Deliver slowly, with conviction]

That idea didn't just build our industry. It built the modern world.

But ideas aren't enough. They need to be tended. They need to be funded. They need to evolve. And they need people—real people, with real lives—who choose to show up and do the work.

[Build to climax]

The question isn't whether open source survives. It will. The question is what shape it takes. Whether it becomes a sustainable ecosystem where maintainers are supported, communities are valued, and AI is a partner, not a threat. Or whether we let it drift into a world of burnout, broken promises, and code that's free in all the wrong ways.

[Final statement - deliver with power]

The future of open source isn't written in code. It's written in the choices we make about who gets paid, what gets built, and how we treat each other while building it.

**It's something we build. Together.**

So let's build something worth having.

[Pause, then:]

Thank you.
