When GitHub Copilot was trained, it ingested 1.2 billion lines of GPL-licensed code. The legal question is murky, but the ethical one is clear: if that model generates a snippet verbatim, should the original maintainer be compensated?

Some propose a **training data dividend**—a micro-payment to projects whose code appears in model outputs. It's not perfect, but it's a start. The people who wrote that code didn't consent to having it used as fuel for models that may eventually replace the value of writing code itself. There's a legitimate argument here about reciprocity, about whether the open source community should benefit from the value being extracted from it.

[Pause]

This isn't a solved problem. And anyone who tells you they have all the answers about AI and open source is selling something.

[Transition]

---

[SECTION 3: A VISION FOR THE NEXT DECADE]

So where does this leave us? Feeling doomed?

[Turn the corner—toward hope and actionable vision]

No. I'm actually optimistic. But my optimism isn't naive. It's grounded in what I see as possible when we make deliberate choices.

Here's what I believe needs to happen in the next decade. I call it the **Three Pillars of Sustainable Open Source**: **Fund the Humans**, **Grow the Community**, **Shape the Tools**. Miss any one, and the structure collapses.

**One: Fund the Humans—professionalize maintenance, not romanticize burnout.**

The volunteer model got us here, but it can't get us to the next level. That means companies need to fund maintainers as legitimate roles—not as side projects, not as hobbies, but as real jobs with real compensation.

Foundations need to step up with sustainable grant funding. We need to treat open source sustainability as infrastructure investment, not charity.

**Two: Grow the Community—build community, not just code.**

The projects that will thrive are the ones that invest in human connection. Not just contributors, but stewards. Mentors. People who onboard new maintainers and build succession plans.

The Rust project doesn't just have contributors—it has working groups, mentorship programs, and an explicit goal of rotating leadership every two years. That's not accidental—it's designed.

The projects that treat their community as an asset—not a resource to be mined—will outlast the ones that don't.

[Strong statement]

**The code is the artifact. The community is the organism.**

**Three: Shape the Tools—AI as a partner, not a takeover.**

Open source communities have agency here. We can set the terms. We can build norms around AI-assisted contribution.

The Python Software Foundation is drafting an **AI Contribution Manifesto**—requiring contributors to disclose AI assistance and banning it entirely for security-critical code. They're writing the rules we all need.

Here's a rule we could adopt tomorrow: All AI-generated PRs must include a **context affidavit**—a brief statement from the human submitter explaining *why* this change fits the project's architecture. Not perfect, but it restores the social contract.

And we can use AI to reduce our maintenance burden—the maintainers of `numpy` are experimenting with AI to auto-generate documentation for undocumented functions. They're reclaiming 15 hours a week—time they're reinvesting in mentorship. The tool isn't the threat; the *unintentional use* is.

The key is intentionality. We get to decide what role AI plays in our communities. We get to write the rules.

**Four: Measure what matters.**

Let's be honest: we've been measuring open source success wrong. Stars? Forks? Downloads? These are vanity metrics. What we should be measuring is sustainability. Maintainer retention. Contributor diversity. Time-to-resolution for issues. Are people staying? Are new voices entering? Is the project still alive in five years?

[Pause]

---

[CONCLUSION - Bring it home with a quotable, memorable ending]

I'll leave you with this.

[Deliver slowly, with conviction]

Open source has always been about a radical idea: that when we share knowledge freely, everyone benefits. That transparency builds trust. That collaboration beats competition.

That idea didn't just build our industry. It built the modern world.

But ideas aren't enough. They need to be tended. They need to be funded. They need to evolve. And they need people—real people, with real lives—who choose to show up and do the work.

[Build to climax]

The question isn't whether open source survives. It will. The question is what shape it takes. Whether it becomes a sustainable ecosystem where maintainers are supported, communities are valued, and AI is a partner, not a threat. Or whether we let it drift into a world of burnout, broken promises, and code that's free in all the wrong ways.

[Final statement - deliver with power]

The future of open source isn't something that happens to us. **It's something we build. Together.**

The future of open source isn't free as in beer, or free as in speech. **It's free as in sustainable.**

[Pause, then:]

Let's build something worth having.

Thank you.

---

*[End of talk]*

Keep them up. Now keep them raised if you couldn't tell me—the person maintaining that dependency—what their name is, or whether they got paid a single dollar to maintain the code your entire business runs on.

[Lower hands slowly]

That's what I thought.

What he discovered would become one of the most terrifying security vulnerabilities in recent memory: a backdoor had been inserted into xz Utils, a compression utility present on virtually every Linux server in the world.

The backdoor wasn't the work of a nation-state hacker. It was the work of a single maintainer—a long-term contributor who had gradually gained trust and then, for reasons we're still understanding, attempted to compromise a piece of critical infrastructure.

[Pause]

Here's what's terrifying about this story: **the project almost didn't have a maintainer at all.** The previous maintainer had essentially stepped away, burned out, looking for someone—anyone—to take over. The attacker saw that vacuum and filled it.

[Pause]

Now, I know this audience. I know many of you build your entire careers on open source. You've contributed to projects, maybe even maintain one. You understand the romance of it—the idea that code should be free, collaborative, universal.

But I'm here today to tell you that romance is under threat. Not from outside forces. Not from some grand conspiracy. But from a perfect storm of economic pressures, shifting technology, and hard truths about what sustainability actually means.

And yes—I'll get to the AI question. Because that's the elephant in every room these days.

[Transition]

---

Let me give you some numbers. Stripe research found that the average large company uses over 600 open source dependencies. Six hundred. Think about the attack surface there. Now think about who maintains those dependencies.

Here's the uncomfortable reality: **most open source maintainers are working essentially for free.** Not because they're naive or don't understand their value—but because the funding mechanisms we've built are broken.

Let's look at what actually sustains projects today. Corporate sponsorships? A handful of companies have stepped up—Google, Microsoft, Red Hat. Their contributions matter. But they're the exception, not the rule. GitHub Sponsors has helped many individual maintainers, but let's be honest: the distribution is brutal. A few projects get meaningful funding. Most get almost nothing.

And then there's the hidden cost we don't talk about enough: **the maintenance burden doesn't scale linearly.** As a project grows, so do issues, pull requests, security vulnerabilities, and community management demands. One person handling 500 issues isn't sustainable. It's not a job—it's a lifestyle that consumes everything else.

I've talked to maintainers who describe themselves as "on call" for their spare time. Who check GitHub before bed, worried about security disclosures. Who haven't taken a real vacation in years because there's no backup.

[Emphatic]

This isn't noble. This is a structural failure.

Here's a concept I want you to take back to your organizations: **the tragedy of the commons.** Companies rationally optimize for free resources. They use open source because it's free. They don't contribute back because... why would they? It's working fine. Until it isn't. Until the maintainer burns out, or walks away, or gets compromised. Each individual company is making the rational choice. But the aggregate is a system that's slowly failing.

[Pause]

I'll leave you with this.

# The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question

*[Note: This script is written for a 15-minute spoken presentation at a tech conference. Estimated delivery time: 14-16 minutes at a conversational pace.]*

---

## Opening

I want to start with a question. How many of you have that one dependency? The one that every project needs, that everyone uses, but that hasn't been updated in three years? The one where the GitHub page just says "looking for maintainers" and has seventeen unresolved security issues.

[PAUSE]

Now—how many of you have *multiple* dependencies like that?

Here's the thing. We've built the entire modern software industry on a foundation held up largely by volunteers. Passionate volunteers, brilliant volunteers—but volunteers nonetheless. People maintaining critical infrastructure on nights and weekends, between full-time jobs, often without any funding at all.

And it's *working*. It's staggeringly successful. Linux runs most of the internet. Python powers half of AI. React, Node, Rust—these projects have transformed what we build and how we build it.

But here's my concern: it's also *breaking*. Quietly, incrementally, project by project. And now there's a new force entering the equation that nobody fully understands yet.

[PAUSE]

This talk is about the intersection of three forces: sustainability, community, and AI. Not because they're separate topics, but because they're *the same* topic. They're all asking the same fundamental question:

What does it mean to build software together in 2025—and what will it mean in 2030?

---

## The Sustainability Crisis

Let me give you some numbers that kept me up at night while preparing this talk.

The OpenSSF estimates that 95% of critical open source projects have fewer than three full-time maintainers. *Critical* projects. The ones your entire infrastructure depends on.

The Linux Foundation's 2023 report found that over 60% of open source maintainers receive no funding whatsoever. Zero. They're doing this purely on passion and goodwill.

And here's the number that should scare you most: the average open source maintainer spends 30 hours a week on their project, but only 5 of those hours are *writing code*. The rest is triage, support, code review, managing contributors, dealing with issues, fighting with companies that use their code without contributing back.

[PAUSE]

We call it "free" software. But somebody's paying. It's just not the people using it.

There's a concept in our industry called the "bus factor"—the number of maintainers who could get hit by a bus before a project fails. For most open source projects, that number is one. One person. One burnout. One family emergency. One career change.

And then what?

I think about this differently now. I've been in this industry for fifteen years. I've built software at startups, at big tech, at companies you've heard of. And I can tell you—we are approaching a generational handoff. The founders of many critical projects are getting older. They're getting tired. They're wondering: *who will carry this forward?*

That's not a rhetorical question. That's an *existential* threat to our industry.

---

## The Community Question

Now, here's what gives me hope. The answer to sustainability isn't *less* open source. It's *better* open source communities.

[PAUSE]

We've spent decades optimizing for code. We measure lines of code, test coverage, performance benchmarks. But we've under-invested in the thing that actually keeps projects alive: *people*.

The most resilient open source projects I've seen aren't the ones with the most stars or the most contributors. They're the ones that have built genuine communities. Communities where newcomers feel welcome. Where contributions are acknowledged. Where the path from user to contributor to maintainer is clear and supported.

Think about what makes a healthy open source community. It's not just technical governance. It's *social* infrastructure. It's mentorship. It's documentation that actually helps new contributors. It's code review that teaches, not just evaluates. It's maintainers who can say "no" without burning bridges. It's clear communication about what's in scope and what isn't.

The projects thriving right now are the ones that have figured this out. Vue.js has a fantastic contributor guide and very clear pathways to becoming a core team member. Rust has built an entire culture around mentorship and welcoming newcomers. These aren't accidents—they're investments in community infrastructure.

[PAUSE]

And here's the thing that engineering leaders in this room need to hear: *you* are part of these communities. Your developers are using open source code every day. Your company benefits from it. And yet, how many of you have sent a single pull request to a project you depend on? How many of you have contributed back—not just with code, but with bug reports, with documentation improvements, with financial support?

The sustainability crisis isn't just a maintainer problem. It's a *user* problem. It's a *corporate* problem. We've built a model where the people who benefit most from open source are often the least likely to give back.

That's not a moral judgment. It's a structural problem. And we need to fix it.

---

## The AI Question

Now let's talk about the thing everyone wants to ask about but nobody wants to admit they're uncertain about: AI.

[PAUSE]

There's a narrative circulating right now that AI will make open source obsolete. Why maintain a library when you can generate the code you need? Why depend on someone else's implementation when AI can write it for you?

I've heard people say: "Open source was a necessary stepping stone. Now we have AI, and we don't need to share code anymore."

I think that's profoundly wrong. But I also think it's wrong for reasons that aren't obvious.

Let me break this down.

First, the *immediate* impact. AI coding assistants are already changing how developers interact with open source. Instead of pulling in a dependency, sometimes it's faster to just generate the function you need. And for some use cases—that's fine. If you need a standard algorithm implementation, AI can probably generate it adequately.

But here's what's interesting: the same AI tools are also *generating* open source code. They're training on open source repositories. They're writing code that gets contributed back—sometimes with human review, sometimes not.

This creates a strange loop. AI generates code trained on open source, which gets contributed back to open source, which trains the next generation of AI. We're not sure what the attractor state of that system is. We don't know if it converges to something better or something worse.

[PAUSE]

But here's what I *do* know.

AI doesn't solve the *trust* problem. It doesn't solve the *maintenance* problem. It doesn't solve the *long-term support* problem.

When you pull in a dependency from a human maintainer, there's someone you can talk to. Someone who understands the code. Someone who will respond when a critical vulnerability is discovered.

AI-generated code doesn't have that. It's a black box. It's someone's intellectual property in a different sense—not copyright, but *comprehension*. Can you debug it? Can you audit it for security? Can you trust it in production?

I think we're going to discover that for critical infrastructure, the answer is: not easily. Not without human maintainers who understand what's happening.

[PAUSE]

The second point is more subtle but maybe more important.

AI is *also* a community phenomenon. The best AI models aren't just trained on code—they're trained on the collective knowledge of open source communities. The documentation, the issues, the discussions, the decisions. That's the secret sauce. That's what makes the models useful.

Which means: open source communities aren't being made obsolete by AI. They're being *embedded* in AI. The question is whether they'll be credited, supported, and compensated for that contribution—or whether it will just be extracted.

That's the fight of the next decade. Not "AI vs open source." But *who controls* the AI that's built on open source, and *who benefits*.

---

## A Vision for the Next Decade

So where does this leave us? Let me propose three concrete shifts I believe we need.

**First: we need to fund the people, not just the code.**

The most impactful thing you can do for a project you depend on is pay the maintainers. Not through some abstract sustainability fund—directly. Sponsors, GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective, whatever works. Make it easy. Make it normal. Make it part of your procurement process.

If your company spends $50,000 on a SaaS license, you can afford to send $500 to the open source projects that license depends on. That's not charity. That's cost of goods sold.

**Second: we need to build community infrastructure like it's product.**

Documentation, contributor guides, mentorship programs, governance structures—these aren't "nice to have." They're the operating system of healthy projects. The best projects already treat them as product. The rest of us need to catch up.

And if you're an engineering leader: your developers are spending time on open source. That's not a distraction from their job—that *is* their job. Building the tools you use is part of building your product.

**Third: we need to shape AI's relationship to open source intentionally.**

This means supporting open source AI projects. It means demanding transparency in what models are trained on. It means building tools that give back to the communities that made them possible. It means not accepting a future where AI companies extract value from open source without reciprocating.

We have agency here. The choices we make now will determine whether AI amplifies open source or replaces it.

---

## Closing

I want to close with a story.

A few years ago, I was talking to a maintainer of a very popular open source library. This person had been maintaining it for over a decade. Ten years of late-night bug fixes. Ten years of ungrateful issues. Ten years of companies using their code in production without a single thank-you.

I asked them: "Why do you keep doing this?"

And they said: "Because someone has to."

[PAUSE]

That answer stuck with me. Not because it's noble—though it is—but because it's *true*. Open source isn't a philosophy experiment. It's infrastructure. It's the foundation of modern software. And somebody has to maintain it.

The question isn't whether open source survives. It will. The question is *who* maintains it, *how*, and *whether* we as an industry have the wisdom to support them.

We built this together. We can sustain it together.

But only if we choose to.

[PAUSE]

Thank you.

---

*[End of script. Approximate word count: 1850]*

We call it the "bus factor," but let's be honest—it's more often the "burnout factor" or the "I-need-to-pay-my-mortgage factor." For most open source projects, that number is one. One person. One burnout. One family emergency. One career change.

This isn't a bug in open source. It's a bug in how we *value* software. We've created a market where consumption is frictionless but contribution is expensive. Every npm install is a one-way street, and we've built a global highway system with no tolls.

# The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question

## Conference Talk Script

---

*[Pause. Make eye contact with the audience.]*

Last year, I got a message from a developer at a mid-sized company. They'd been using a popular open source library in their production system for three years. It had twelve thousand stars on GitHub. It was maintained by one person—a developer in Germany who had, in their words, "simply stopped responding."

No warning. No handoff. No goodbye. Just silence.

The library wasn't abandoned because it was bad. It was abandoned because its maintainer got burned out, got a new job, had a kid—pick a reason. The reason doesn't matter. What matters is that this company's production system now depended on code that no one was watching anymore.

This is the reality of open source in 2024. We build our entire digital infrastructure on borrowed time and borrowed goodwill.

*[Pause.]*

I'm here to talk about what we do next.

---

## The Sustainability Crisis No One Wants to Name

Let's start with some honesty. Open source has a sustainability problem, and we've been pretending it will solve itself.

I don't mean funding—though that's part of it. I mean *human* sustainability. The fundamental model where a handful of overworked maintainers keep the world's software running is breaking. It's been breaking for years. We just haven't wanted to look at it directly.

Consider the math. The Linux Foundation's latest report shows there are now over 200 million open source repositories on GitHub alone. But the median number of contributors to a repository is—wait for it—one. One person. And for a significant percentage of critical infrastructure, that one person is unpaid, unsupported, and running on passion and caffeine.

The "bus factor" in much of our infrastructure is genuinely one. One person gets hit by a bus, one person burns out, one person decides they need to sleep at night—and suddenly thousands of projects have no maintainer.

I've heard people say, "Well, if it's important, someone will step up." That's not a strategy. That's a prayer.

And here's what keeps me up at night: we're not just talking about hobby projects anymore. We're talking about the actual substrate of modern civilization. Healthcare systems. Financial infrastructure. Transportation. The code that runs our power grids. All of it built on the labor of people who, by any rational measure, should have quit years ago.

The OpenSSF estimates that over 95% of critical open source projects are understaffed. That's not a minority problem. That's an industry-wide crisis wearing a hoodie and pretending everything is fine.

---

## The Corporate Free-Ride

Now, here's where it gets uncomfortable.

A lot of companies—companies making billions of dollars—have built their entire business models on open source code that they have contributed almost nothing back to. They've taken the "move fast and break things" mentality and applied it to their relationship with the community. Use the code. Disrupt the market. Let someone else worry about the maintenance.

This isn't a lecture about corporate responsibility—though we can have that conversation. This is about incentives.

When companies treat open source as a cost center to be minimized rather than a dependency to be invested in, they're making a rational choice in the short term. But they're also digging their own grave. The security vulnerabilities, the maintenance debt, the technical decayed that no one is addressing—it's all accumulating. And it's going to come due.

The organizations that will thrive in the next decade are the ones that figure out how to make open source investment a strategic priority—not because it's morally right, but because it's existentially necessary.

---

## The AI Question

And then there's AI.

*[Let that sit for a moment.]*

I've been thinking about this a lot, because AI is going to reshape open source in ways we don't fully understand yet. And I think there are two competing narratives that are both wrong.

Narrative one: AI is going to automate away the need for open source. Why rely on a community when you can generate code on demand? Just ask Copilot to write your database driver. Problem solved.

Narrative two: AI makes open source *more* important, because we need the human oversight, the community governance, the ethical frameworks that AI systems can't provide.

The truth, as always, is more complicated. And more interesting.

AI code generation is genuinely useful. I'm not going to stand here and tell you that LLMs aren't helping developers write code faster. They are. I've used them. I have a complicated relationship with that fact, but I can't deny it.

But here's what's happening that nobody's talking about: AI-generated code has an *assumption problem*. It assumes that code exists in a vacuum—that the hard part of software engineering is typing the characters. It's not. The hard part is understanding the domain, the tradeoffs, the edge cases, the *context* that makes code actually work in production.

AI can generate a function that looks right. It cannot generate the institutional knowledge of why that function was written this way instead of that way. It cannot generate the relationships between maintainers who know, "Oh, that change will break this other thing because of the thing that happened in 2019." It cannot generate trust.

And here's the deeper problem: AI models are trained on open source code. A lot of it. And the legal and ethical frameworks for this have not been figured out. We're in a period where the largest companies in the world are building trillion-dollar businesses on the labor of open source communities who never consented to that use.

That is a conversation we need to have. Not as a sidebar. As a central question.

---

## The Path Forward

So what do we do?

I want to propose a vision—not a policy, not a mandate, but a vision—for how open source can thrive in the next decade.

First, we need to treat sustainability as engineering, not charity. This means applying the same rigor we apply to our code to our community structures. What does bus factor look like when we engineer it intentionally? How do we build redundancy into human systems the way we build redundancy into code? This is a design problem, and we should approach it as one.

Second, we need new funding models that don't depend on the kindness of strangers. I'm excited about things like GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective, and the various foundation models—but we need more. We need companies to treat open source sustainability as a line item, not a nice-to-have. The projects that survive won't be the ones with the most passionate maintainers. They'll be the ones with sustainable funding structures.

Third—and this is the hardest one—we need to rebuild the social contract of open source. The idea that code should be free in all senses has been powerful, but it's also allowed companies to extract value while externalizing costs. I'm not proposing we abandon the spirit of open source. I'm proposing we update it for an era where the stakes are higher and the players are more sophisticated.

And finally, we need to embrace AI as a tool while defending what makes open source valuable in the first place. The community. The shared ownership. The human connection that turns code into something more than code.

---

## The Thing That Can't Be Automated

Let me end with this.

A few months ago, I was at a conference—a different one, different city—and I found myself in a hallway conversation with a maintainer of a project I use. We talked about the code, sure. But we also talked about their kids, their job, why they started the project in the first place. There was a moment—maybe it was the third beer, maybe it was just the hour—where they said something that stuck with me.

They said, "You know what nobody talks about? It's not the code. It's the people who show up. It's the person who files the first good bug report. It's the person who writes the documentation when you're exhausted. It's the community that makes you feel like you're not doing this alone."

*[Pause.]*

AI can write code. It can probably write better code than it could a year ago, and it'll be better still a year from now.

But it can't show up at 2 AM when something is on fire. It can't mentor a new contributor who just made their first pull request. It can't look at a stranger on the internet and say, "I see you. I know what you're going through. Let's figure this out together."

That's the thing that can't be automated. That's the thing worth saving.

The future of open source isn't a technology question. It's a human question. And the answer is us.

*[Pause.]*

Thank you.

---

*[End of talk. Approximate runtime: 14-15 minutes.]*

# The Future of Open Source: Sustainability, Community, and the AI Question

## Conference Talk Script

---

*[Pause. Make eye contact with the audience.]*

Last year, I got a message from a developer at a mid-sized company. They'd been using a popular open source library in their production system for three years. It had twelve thousand stars on GitHub. It was maintained by one person—a developer in Germany who had, in their words, "simply stopped responding."

No warning. No handoff. No goodbye. Just silence.

The library wasn't abandoned because it was bad. It was abandoned because its maintainer got burned out, got a new job, had a kid—pick a reason. The reason doesn't matter. What matters is that this company's production system now depended on code that no one was watching anymore.

Now, here's what that looked like in practice. The pagers went off at 3 AM. The CTO was on the call. They traced the stack trace down fifteen layers to a library maintained by someone they'd never met, in a timezone they couldn't pronounce, and realized: no one was coming. No one could come. The only person who understood this code was probably sleeping soundly in Berlin, done with this whole thing.

This is the reality of open source in 2024. We build our entire digital infrastructure on borrowed time and borrowed goodwill.

*[Pause.]*

I'm here to talk about what we do next.

---

## The Sustainability Crisis No One Wants to Name

Let's start with some honesty. Open source has a sustainability problem, and we've been pretending it will solve itself.

I don't mean funding—though that's part of it. I mean *human* sustainability. The fundamental model where a handful of overworked maintainers keep the world's software running is breaking. It's been breaking for years. We just haven't wanted to look at it directly.

Consider the math. The Linux Foundation's latest report shows there are now over 200 million open source repositories on GitHub alone. But the median number of contributors to a repository is—wait for it—one. One person. And for a significant percentage of critical infrastructure, that one person is unpaid, unsupported, and running on passion and caffeine.

The "bus factor" in much of our infrastructure is genuinely one. One person gets hit by a bus, one person burns out, one person decides they need to sleep at night—and suddenly thousands of projects have no maintainer.

I've heard people say, "Well, if it's important, someone will step up." That's not a strategy. That's a prayer.

And here's what keeps me up at night: we're not just talking about hobby projects anymore. We're talking about the actual substrate of modern civilization. Healthcare systems. Financial infrastructure. Transportation. The code that runs our power grids. All of it built on the labor of people who, by any rational measure, should have quit years ago.

The OpenSSF estimates that over 95% of critical open source projects are understaffed. That's not a minority problem. That's an industry-wide crisis wearing a hoodie and pretending everything is fine.

Now, let me tell you about the XZ Utils backdoor. If you don't know it, you should. Earlier this year—or was it last year? Time blurs—a longtime open source maintainer was exhausted. He'd been maintaining this compression library for decades, essentially for free. And a "helpful" stranger stepped in to contribute. The stranger gained his trust. They became a co-maintainer.

That stranger inserted a backdoor into the supply chain that nearly shipped to every Linux system in the world. Think about that. We came within weeks of a compromise that would have affected virtually every SSH server on the planet. Not because of a sophisticated cyberattack. Because a maintainer was tired.

This is what burnout looks like in the age of supply chain security. It's not just that projects die. It's that exhausted maintainers become attack vectors.

There's also what I call the **Entitlement Curve**—the way some users treat maintainers not as volunteers, but as unpaid vendors. I've seen GitHub issues that read like customer service complaints from hell. "Your library broke my production system. Fix it now. I've been waiting four hours." Four hours. For code someone gave you for free.

The emotional toll of this is invisible but devastating. Maintainers aren't just writing code; they're absorbing the stress of thousands of strangers who've built businesses on their labor. That doesn't scale. Nothing human scales to that.

---

## The Corporate Free-Ride

Now, here's where it gets uncomfortable.

A lot of companies—companies making billions of dollars—have built their entire business models on open source code that they have contributed almost nothing back to. They've taken the "move fast and break things" mentality and applied it to their relationship with the community. Use the code. Disrupt the market. Let someone else worry about the maintenance.

This isn't a lecture about corporate responsibility—though we can have that conversation. This is about incentives.

When companies treat open source as a cost center to be minimized rather than a dependency to be invested in, they're making a rational choice in the short term. But they're also digging their own grave. The security vulnerabilities, the maintenance debt, the technical decay that no one is addressing—it's all accumulating. And it's going to come due.

Remember the `colors.js` incident? A maintainer, frustrated with corporate extraction, pushed a malicious update that broke thousands of applications. Was it the right thing to do? Probably not. But it was a symptom of a broken relationship between companies and the communities they depend on.

The organizations that will thrive in the next decade are the ones that figure out how to make open source investment a strategic priority—not because it's morally right, but because it's existentially necessary.

---

## The AI Question

And then there's AI.

*[Let that sit for a moment.]*

I've been thinking about this a lot, because AI is going to reshape open source in ways we don't fully understand yet. And I think there are two competing narratives that are both wrong.

Narrative one: AI is going to automate away the need for open source. Why rely on a community when you can generate code on demand? Just ask Copilot to write your database driver. Problem solved.

Narrative two: AI makes open source *more* important, because we need the human oversight, the community governance, the ethical frameworks that AI systems can't provide.

The truth, as always, is more complicated. And more interesting.

AI code generation is genuinely useful. I'm not going to stand here and tell you that LLMs aren't helping developers write code faster. They are. I've used them. I have a complicated relationship with that fact, but I can't deny it.

But here's what's happening that nobody's talking about: AI-generated code has an *assumption problem*. It assumes that code exists in a vacuum—that the hard part of software engineering is typing the characters. It's not. The hard part is understanding the domain, the tradeoffs, the edge cases, the *context* that makes code actually work in production.

AI can generate a function that looks right. It cannot generate the institutional knowledge of why that function was written this way instead of that way. It cannot generate the relationships between maintainers who know, "Oh, that change will break this other thing because of the thing that happened in 2019." It cannot generate trust.

And here's the deeper problem: AI models are trained on open source code. A lot of it. And the legal and ethical frameworks for this have not been figured out. We're in a period where the largest companies in the world are building trillion-dollar businesses on the labor of open source communities who never consented to that use.

That is a conversation we need to have. Not as a sidebar. As a central question.

But here's what keeps me up at night regarding AI, and it's more immediate: **the noise-to-signal ratio is becoming existential.**

Maintainers are already drowning in low-quality contributions. People using AI to "fix" typos, to refactor code they don't understand, to farm contribution credits for their resumes. I've talked to maintainers who now receive fifty AI-generated pull requests a day. Fifty. For a project maintained by one person in their spare time.

How do you review that? How do you maintain quality when the volume of "contributions" has become noise? AI isn't just writing code—it's generating a firehose of synthetic engagement that threatens to drown the very communities it claims to empower.

And there's the Ouroboros problem—the snake eating its own tail. If open source maintainers quit because they're overwhelmed by AI spam and burnout, AI models will have nothing new to train on. AI *needs* human open source to survive. But right now, it's killing the ecosystem that feeds it.

---

## The Path Forward

So what do we do?

I want to propose a vision—not a policy, not a mandate, but a vision—for how open source can thrive in the next decade.

First, we need to treat sustainability as engineering, not charity. This means applying the same rigor we apply to our code to our community structures. What does bus factor look like when we engineer it intentionally? How do we build redundancy into human systems the way we build redundancy into code? This is a design problem, and we should approach it as one.

And I don't mean this abstractly. I mean: on Monday, I want every Engineering Manager in this room to audit your dependency tree. Find the projects you depend on that have a bus factor of one. Then sponsor three of them. Not with a Slack message. With money. With maintainers. With a commitment that says, "We need you to stay alive, and we're willing to invest in that."

Second, we need new funding models that don't depend on the kindness of strangers. I'm excited about things like GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective, and the various foundation models—but we need more. We need companies to treat open source sustainability as a line item, not a nice-to-have. We need procurement policies that refuse to use software with a bus factor of one. We need sovereign tech funds—like Germany is deploying—to treat open source infrastructure as national security.

The projects that survive won't be the ones with the most passionate maintainers. They'll be the ones with sustainable funding structures.

Third—and this is the hardest one—we need to rebuild the social contract of open source. The idea that code should be free in all senses has been powerful, but it's also allowed companies to extract value while externalizing costs. I'm not proposing we abandon the spirit of open source. I'm proposing we update it for an era where the stakes are higher and the players are more sophisticated.

And finally, we need to embrace AI as a tool while defending what makes open source valuable in the first place. The community. The shared ownership. The human connection that turns code into something more than code.

---

## The Thing That Can't Be Automated

Let me end with this.

A few months ago, I was at a conference—a different one, different city—and I found myself in a hallway conversation with a maintainer of a project I use. We talked about the code, sure. But we also talked about their kids, their job, why they started the project in the first place. There was a moment—maybe it was the third beer, maybe it was just the hour—where they said something that stuck with me.

They said, "You know what nobody talks about? It's not the code. It's the people who show up. It's the person who files the first good bug report. It's the person who writes the documentation when you're exhausted. It's the community that makes you feel like you're not doing this alone."

*[Pause.]*

AI can write code. It can probably write better code than it could a year ago, and it'll be better still a year from now.

But it can't show up at 2 AM when something is on fire. It can't mentor a new contributor who just made their first pull request. It can't look at a stranger on the internet and say, "I see you. I know what you're going through. Let's figure this out together."

That's the thing that can't be automated. That's the thing worth saving.

The future of open source isn't a technology question. It's a human question.

And the answer is us.

*[Pause.]*

Thank you.

---

*[End of talk. Approximate runtime: 15 minutes.]*

And here's what keeps me up at night: we're not just talking about hobby projects anymore. We're talking about the actual substrate of modern civilization. Healthcare systems. Financial infrastructure. Transportation. The code that runs our power grids. All of it built on the labor of people who, by any rational measure, should have quit years ago.

The OpenSSF estimates that over 95% of critical open source projects are understaffed. That's not a minority problem. That's an industry-wide crisis wearing a hoodie and pretending everything is fine.

Now, here's where I want to add some texture to this conversation. Not all sustainability models are created equal. We've seen the "Hero Maintainer" model fail—brilliant individuals carrying entire ecosystems on their backs until they can't anymore. But we've also seen alternatives work.

Look at the Apache Software Foundation, or the Linux Foundation, or the Python Software Foundation. These aren't perfect—nothing is—but they provide something that individual maintainers can't: institutional continuity. When a project is under a foundation, it survives personnel changes. It has legal standing. It has funding mechanisms. The bus factor becomes, well, a *factor* rather than a catastrophe.

Contrast that with the project that was acquired by a corporation, only to be "sunsetted" when the company's priorities shifted. Or the project whose maintainer went silent after a burnout episode. The foundation model isn't the only answer, but it's a proven one.

And here's the deeper point: we need to stop treating sustainability as an afterthought and start treating it as a *design problem*. What does bus factor look like when we engineer it intentionally? How do we build redundancy into human systems the way we build redundancy into code? This is a design problem, and we should approach it as one.

---

## The Corporate Free-Ride

Now, here's where it gets uncomfortable.

A lot of companies—companies making billions of dollars—have built their entire business models on open source code that they have contributed almost nothing back to. They've taken the "move fast and break things" mentality and applied it to their relationship with the community. Use the code. Disrupt the market. Let someone else worry about the maintenance.

This isn't a lecture about corporate responsibility—though we can have that conversation. This is about incentives.

When companies treat open source as a cost center to be minimized rather than a dependency to be invested in, they're making a rational choice in the short term. But they're also digging their own grave. The security vulnerabilities, the maintenance debt, the technical decay that no one is addressing—it's all accumulating. And it's going to come due.

Let me give you a concrete example. Remember Log4Shell? The vulnerability that sent every security team in the world into a tailspin? That was a critical piece of infrastructure maintained by volunteers. The maintainers weren't negligent—they were overwhelmed. They were managing a project used by millions of systems with the resources of a small team and the gratitude of absolutely no one who was paying them.

The organizations that will thrive in the next decade are the ones that figure out how to make open source investment a strategic priority—not because it's morally right, but because it's existentially necessary.

And I know what some of you are thinking. You're thinking, "We can't possibly pay for every library we use. There are hundreds of them." And you're right. That's not what I'm suggesting.

Here's a concrete proposal: the 20% Rule. Companies should mandate that 20% of engineering time be spent maintaining the dependencies they use. Not just reporting bugs—actually contributing back. Documentation. Testing. Security audits. Code contributions. This isn't charity. This is operational insurance. The more you invest in the infrastructure you depend on, the more reliable your systems become.

You can argue about the percentage. But the principle is sound: if you're using it, you're responsible for it. That's what it means to be a good citizen of the ecosystem.

---

## The AI Question

And then there's AI.

*[Let that sit for a moment.]*

I've been thinking about this a lot, because AI is going to reshape open source in ways we don't fully understand yet. And I think there are two competing narratives that are both wrong.

Narrative one: AI is going to automate away the need for open source. Why rely on a community when you can generate code on demand? Just ask Copilot to write your database driver. Problem solved.

Narrative two: AI makes open source *more* important, because we need the human oversight, the community governance, the ethical frameworks that AI systems can't provide.

The truth, as always, is more complicated. And more interesting.

AI code generation is genuinely useful. I'm not going to stand here and tell you that LLMs aren't helping developers write code faster. They are. I've used them. I have a complicated relationship with that fact, but I can't deny it.

But here's what's happening that nobody's talking about: AI-generated code has an *assumption problem*. It assumes that code exists in a vacuum—that the hard part of software engineering is typing the characters. It's not. The hard part is understanding the domain, the tradeoffs, the edge cases, the *context* that makes code actually work in production.

Let me give you an example. I once watched an AI generate a currency conversion function. It was syntactically perfect. It handled all the standard cases. It even had tests.

What it didn't handle was a specific country's tax laws that required a particular rounding behavior that only existed because of a historical regulation from 1987 that was documented nowhere in the code, only in the institutional knowledge of the team that had been maintaining it for fifteen years.

AI can generate a function that looks right. It cannot generate the institutional knowledge of why that function was written this way instead of that way. It cannot generate the relationships between maintainers who know, "Oh, that change will break this other thing because of the thing that happened in 2019." It cannot generate trust.

And here's the deeper problem that keeps me up at night: AI models are trained on open source code. A lot of it. And the legal and ethical frameworks for this have not been figured out. We're in a period where the largest companies in the world are building trillion-dollar businesses on the labor of open source communities who never consented to that use.

That is a conversation we need to have. Not as a sidebar. As a central question.

There's another issue I want to raise, and it's more technical. What happens when AI-generated code starts flooding open source repositories? What happens when maintainers are overwhelmed with AI-generated pull requests that look correct but contain subtle bugs, hallucinated dependencies, or security vulnerabilities that slip through?

I've seen this start to happen. Maintainers already struggle to keep up with human contributions. Add AI to the mix, and the signal-to-noise ratio becomes a nightmare. This is the "hallucinated maintenance" problem—AI generating the *appearance* of maintenance without the substance. And it's a threat we need to start thinking about seriously.

---

## The Path Forward

So what do we do?

I want to propose a vision—not a policy, not a mandate, but a vision—for how open source can thrive in the next decade.

First, we need to treat sustainability as engineering, not charity. This means applying the same rigor we apply to our code to our community structures. What does bus factor look like when we engineer it intentionally? How do we build redundancy into human systems the way we build redundancy into code? This is a design problem, and we should approach it as one.

Second, we need new funding models that don't depend on the kindness of strangers. I'm excited about things like GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective, and the various foundation models—but we need more. We need companies to treat open source sustainability as a line item, not a nice-to-have. The projects that survive won't be the ones with the most passionate maintainers. They'll be the ones with sustainable funding structures.

Third—and this is the hardest one—we need to rebuild the social contract of open source. The idea that code should be free in all senses has been powerful, but it's also allowed companies to extract value while externalizing costs. I'm not proposing we abandon the spirit of open source. I'm proposing we update it for an era where the stakes are higher and the players are more sophisticated.

Fourth—and this is where I want to challenge the room—we need to hold AI companies accountable for what they're building on. The training data question isn't abstract. It's a labor question. It's a consent question. And it's one we're going to have to answer.

And finally, we need to embrace AI as a tool while defending what makes open source valuable in the first place. The community. The shared ownership. The human connection that turns code into something more than code.

---

## The Thing That Can't Be Automated

Let me end with this.

A few months ago, I was at a conference—a different one, different city—and I found myself in a hallway conversation with a maintainer of a project I use. We talked about the code, sure. But we also talked about their kids, their job, why they started the project in the first place.

I remember the way the light caught their face when they talked about the first person who ever filed a bug report. Not a complaint—a genuine, thoughtful bug report that made them feel like someone else actually *cared* about what they had built. That was the moment, they told me, that they knew this mattered to someone beyond themselves.

There was a moment—maybe it was the third beer, maybe it was just the hour—where they said something that stuck with me.

They said, "You know what nobody talks about? It's not the code. It's the people who show up. It's the person who files the first good bug report. It's the person who writes the documentation when you're exhausted. It's the community that makes you feel like you're not doing this alone."

I think about that a lot. About what it means to show up for each other. About what it means to build something together.

*[Pause.]*

AI can write code. It can probably write better code than it could a year ago, and it'll be better still a year from now.

But it can't show up at 2 AM when something is on fire. It can't mentor a new contributor who just made their first pull request and is terrified they're going to embarrass themselves. It can't look at a stranger on the internet and say, "I see you. I know what you're going through. Let's figure this out together."

That's the thing that can't be automated. That's the thing worth saving.

The future of open source isn't a technology question. It's a human question. And the answer is us.

*[Pause.]*

Thank you.

---

That package handles encryption for 40% of the Fortune 500's customer data.

*[Pause.]*

He's not irresponsible. He's just tired. And we never noticed because we were too busy building features on top of his free labor.

This is the reality of open source in 2024. We've built civilization on a volunteer's weekend project.

I'm here to talk about what we do next.

---

## The Sustainability Crisis No One Wants to Name

Let's start with some honesty. Open source has a sustainability problem, and we've been pretending it will solve itself.

I don't mean funding—though that's part of it. I mean *human* sustainability. The fundamental model where a handful of overworked maintainers keep the world's software running is breaking. It's been breaking for years. We just haven't wanted to look at it directly.

Consider the math. The Linux Foundation's latest report shows there are now over 200 million open source repositories on GitHub alone. But the median number of contributors to a repository is—wait for it—one. One person. And for a significant percentage of critical infrastructure, that one person is unpaid, unsupported, and running on passion and caffeine.

The "bus factor" in much of our infrastructure is genuinely one. One person gets hit by a bus, one person burns out, one person decides they need to sleep at night—and suddenly thousands of projects have no maintainer. That's not a metaphor. It's a business continuity plan that doesn't exist.

And here's what keeps me up at night: we're not just talking about hobby projects anymore. We're talking about the actual substrate of modern civilization. Healthcare systems. Financial infrastructure. Transportation. The code that runs our power grids. All of it built on the labor of people who, by any rational measure, should have quit years ago.

The OpenSSF estimates that over 95% of critical open source projects are understaffed. That's not a minority problem. That's an industry-wide crisis wearing a hoodie and pretending everything is fine.

Let me give you a concrete example. Remember left-pad? In 2016, a single maintainer unpublished their npm package—two lines of code that padded strings. Two point five million builds broke in eleven minutes. Airbnb, Netflix, Spotify—everything just stopped working. That's what technical debt becomes when it becomes a technical default.

Or Heartbleed. A single volunteer maintainer introduced a vulnerability that exposed the private keys of half the internet. Or Log4Shell—that one hurt for months. The pattern is always the same: a small number of exhausted humans, responsible for infrastructure that affects billions, with no redundancy, no backup, no safety net.

---

## The Corporate Free-Ride

Now, here's where it gets uncomfortable.

A lot of companies—companies making billions of dollars—have built their entire business models on open source code that they have contributed almost nothing back to. They've taken the "move fast and break things" mentality and applied it to their relationship with the community. Use the code. Disrupt the market. Let someone else worry about the maintenance.

This isn't a lecture about corporate responsibility—though we can have that conversation. This is about incentives.

When companies treat open source as a cost center to be minimized rather than a dependency to be invested in, they're making a rational choice in the short term. But they're also digging their own grave. The security vulnerabilities, the maintenance debt, the technical decay that no one is addressing—it's all accumulating. And it's going to come due.

The organizations that will thrive in the next decade are the ones that figure out how to make open source investment a strategic priority—not because it's morally right, but because it's existentially necessary.

Foundations like Apache, Eclipse, and CNCF have shown us something important: collective governance works. When projects move under foundation umbrellas, they gain institutional longevity. They get legal protection. They develop proper security processes. That's not the only answer, but it's part of one.

---

## The AI Question

And then there's AI.

*[Let that sit for a moment.]*

I've been thinking about this a lot, because AI is going to reshape open source in ways we don't fully understand yet. And I think there are two competing narratives that are both wrong.

Narrative one: AI is going to automate away the need for open source. Why rely on a community when you can generate code on demand? Just ask Copilot to write your database driver. Problem solved.

Narrative two: AI makes open source *more* important, because we need the human oversight, the community governance, the ethical frameworks that AI systems can't provide.

The truth, as always, is more complicated. And more interesting.

AI code generation is genuinely useful. I'm not going to stand here and tell you that LLMs aren't helping developers write code faster. They are. I've used them. I have a complicated relationship with that fact, but I can't deny it.

But here's what's happening that nobody's talking about: AI-generated code has an *assumption problem*. It assumes that code exists in a vacuum—that the hard part of software engineering is typing the characters. It's not. The hard part is understanding the domain, the tradeoffs, the edge cases, the *context* that makes code actually work in production.

AI can generate a function that looks right. It cannot generate the institutional knowledge of why that function was written this way instead of that way. It cannot generate the relationships between maintainers who know, "Oh, that change will break this other thing because of the thing that happened in 2019." It cannot generate trust.

AI knows the syntax but not the scars.

And here's the deeper problem—and this is where it gets legally and ethically messy. AI models are trained on open source code. A lot of it. Massive amounts. And the legal and ethical frameworks for this have not been figured out. We're in a period where the largest companies in the world are building trillion-dollar businesses on the labor of open source communities who never consented to that use.

There are lawsuits right now. There are licensing debates that are getting heated. There are new licenses being proposed—Anti-AI licenses, RAIL licenses, various forms of "no training on this code" restrictions. Some of them are effective. Many of them are toothless. The legal landscape is a mess, and it's going to get messier before it gets clearer.

But here's the thing nobody's talking about. AI isn't just changing how we write code—it's changing how we *maintain* it. Last month, a maintainer I know received forty-seven AI-generated PRs in one weekend. All of them passed the tests. None of them fixed the actual problem.

On the other hand—AI can help. Automated testing, documentation generation, issue triage. There are maintainers using AI right now to do their jobs better. Not to replace the community, but to amplify it. That's the version of AI I want to see. Not the version that automates us out of the equation, but the version that handles the busywork so we can handle the human work.

---

What does bus factor look like when we engineer it intentionally? How do we build redundancy into human systems the way we build redundancy into code? This is a design problem, and we should approach it as one.

This is your sustainability checklist: automated testing, contributor onboarding docs, governance models, funding diversification. If your project doesn't have these, you're one burned-out maintainer away from crisis.

Second, we need new funding models that don't depend on the kindness of strangers. I'm excited about things like GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective, and the various foundation models—but we need more. We need companies to treat open source sustainability as a line item, not a nice-to-have. Sustainability isn't charity—it's infrastructure insurance. The projects that survive won't be the ones with the most passionate maintainers. They'll be the ones with sustainable funding structures.

Third—and this is the hardest one—we need to rebuild the social contract of open source. The idea that code should be free in all senses has been powerful, but it's also allowed companies to extract value while externalizing costs. I'm not proposing we abandon the spirit of open source. I'm proposing we update it for an era where the stakes are higher and the players are more sophisticated.

And finally, we need to embrace AI as a tool while defending what makes open source valuable in the first place. The community. The shared ownership. The human connection that turns code into something more than code.

---

## Choose Your Own Adventure

Now here's where I get practical. Different people in this room have different jobs, different leverage, different responsibilities. So let me speak to each of you.

If you're an individual developer: Start measuring your dependencies' health. Create a DEPENDENCY_HEALTH.md in your repos. Track: last commit, maintainer responsiveness, funding status, bus factor. I'm serious. Do it this week.

If you're a startup CTO: Budget 5% of engineering time for upstream contributions. Not charity—insurance. Calculate your "open source exposure"—what percentage of your codebase you don't control. Then act accordingly.

If you're an enterprise architect: Push for Open Source Program Offices. Join foundations. Treat open source like any other vendor relationship—except this vendor is also your business partner and your competitor.

---

## The Thing That Can't Be Automated

Let me end with this.

A few months ago, I was at a conference—a different one, different city—and I found myself in a hallway conversation with a maintainer of a project I use. We talked about the code, sure. But we also talked about their kids, their job, why they started the project in the first place. There was a moment—maybe it was the third beer, maybe it was just the hour—where they said something that stuck with me.

They said, "You know what nobody talks about? It's not the code. It's the people who show up. It's the person who files the first good bug report. It's the person who writes the documentation when you're exhausted. It's the community that makes you feel like you're not doing this alone."

*[Pause.]*

AI can write code. It can probably write better code than it could a year ago, and it'll be better still a year from now.

But it can't show up at 2 AM when something is on fire. It can't mentor a new contributor who just made their first pull request. It can't look at a stranger on the internet and say, "I see you. I know what you're going through. Let's figure this out together."

That's the thing that can't be automated. That's the thing worth saving.

The future of open source isn't written in code. It's written in the 2 AM Slack messages between strangers who've become teammates. In the PR review that teaches more than it criticizes. In the moment when someone says, "I've got this—go sleep."

AI can write our functions. But it can't write our future. That requires humans who show up, not just code that compiles.

The next decade of open source depends on what it always has: not better technology, but better humans.

We're not just maintaining code. We're maintaining the infrastructure of human connection that makes all of this possible.

Don't just contribute code. Contribute to the thing that makes the code matter.

Show up. The future is being maintained by whoever shows up.

Thank you.

---

*[End of talk. Approximate runtime: 14-15 minutes.]*

*Emotional sustainability* means the maintainer can take a vacation without checking GitHub every thirty minutes. It means not treating burnout as a badge of honor.

*Technical sustainability* means the codebase can evolve without a complete rewrite. It means not accumulating so much technical debt that future maintainers just walk away.

*Governance sustainability* means decisions don't bottleneck on one person. It means knowing who can merge a PR at 3 AM when a vulnerability drops.

Most projects fail on just one of these. But we pretend they're all the same problem.

*[Pause.]*

I want you to go back to your teams and audit your dependencies. If a project has fewer than three maintainers and no funding model, flag it. That's not a code smell. That's organizational risk. Your dependency tree is a social graph, and right now it's a pyramid scheme.

---

## The Corporate Free-Ride

Now, here's where it gets uncomfortable.

*[Look around. Pause.]*

How many of you work at companies that use open source?

*[Pause. Gesture to keep hands up.]*

Now keep your hand up if your company pays a full-time maintainer of a project you don't own.

*[Pause. Let the visual land.]*

That's what I thought.

A lot of companies—companies making billions of dollars—have built their entire business models on open source code that they have contributed almost nothing back to. They've taken the "move fast and break things" mentality and applied it to their relationship with the community. Use the code. Disrupt the market. Let someone else worry about the maintenance.

We've confused "free as in speech" with "free as in unpaid labor."

This isn't a lecture about corporate responsibility—though we can have that conversation. This is about incentives.

When companies treat open source as a cost center to be minimized rather than a dependency to be invested in, they're making a rational choice in the short term. But they're also writing their own technical debt. The security vulnerabilities, the maintenance debt, the technical decay that no one is addressing—it's all accumulating. And it's going to come due.

The organizations that will thrive in the next decade are the ones that figure out how to make open source investment a strategic priority—not because it's morally right, but because it's existentially necessary.

---

## The AI Question

And then there's AI.

*[Let that sit for a moment.]*

I've been thinking about this a lot, because AI is going to reshape open source in ways we don't fully understand yet. And I think there are three tensions we need to navigate—not two narratives that are both wrong.

*Tension one: automation vs. oversight.* AI code generation is genuinely useful. I'm not going to stand here and tell you that LLMs aren't helping developers write code faster. They are. I've used them. I have a complicated relationship with that fact, but I can't deny it.

But here's what's happening that nobody's talking about: AI-generated code has an *assumption problem*. It assumes that code exists in a vacuum—that the hard part of software engineering is typing the characters. It's not. The hard part is understanding the domain, the tradeoffs, the edge cases, the *context* that makes code actually work in production.

AI can write code. It cannot write a community charter.

*Tension two: abundance vs. fragility.* Last month, a maintainer I know used AI to auto-respond to 200 duplicate issues in a weekend—work that would have burned them out. But the AI also suggested a "fix" that would have introduced a subtle security vulnerability. The community caught it. That's the pattern: AI handles the scale, humans handle the stakes.

*Tension three: consent vs. extraction.* AI models are trained on open source code. A lot of it. And the legal and ethical frameworks for this have not been figured out. We're in a period where the largest companies in the world are building trillion-dollar businesses on the labor of open source communities who never consented to that use.

And right now, we're seeing the first wave of responses. The Anti-Capitalist Software License. Projects adding "no AI training" clauses. Creative Commons debating new variants. This is happening *right now*, and it's going to reshape what "open" means.

That is a conversation we need to have. Not as a sidebar. As a central question.

---

## Open Source 2.0: The Path Forward

So what do we do?

I want to propose a vision—not a policy, not a mandate, but a vision—for how open source can thrive in the next decade. Call it Open Source 2.0.

First, we need to treat sustainability as engineering, not charity. This means applying the same rigor we apply to our code to our community structures. What does bus factor look like when we engineer it intentionally? How do we build redundancy into human systems the way we build redundancy into code? This is a design problem, and we should approach it as one.

Second, we need new funding models that don't depend on the kindness of strangers. I'm excited about things like GitHub Sponsors, Open Collective, and the various foundation models—but we need more. We need companies to treat open source sustainability as a line item, not a nice-to-have. The projects that survive won't be the ones with the most passionate maintainers. They'll be the ones with sustainable funding structures.

Third—and this is the hardest one—we need to rebuild the social contract of open source. The idea that code should be free in all senses has been powerful, but it's also allowed companies to extract value while externalizing costs.

This means every Fortune 500 company using open source should have a published policy on upstream contributions. It means maintainers should have the right to be paid for their time without being called "sellouts." It means we stop treating burnout as a badge of honor.

We need a Maintainer's Bill of Rights. Not because it's politically correct, but because it's the only way the lights stay on.

And finally, we need to embrace AI as a tool while defending what makes open source valuable in the first place. The community. The shared ownership. The human connection that turns code into something more than code.

*[Pause.]*

Imagine it's 2029. A critical vulnerability drops in a library used by half the Fortune 500. Instead of one maintainer waking up to three thousand panicked issues, a funded security team at five major companies coordinates a response through a shared governance board. The fix ships in six hours. Contributors from around the world collaborate in real-time, not because they're on call, but because they *want* to—because the project has invested in them as much as they've invested in the code.

That's what thriving looks like.

---

## The Thing That Can't Be Automated

Let me end with this.

A few months ago, I was at a conference—a different one, different city—and I found myself in a hallway conversation with a maintainer of a project I use. We talked about the code, sure. But we also talked about their kids, their job, why they started the project in the first place. There was a moment—maybe it was the third beer, maybe it was just the hour—where they said something that stuck with me.

They said, "You know what nobody talks about? It's not the code. It's the people who show up. It's the person who files the first good bug report. It's the person who writes the documentation when you're exhausted. It's the community that makes you feel like you're not doing this alone."

*[Pause.]*

The best code review isn't catching a bug. It's telling a new contributor: *You belong here.*

AI can write code. It can probably write better code than it could a year ago, and it'll be better still a year from now.

But it can't show up at 2 AM when something is on fire. It can't mentor a new contributor who just made their first pull request. It can't look at a stranger on the internet and say, "I see you. I know what you're going through. Let's figure this out together."

That's the thing that can't be automated. That's the thing worth saving.

The future of open source isn't a technology question. It's a human question. And the answer is us.

*[Pause.]*

Thank you.

---

*[End of talk. Approximate runtime: 14-15 minutes.]*

---

*[Pause. Make eye contact with the audience.]*

It was maintained by one person—a developer in Germany who had, in their words, "simply stopped responding."

No warning. No handoff. No goodbye. Just silence.

The library wasn't abandoned because it was bad. It was abandoned because its maintainer got burned out, got a new job, had a kid—pick a reason. The reason doesn't matter. What matters is that this company's production system now depended on code that no one was watching anymore.

It's the slow accumulation of 47 open issues, 12 of which are effectively tech support requests from people treating you like an unpaid contractor. It's the 3 AM notification from a Fortune 500 company whose production is down, written in a tone that suggests you owe them something. Narrative two: AI makes open source *more* important, because we need the human oversight, the community governance, the ethical frameworks that AI systems can't provide.

---

Second, we need funding models that don't depend on the kindness of strangers—and that go beyond individual sponsorships. Third, we need to rebuild the social contract of open source. The old model—use the code for free, contribute when you have time—worked when the stakes were lower. Now the stakes are everything. Not "good first issues," but senior engineers doing the unglamorous work of release management and security patches. We need to normalize "corporate maintainership" as a standard cost of doing business.

And finally, we need to embrace AI as a tool while defending what makes open source valuable in the first place. The community. The shared ownership. The human connection that turns code into something more than code.

---

## The Thing That Can't Be Automated

Let me end with this.

A few months ago, I was at a conference—a different one, different city—and I found myself in a hallway conversation with a maintainer of a project I use. We talked about the code, sure. But we also talked about their kids, their job, why they started the project in the first place. There was a moment—maybe it was the third beer, maybe it was just the hour—where they said something that stuck with me.

They said, "You know what nobody talks about? It's not the code. It's the people who show up. It's the person who files the first good bug report. It's the person who writes the documentation when you're exhausted. It's the community that makes you feel like you're not doing this alone."

*[Pause.]*

AI can write code. It can probably write better code than it could a year ago, and it'll be better still a year from now.

But it can't show up at 2 AM when something is on fire. It can't mentor a new contributor who just made their first pull request. It can't look at a stranger on the internet and say, "I see you. I know what you're going through. Let's figure this out together."

That's the thing that can't be automated. That's the thing worth saving.

The future of open source isn't in the models we train. It's in the relationships we maintain. And maintenance, unlike code, cannot be generated. It can only be given.

*[Pause.]*

Thank you.

---
